Pain was measured with the same instrument at the same time points in both groups, and the analysis uses the same mixed-effects model. Nothing suggests that the method or threshold differed between arms.

The comparator was an open-label placebo with education about placebo effects, and the PRT arm received an active, 8-session therapy that explicitly aims to change how participants interpret pain. Participants' beliefs about benefit could therefore plausibly differ between arms and influence the self-rated pain scores that drive the effect estimate. The size and direction of any such expectation effect are not measured in the sources.
Pain intensity is a participant-reported outcome. Participants who knew their group could rate their pain differently because of their expectations, so influence on assessment is possible.

The outcome is the pre-specified Brief Pain Inventory average pain over the last week on a 0-10 numerical rating scale, the same measure as the primary outcome in the Methods. No inspected passage describes the instrument as inappropriate or insensitive to the expected effect; the 0-10 scale is also fine enough to detect the reported between-group differences.

The reported estimate comes from the ITT mixed-effects model with age and sex covariates and a random participant intercept (eh_2da742228211cf8e). This matches the primary ITT analysis planned in the protocol (protocol p.8, lines 32-35 and 43-46). The protocol also planned a per-protocol secondary analysis, but a lexical search found no per-protocol result in the main article, and none in supplement 2. There is no evidence that a per-protocol analysis was run and withheld, or that the reported ITT analysis was chosen for its results.

Table 2 reports all six pain intensity time points for PRT vs placebo: posttreatment, 1, 2, 3, 6 and 12 months, each with a Hedges g. So no eligible pain measurement is omitted. The approved 12-month estimate (g -0.70) is smaller than the 1-month (-0.83) and posttreatment (-1.14) estimates, so choosing it does not favour the most favourable effect, and nothing in the Sources indicates selection on results.

The registry record (first submitted 2017-09-13, start 2017-08-07 actual) lists one primary outcome: BPI-SF pain at about 1 month post-randomization only, with no 12-month time frame. Protocol v4.4 (dated September 5, 2018) names the post-treatment MRI endpoint, about 5 weeks after randomization, as primary, and says 1-year follow-up 'may be included in the main analysis or presented in a separate manuscript'. The report's Methods also define the primary outcome as the 1-month posttreatment score, yet the approved Result is the 12-month PRT vs placebo estimate (g -0.70). The report gives no result-independent reason for that departure. Both the registry and the protocol postdate the start of enrolment, so neither can show that the 12-month analysis was fixed before unblinded data were available.

Table 2 (p. 5, lines 87-115) reports baseline characteristics for 12 placebo and 13 zonisamide patients. Age (61.5 vs 55.9, P = 0.18), BMI (31.7 vs 36.8, P = 0.20), baseline VAS (63.9 vs 58.9, P = 0.31), baseline Likert (6.63 vs 6.45, P = 0.60) and sex (P = 0.38 to 1.0) show no significant imbalance, and the text states the demographics and pain features were similar (p. 5, lines 76-79). The 13 vs 12 group sizes match the 1:1 block design. Nothing suggests a randomization failure.

The report says the placebo capsule contained lactulose and the zonisamide capsule was 'double-encapsulated so as to appear identical to the placebo' (p. 4, lines 25-29). This shows the drug was masked but does not describe how assignments were made or delivered: no central or remote allocation, no sequentially numbered or sealed containers, and no statement on who held the sequence or who enrolled participants. Identical masking alone does not establish concealment before assignment, and nothing supports a probable answer.

The report states the trial was randomized and that patients were 'randomized in blocks of 6' (p. 4, lines 7-8), but does not say that the order of allocations within blocks was random, nor name any generation method (computer, table, coin, etc.). Per guidance section 4.3.1.1, blocked allocation without an explicit random within-block order should be answered 'No information'. The circumstances (single-centre pilot, no protocol or SAP captured) give no basis for a probable answer.

The reported analysis population, ITT-E, is defined as patients 'who received study drug and had at least one post-treatment efficacy evaluation' (page 4). Figure 1 shows 13 randomized to zonisamide, 12 receiving at least one dose, and 11 included in the efficacy measure; the placebo arm shows 12 randomized, 12 dosed and 12 included (page 6). Excluding a randomized zonisamide participant who never received study drug is an exclusion based on intervention received, which section 5.3.1 treats as inappropriate. The report does not give the reason, so the exclusion may instead reflect missing outcome data, which would make it an acceptable modified ITT. The exclusion is also confined to one arm.

The report states that patients were assigned 'in a double-blind fashion' (page 4) and that zonisamide was double-encapsulated 'so as to appear identical to the placebo' (page 4), so the capsules were matched. Nothing reports that participants guessed or were told their allocation. Zonisamide-specific adverse events (dizziness, jitteriness, restlessness/insomnia, balance problems; page 7) could allow some participants to infer allocation, but the report does not say participants recognised them as drug-specific.

The report describes double-blind assignment and identically appearing capsules (page 4), which supports blinding of those administering the drug. The report does not say explicitly which personnel were masked, and allocation concealment is not established, so the answer rests on the identical-capsule description.

The ITT-E analysis excludes two of 13 randomized zonisamide participants and none in placebo (page 6 flow chart), about 15% of that arm and 8% of all randomized participants. With only 3 responders in the zonisamide group and 0 in placebo, and P = 0.09 (page 6), one participant can change the responder proportion materially: 3 of 11 becomes 3 of 12 (25%) or 4 of 12 (33%) depending on that participant's outcome. Given the small counts and the borderline P value, the exclusion has potential for a substantial impact on the result, though the direction is unknown.

The reported ITT-E responder analysis includes 11 of 13 randomized zonisamide participants and 12 of 12 placebo participants (page 6 flow chart; page 4 ITT-E definition). Two zonisamide participants (about 15% of that arm, 8% overall) are missing from the analysis: one never received study drug and one withdrew without a post-treatment efficacy evaluation. With only 3 responders in the zonisamide arm, two missing participants are not small enough that their outcomes could make no important difference, so 'nearly all' is not met.

The report gives no sensitivity analysis of the responder outcome under plausible values for the missing participants. The main efficacy analysis uses last-observation-carried-forward imputation (page 4), which section 6.1.6 and Box 8 state should not be assumed to correct for bias. The observed-data responder analysis (3 of 7 versus 0 of 11; page 6) restricts to maintenance participants and does not model the missing participants' outcomes, so it is not evidence against bias from missingness.

Withdrawal proportions differ sharply between groups (8 of 13 zonisamide versus 1 of 12 placebo; page 6 flow chart). Reported reasons also differ by group: drug-related adverse events account for the zonisamide withdrawals (drug rash, headache, jitteriness and metallic taste, irritability and insomnia; page 7), whereas the single placebo withdrawal was for protocol violation (page 6). Under section 6.1.4.2, reasons related to adverse experiences of one intervention and differing between groups are the pattern most likely to bias the result, and the proportion missing differs between groups. This meets the reasons for answering Yes.

Withdrawal was common in the zonisamide arm (8 of 13 withdrawn; 5 completed) and rare in placebo (1 of 12 withdrawn, for protocol violation; page 6 flow chart). Among zonisamide withdrawals, the report attributes four to probably drug-related adverse events, including drug rash, headache, jitteriness and irritability/insomnia (page 7). Withdrawal for adverse effects of the drug is plausibly related to the participant's health status and therefore to the responder outcome, so missingness could depend on the true value.

The outcome is participant-reported: the participant is the assessor, and the sources describe the trial as double-blind with a matching placebo capsule that was identical in appearance (eh_b7c017390e6833dc, p4). The sources report no unblinding of the participants or of the outcome recording. However, adverse effects that occurred only in the zonisamide arm (dizziness, jitteriness, restlessness/insomnia, balance/equilibrium; eh_f599b2e857a22227, p7) could have revealed assignment to participants. The sources do not report any formal assessment of blinding success or treatment guesses, so awareness is probably not present but is not fully excluded. The overlap with Domain 2 is recorded there and is not counted again as a separate mechanism here.

Both groups completed the same daily pain diary (VAS and Likert, eh_b7c017390e6833dc, p4) with the same weekly averaging and the same 50% responder threshold (eh_975c987146505a4f and eh_b343e6e8359527e6, p5). Participants were recording their own pain under the same instruments on the same schedule, so the sources describe no difference in measurement method, threshold or timing between the zonisamide and placebo groups. The responder endpoint was analysed as a comparison of responder proportions across groups with the same definition (eh_b343e6e8359527e6, p5).

The responder outcome is a pain-intensity response: at least 50% reduction from baseline in daily pain ratings, averaged from the VAS (0-100) and the Likert (0-10) diary scores (eh_b7c017390e6833dc, p4). The responder threshold of at least 50% reduction in pain score is described as an alternative response definition used in other pain studies (eh_975c987146505a4f, p5). Daily diary pain ratings are a sensitive and standard way to capture the pain-reduction effect this outcome targets, and the report states that VAS and Likert yield identical responder results (eh_f599b2e857a22227, p7). Nothing in the sources indicates the instrument was inappropriate for measuring pain response. The question does not assess whether a post hoc responder endpoint is a sensible choice of outcome, which is addressed in Domain 5.

The responder result is reported under two analysis approaches: an intent-to-treat analysis with imputation and an observed-data analysis of patients with at least one week of maintenance data (eh_f599b2e857a22227, p7, Figure 3 legend). Both are presented in the report, with ITT P = 0.09 and observed-data P = 0.04. The assessed result, ITT-E 3 of 11 vs 0 of 12 (P = 0.09), is the less favourable of the two, which argues against selection of the most favourable analysis. The report states that several alternative analyses were run (eh_975c987146505a4f, p5), and their existence is not disputed, but the sources report the responder analyses that were run without omission of a responder analysis of the same definition. Whether other adjusted or differently defined responder analyses exist is not established.

Within the requested definition (at least 50% reduction in pain from baseline to the final week), the report gives one responder definition with one time window. Both VAS and Likert daily scores are stated to yield identical responder results (eh_f599b2e857a22227, p7, Figure 3 legend), so the scale choice does not create alternative responder results. The responder result is reported for the ITT-E population and for the observed maintenance population (eh_e45ccd0123b38935, p6; eh_f599b2e857a22227, p7), and both are presented rather than only the favourable one. Other pain measures (the continuous change from baseline and weekly means) are in the same domain, but they are a different outcome from the requested responder analysis, so they are not treated as eligible alternatives here.

The authors describe the ≥50% responder analysis as post hoc: "A post hoc analysis was also performed using a ≥50% reduction in pain score as the cutoff for response" (eh_975c987146505a4f, p5). The primary efficacy measure is a different analysis, the baseline-to-maintenance change with LOCF for ITT-E, and the responder analysis is reported separately (eh_b7c017390e6833dc, p4; eh_e45ccd0123b38935, p6). A responder analysis described by the authors as post hoc was therefore not part of the analysis plan they specified, and the report does not present it as one. No dated protocol, SAP or registry entry specifying this responder analysis is among the captured Sources, so whether a pre-specified plan existed cannot be confirmed. The tentative framing of the pilot (eh_e45ccd0123b38935, p6) is consistent with a result that was not pre-specified.

Age, sex, pain intensity and duration, cause of pain, area of pain and concomitant analgesics did not differ between groups (Table 1, p5 l54-57). Groups were 34 and 34 at randomisation, and no baseline imbalance is reported that suggests a problem with the randomization process (p5 l43-58).

An independent pharmacist, with no other role in the study or data analysis, prepared a concealed allocation schedule; the allocation code was kept in a sealed envelope until the end of the study; site pharmacists prepared the syringes, so injecting physicians could not see the treatment; and the solutions were transparent and indistinguishable (p3 l4-20). Allocation was therefore controlled by an independent unit, not by enrolment staff.

The main report states that participants were randomly assigned (1:1) by block randomisation according to a centralised schedule, and that the treatments were randomly assigned in blocks of four to a consecutive series of numbers (p2 l47-49; p3 l4-10). A random component is explicit, so the sequence is random.

The Result is based on the intention-to-treat population of 34 (botulinum toxin A) and 32 (placebo), with week-24 values carried forward by LOCF (p4 l40-44). Of 68 randomised, one participant withdrew on the day of the first administration and one did not complete any pain diary (p5 l43-50). Both were excluded because they lacked outcome data, which is a modified ITT exclusion that the guidance treats as appropriate for this domain, with missing outcome data assessed in Domain 3. The analysis did not use per-protocol or as-treated grouping. The report describes the analysis as intention-to-treat, not explicitly as modified ITT, so this is Probably yes.

Active and placebo solutions were transparent and indistinguishable, and all patients and investigators were masked to assignment (p3 l4-20). The registry records quadruple masking of participants, care providers, investigators and outcome assessors. The report acknowledges a risk of unmasking from skin changes (wrinkles or colour) after subcutaneous toxin, but states that neither patients nor investigators reported recognising the treatment for this reason (p10 l26-30). No participant guessing data are reported, so this answer is Probably no rather than No.

Site pharmacists who were not otherwise involved in the study prepared the syringes, so the physicians injecting could not recognise the treatment. Those injecting were not involved in subsequent assessments. The allocation code was kept in a sealed envelope until the end of the study (p3 l4-20). The registry lists care providers and investigators as masked. Carers and people delivering interventions therefore had no route to knowing assignment during the trial.

Of 68 randomised, 66 were analysed. The flow shows 34 placebo participants randomised and 32 included, so both participants excluded for lacking outcome data were in the placebo arm, and none in the botulinum toxin A arm (p4 l77-90; p5 l43-50). That is 2 of 34 placebo participants (6%) and 2 of an observed 15 responders. Among the 66 analysed, week-24 values not observed were carried forward by LOCF, and the number of carried-forward week-24 values is not reported in the main text. Weekly pain records were 7.9% missing (131 of 1650), and visit records 7.3% missing (29 of 396), concentrated late in the study (supplement Web Extra file 10). For a dichotomous outcome, the two excluded placebo participants are not negligible relative to 15 observed responders: if both were responders, the placebo response would rise from 15.6% to 20.6% and the observed difference would fall from about 13.8 to 8.8 percentage points. Data were therefore not available for nearly all randomised participants.

Sensitivity analyses with three other imputation methods (linear interpolation, maximum likelihood, and multiple imputation by MCMC) gave results similar to LOCF (supplement Web Extra file 9; main report p10 l26-34). These methods all assume the missing values are missing at random, so they show that the imputation method does not change the estimate under that assumption; they do not test whether missingness depended on the outcome. The investigators also acknowledge that LOCF can overestimate efficacy (p10 l22-26). The guidance says LOCF and imputation based on intervention group alone should not be assumed to correct bias. No sensitivity analysis examined a plausible not-at-random scenario, such as assuming dropouts in the placebo arm were non-responders.

The reported reasons for missingness relate to the outcome: three placebo participants left the study prematurely with pain worse at 24 weeks (supplement Web Extra file 6). Missingness was also more frequent in the placebo arm (p=0.043) and concentrated late in follow-up (supplement Web Extra file 10). Participants whose pain worsened leaving the placebo arm is the pattern the guidance identifies as likely to bias the estimate. The primary analysis (LOCF) does not account for this dependence, and the investigators note that LOCF may overestimate efficacy.

Missingness was mostly due to dropouts and was more prevalent at the end of the 24-week period and in the placebo group (supplement Web Extra file 10). Three placebo participants with 30% pain worse stopped the study prematurely (supplement Web Extra file 6, eh_73fd5c139d0c5851). Loss to follow-up in a pain trial could plausibly relate to a participant's pain, so missingness could depend on the true week-24 value.

For this participant-reported outcome the assessor is the participant. The report states that all patients and investigators were masked to treatment assignment, with identical transparent solutions prepared by pharmacists who took no other part in assessment (eh_8541ee2f0d65d951). The registry lists masking as quadruple, with participants, care providers, investigators and outcomes assessors all masked (eh_a586b39e4b741f15). The authors acknowledge a risk of unmasking from skin changes after subcutaneous injection, but they state that neither patients nor investigators reported recognising the treatment (eh_e5aa3885b731f31e). That is a residual concern, not evidence that the participants knew the assignment, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

Pain was measured the same way in both arms: a daily diary of pain scores summarised as weekly means, with the same visit and follow-up schedule after the same two administrations 12 weeks apart (eh_8541ee2f0d65d951; eh_73fd5c139d0c5851). Both groups received identical-looking syringes and the same schedule, so the injection visits did not add extra contacts in one arm. The outcome is pre-specified, and the captured text reports no difference in measurement thresholds, timing or detection opportunities between groups. Differential loss to follow-up is a missing-data issue assessed in Domain 3, not a difference in how the outcome was measured.

The outcome is the proportion of participants with at least a 50% reduction in self-reported pain intensity at week 24, from a Brief Pain Inventory average pain score on a 0-10 numerical rating scale (eh_415f5ec0b2f07e4a; main p3 l88-93). Pain was recorded in diaries as weekly mean scores (supplement Web Extra file 6, eh_73fd5c139d0c5851). This is the standard participant-reported pain measure for a pain trial, and the threshold is a sensible responder definition. The captured text gives no reason to think the instrument is insensitive to effects of this size or has poor validity. The primary outcome is pre-specified, so the screening question does not point to an inappropriate method.

The responder comparison could have been analysed in several ways: ITT with LOCF, other imputation methods, and adjusted or unadjusted models. The report states that the authors 'used several robust statistical models' (eh_e5aa3885b731f31e), but the captured text does not say which models were planned or reported for the responder outcome. The reported estimate is the ITT LOCF comparison (eh_676840d75be7290a), and a post-hoc sensitivity analysis with three other imputation methods gave similar results (eh_dbc32cf12ff994d7). No analysis plan is captured to show which analyses were pre-specified, so whether the reported analysis was chosen from several eligible analyses cannot be determined. The sensitivity results and the null responder finding argue against selection on favourable results, but they do not settle the question.

The registry lists two pain outcomes relevant to this result: the primary daily diary average pain score and a 24-week pain-relief outcome (eh_a586b39e4b741f15). The report presents both, and reports the 50% responder result explicitly with its null p value of 0.2 (eh_791f79717f07213f). It also reports 30%, 50%, 70% relief and pain worse on the same diary data (eh_73fd5c139d0c5851). Reporting every responder threshold and reporting a null result for the one selected for this Result argues against selection of the favourable measurement. Because the registered 24-week outcome does not name a responder threshold, the match between intention and report is not fully confirmed.

No protocol, SAP or dated analysis plan is captured. The registry record has no linked documents (provenance capture, status no_linked_documents_in_current_record), so the only pre-specification source is the ClinicalTrials.gov entry. That entry was first submitted on 2010-11-30, but the recorded start is 2010-10, so it was filed after enrolment began and could not fix the analysis before unblinded outcome data were available. The registry lists the primary outcome as average daily diary pain and a 24-week pain-relief outcome as a registered other outcome (eh_a586b39e4b741f15). The report's responder analysis is the ITT LOCF comparison (eh_676840d75be7290a). Under the guidance, a registry entry filed after enrolment without an earlier protocol or SAP gives no information on whether the analysis was fixed in advance.

Baseline Table 1 (ITT, n = 49 M1, 52 DLPFC, 48 sham) shows similar age (56.7, 56.5, 52.9 years), sex (57.1%, 55.8%, 52.1% female), pain duration, average pain intensity (7.0, 6.5, 6.9 out of 10), pain interference, DN4, NPSI and BDI. Pain condition proportions are similar across arms. The reported differences look compatible with chance and do not suggest a problem with randomization.

Allocation was centralized at the Clinical Research Unit of the coordinating centre, and identification numbers were reported by study staff on an eCRF, so the sequence was not generated at the enrolling sites. The active/sham assignment was stored on a blinded USB flash drive prepared for each patient. The report does not state explicitly that the sequence was hidden from enrolling staff until registration or describe the envelope or container safeguards, so Probably yes rather than Yes.

The Methods (main article p. 3) state that a computer-based algorithm generated random permuted blocks, stratified by study centre, with a 1:1 first randomization and a 0.67:0.33 re-randomization to active or sham. A computer random component is a Yes under the signalling-question criteria.

Results (p. 5, lines 36-60) state that the modified ITT population of 149 patients was analysed as 49 M1, 52 DLPFC and 48 sham, with the three excluded patients withdrawing consent before assignment (Fig. 2, footnote 2). The Methods state that the analysis used all patients in their randomized groups, with missing outcome data handled under Domain 3. The completer restriction used for the responder proportion in the Discussion is a missing-data restriction and belongs to Domain 3, but the responder denominators per arm are not reported, so Probably yes rather than Yes.

The Methods (p. 3) describe a double-sided active/placebo coil with identical sides, a sound matched across sides, and low-intensity scalp electrical stimulation synchronized to pulses in all arms, which the authors say ensured double blinding. The blinding questionnaire (p. 6, lines 21-27) shows that 58% of M1 and 44% of sham participants thought they had received active treatment, and 39% and 56% thought they had received sham. That is consistent with participants not knowing their assignment, though not proof.

The Methods (p. 3) state that the active or sham assignment was saved on a USB drive blinded to the investigators, with a personalized coloured patch for the target. The sound and the electrical scalp stimulation were the same across arms, which the authors say fully ensured double blinding for the patient and operator.

Only 93 of 149 modified-ITT participants (62%) are reported at Weeks 22 and 25 (p6 Figure 2 footnote; p5 lines 57-59 give 138 (93%) after five sessions and 130 (87%) at Week 4). The responder proportions (44.7% vs 12%) are reported for patient completers (p7 Discussion, eh_52b50ee68c221f59), so about 38% of randomized participants have no observed Week 25 outcome in the reported analysis. Imputed values count as missing under this question, and the between-session mean imputation (p5 lines 19-21) does not supply an observed Week 25 outcome. Nearly all outcome data are not available.

The trialists state that early dropouts before 25 weeks 'were not missing at random since they were not equally distributed within groups', that these data 'were not imputed because no satisfactory method exists to handle them appropriately', and were censored at the last visit (p5 lines 21-25). The only imputation reported is simple mean imputation of between-session missing data, which is assumed MAR (p5 lines 19-21) and does not address Week 25 dropouts. No sensitivity analysis for the Week 25 responder outcome was found in the supplement (zero-hit receipt sr_3026e05d027323cd, which is a bounded lexical search, not evidence of absence). Therefore no evidence shows the result is robust to missing outcome data.

Reasons 2 and 3 of Box 8 apply: the reported reasons for missing outcome data are outcome-related (lack of efficacy) and differ between arms, with 25% of sham-rTMS participants and 2% of M1-rTMS participants stopping for lack of efficacy after the early period (p5 lines 64-68, P = 0.005). Reason 1 also applies in part: the proportion of dropouts before 25 weeks differs between arms (21.4% for M1-rTMS, P = 0.028; p5 lines 60-61). The analysis did not account for the characteristics that explain this relation (the trialists use censoring at last visit, p5 lines 24-25), so the answer is not 'No'.

The trialists report that dropouts 'did not occur at random' (p5 lines 61-62). Later dropouts were mainly due to lack of efficacy: 1 patient (2%) in M1-rTMS, 9 (17.3%) in DLPFC-rTMS and 12 (25%) in sham-rTMS (p5 lines 64-68). Lack of efficacy is an outcome-related reason for missingness, so missingness of the pain-relief outcome could depend on its true value.

The participant is the outcome assessor for the patient-reported pain relief scale (p3 Figure 1 legend and the Method for the 0-100% scale, eh_27ee09853ffa0081). The abstract states that patients and investigators were blind to treatment allocation (eh_2fa94317a920020f), and the authors state the double-blind procedure was fully ensured with identical-looking active and placebo coil sides and synchronized scalp stimulation in all arms (p3, eh_27ee09853ffa0081). The blinding questionnaire at Week 25 shows no significant difference between arms in guesses (P = 0.33 to 0.42 in Supplementary Table 4). This supports a probable no for awareness. The questionnaire also shows partial correct guessing, which is recorded as counterevidence.

The same measures (pain relief 0-100%, pain intensity, PGIC/CGIC) were collected at the same visits in all arms, with extended and shorter visits defined by the schedule and not by arm (p5 lines 1-18; Figure 1 legend on p3 in eh_27ee09853ffa0081). The protocol kept the number and timing of visits and sessions equal across arms, and assessment was not described as changing with arm. No passage reports differential detection or additional encounters for pain relief in one arm.

The Week 25 responder proportion is derived from the 0-100% pain relief scale, which the trial used as a standard secondary measure with the same instruments at each visit (p5 lines 1-5 and 14-18 list the pain relief (0-100%) measure among the continuous secondary measures and state its use for the Week 25 NNT). The method is not reported as unsuited to detect plausible effects; the Discussion says the 0-100% pain relief scale was more sensitive to treatment than the NRS (p7, eh_52b50ee68c221f59). The question concerns the method, not the choice of outcome, so this answer does not depend on whether the responder dichotomy is an appropriate summary.

The registry lists the responder outcome at two cut-points (30% and 50% improvement), which are two eligible analyses of one measurement (sh_00bf02240e6904fe lines 118-122). Only the 50% threshold is reported, and only on the 0-100% relief scale (eh_52b50ee68c221f59). The bounded search of the main article (sr_192a5ae98f7e3255) found no other responder result, and the supplement search (sr_16d17693146a09b8) returned no hits, so no 30% or NRS-based responder result is captured. The sensitivity analyses in the Methods cover the primary outcome only (p4 lines 125-127), so no comparable analysis is reported for the responder dichotomy. The 50% responder result is the most favourable headline the report gives, so selection of the reported cut-point on the basis of results is plausible.

The registry names the responder outcome with two thresholds (30% and 50% improvement in pain) at the same time point (sh_00bf02240e6904fe lines 118-122). The main article reports only one responder proportion, the 50% threshold on the 0-100% pain relief scale (44.7% vs 12%, p7 Discussion, eh_52b50ee68c221f59). A bounded search of the main article for 'responders' (sr_192a5ae98f7e3255) returned only the Discussion passage, and the supplement search for 'responder' returned no hits (sr_16d17693146a09b8). So the 30% responder result and any responder proportion on the NRS pain-intensity scale are not reported in the captured Sources. The Discussion states that NRS effects were moderate (NNT 7.7) and justifies the relief scale as more sensitive, citing earlier studies, which reads as a results-informed choice of measurement. The reported measurement is the one with the most favourable NNT (3.1).

The registry record was first submitted 2013-11-07, before the 2014-03 start (sh_00bf02240e6904fe p1 lines 21-30), and lists Secondary outcome 3 as 'Proportion of responders to rTMS', defined as pain improved by at least 30% and at least 50% from baseline, at the end of treatment (25 weeks) (lines 118-122). The reported Result is the 50% threshold on the 0-100% pain relief scale at Week 25. The report's Methods list the pain relief scale as a secondary outcome (p4 lines 39-42), but the Methods (p4 lines 27-127) describe no responder analysis or threshold, and the 30% responder analysis is not reported anywhere in the main article or supplement. No protocol or SAP is linked to the registry record (sh_480f1370e272f651), so the analysis cannot be checked against a finalized plan. The reported analysis therefore departs from the registered responder outcome without a stated result-independent reason. The registry does not name the scale, which leaves a degree of uncertainty.

Table 1 (main article p.5) shows similar baseline characteristics across arms: HbA1c 8.04 (0.65), 8.04 (0.61) and 8.05 (0.66) %; bodyweight 92.87, 91.07 and 90.50 kg; metformin use 94%, 96% and 96%. Group sizes (142, 142, 140) match the 1:1:1 intent. No imbalance suggests a problem with randomisation. The main text says baseline characteristics were similar between groups.

Allocation was made by a remote interactive web-response system (IWRS) that assigned numbered cartons to each patient (main article p.3 lines 34-51; protocol section 6.2, Prot_001 p.27). Site staff entered the patient and received the carton assignment from the system. This is the remote, centrally administered allocation that Box 4 lists as Yes. Blinding is a separate domain question and does not affect this answer.

The main report states that randomisation used 'a computer-generated random sequence' via an interactive web-response system (main article p.3, lines 34-51). Protocol section 6.2 (Prot_001 p.27) says assignment 'will be determined by a computer-generated random sequence', with block randomisation at country level. A computer-generated random sequence is a random component, so the answer is Yes.

The reported population for this result is participants who received at least one dose of study drug, with 142, 141 and 140 per arm (eh_ecf6a2b6760b5472). One randomised 0.75 mg participant received no study drug and was excluded from the ITT population (eh_a54e3f2ee2f7afad). That exclusion reflects non-receipt of any dose, not outcome missingness, and the 0.75 mg denominator of 141 is the dosed population. A dosed-population analysis for a safety outcome is a reasonable analysis set, but it is not the randomised ITT set the guidance treats as appropriate, so the probable answer is no rather than yes. The randomised count of 142 in the 0.75 mg arm is recorded at eh_dfa892fb82c3869c.

The trial was double-blind: participants received identical-looking cartons assigned by the sponsor's IWRS (eh_e4212a0bb6d3c257), and assignment was blinded to patients and investigators until the end of the study (eh_59bf8700bf9112c7). No passage reports that participants were aware of their assigned intervention. Whether gastrointestinal side effects could have let participants infer allocation is not reported.

Investigators and trial personnel were blinded: the assignment was blinded to patients and investigators until the end of the study (eh_59bf8700bf9112c7), and the protocol describes a double-blind study with IWRS-generated allocation of blinded study drug cartons (eh_e4212a0bb6d3c257).

One of 142 randomised participants in the 0.75 mg arm (0.7%) was excluded from the dosed population (eh_a54e3f2ee2f7afad). For a single serious adverse event with 1 event in 283 dulaglutide-treated participants and 0 in the placebo arm, one excluded participant is unlikely to shift the result materially. The exclusion is documented as the population description for this result (eh_ecf6a2b6760b5472).

The registered outcome is reported as counts per arm over participants who received at least one dose of study drug, with denominators 142, 141 and 140 (eh_4edc31caf9d1a766; eh_ecf6a2b6760b5472). The result line for gastrointestinal haemorrhage reports the same denominators (eh_2bbda3e08da2a64f). Of 424 randomised participants, 423 are in these denominators. The one randomised participant without reported outcome data is the 0.75 mg participant who received no study drug (eh_a54e3f2ee2f7afad). Adverse-event collection is defined for dosed participants (eh_ecf6a2b6760b5472), so this participant has no reported safety outcome. Missing outcome data are therefore 1 of 424 randomised (0.2%). Calling this nearly all randomised participants is a judgement: with only 1 event observed in the dulaglutide arms, one missing participant could in principle change a count. The trial's own reporting, however, does not indicate any loss to follow-up in the safety population, and the excluded participant received no drug. The participant flow for completion and withdrawal was not in the captured supplement and the registry participant flow was not read, so this judgement rests on the denominators.

The assignment was blinded to patients and investigators until the end of the study (eh_59bf8700bf9112c7), and the trial was double-blind with IWRS-assigned cartons (eh_e4212a0bb6d3c257). Investigators record serious adverse events, so the outcome assessors (the site investigators and clinical staff) were blinded to assigned intervention. The reported event is an adverse-event record rather than a judgement-based clinical decision by an unblinded care provider.

All arms received the same once-weekly subcutaneous injection schedule, with blinded cartons of study drug (eh_10929e93d663553c). Placebo-matched blinding means the three arms received the same contact and monitoring structure, so there is no stated mechanism by which a haemorrhage event would be ascertained more often in one arm. The serious adverse event row is reported with identical denominators per arm (eh_2bbda3e08da2a64f). Ascertainment is systematic (SYSTEMATIC_ASSESSMENT), not passive, which reduces the diagnostic detection bias that the guidance describes for passively collected events.

The outcome is a serious adverse event recorded in the ClinicalTrials.gov results under the Gastrointestinal disorders SOC with the term Gastrointestinal haemorrhage, coded with MedDRA 20.0 by systematic assessment (eh_2bbda3e08da2a64f). Systematic assessment of the serious adverse event list is a standard, pre-specified way of ascertaining events in a registered trial, so the method is unlikely to be unsuitable for detecting a haemorrhage of this type. The population is the dosed participants (eh_ecf6a2b6760b5472). The question does not ask whether the choice of a single haemorrhage term reflects all gastrointestinal adverse events, which is a matter of outcome definition rather than measurement method.

The reported result is a participant count with at least one serious AE per arm. Protocol 9.5.2 and SAP section 5.15 specify AE counts and proportions per treatment group, with chi-square comparisons, and no alternative analysis of this count (for example adjusted or time-to-event versions) is specified (eh_6fcd1b8b5f906d29, eh_ee10aa8261daab60). The text does not show multiple eligible analyses of the haemorrhage event that were calculated and only one reported. Denominators 142, 141 and 140 match the safety population in the main article (eh_ecf6a2b6760b5472).

Eligible measurements of the GI AE domain, judged from the requested outcome of gastrointestinal adverse events, include all GI preferred terms. The record reports GI terms without apparent omission: diarrhoea 8/142, 14/141, 4/140 and nausea 21/142, 7/141, 5/140 in the non-serious AE table (eh_2c46fd9653d0fabb), and the serious haemorrhage term 0/142, 1/141, 0/140 (eh_2bbda3e08da2a64f). Protocol 9.5.2 specifies PT-level reporting of all AEs and SAEs (eh_6fcd1b8b5f906d29). The reported measurement was therefore not chosen from a subset of GI terms; the trialists reported all GI terms that occurred. The main article lists cholelithiasis and appendicitis as GI events of special interest (eh_d88741cd60f7a4d9) and states no cholelithiasis cases (eh_6baef819d4f03f5f), which is not a selection of the registered GI measurements.

Protocol version (a), H9X-MC-GBGE(a), carries an approval date of 21-Aug-2015 (eh_a24c344f8badf11e). Randomisation began on Dec 7, 2015 (eh_dfa892fb82c3869c), so this version was dated before unblinded outcome data existed. Its section 9.5.2 specifies that AEs and SAEs will be coded to MedDRA preferred term and SOC, with counts and proportions per treatment group (eh_6fcd1b8b5f906d29). The reported measure, participants with a serious AE of gastrointestinal haemorrhage per arm, matches that plan. Version (b), approved 28-Mar-2016 (eh_0e164fa769deeb1d), carries the same 9.5.2 wording (eh_9358c5d484acae6a), so the plan was not changed after enrolment for this measure. The SAP section on AE summaries is consistent (eh_ee10aa8261daab60). The SAP itself is not dated in the sources, and the registry record does not register AE outcomes.

Baseline Table 1 shows well-balanced groups: 144 dulaglutide versus 147 placebo (close to the intended 1:1), mean age 57.8 versus 58.3 years, HbA1c 8.6 versus 8.6 percent, and similar diabetes duration, insulin dose and OAD use. The reported differences are small and compatible with chance; none indicates a problem with randomization.

Allocation was made through an interactive web response system (IWRS), a remote service that is not controlled by enrolling staff. The SAP states that treatment assignments were blinded and that the randomization table was visible only to a minimal number of sponsor personnel. Together these describe remote, centrally controlled allocation that conceals the next assignment from enrolling investigators.

The main article states that randomization used a computer-generated random sequence with an interactive web response system, stratified by HbA1c and OAD use, at 1:1 allocation. A computer-generated random sequence is a random component, so the sequence is random.

The efficacy and safety analyses used all randomized patients who received at least one dose of study drug for their assigned arm (intention-to-treat population). All 291 randomized participants were included in the ITT population, and the registry AE table reports the analysis population as all randomized participants (denominators 144 and 147). No participants were removed after randomization for the reported AE counts.

The main article states that treatment allocation was masked from patients, and identical cartons with unmarked injection devices were used to preserve blinding. Injection devices are identical, and the placebo is a matching once-weekly injection. Nothing in the Sources reports that participants learned their assignment, although GLP-1 receptor agonist side effects can in principle reveal the assigned intervention.

Investigators, patients and sponsor staff involved in treatment or clinical evaluation were masked, and the study drug was supplied in identical cartons with unmarked devices. The SAP describes assignments as blinded to investigators until study end, with emergency unblinding allowed only when a patient's well-being requires it.

The approved Result is the registry AE count per arm, and the registry AE table reports the at-risk denominators as 144 (dulaglutide) and 147 (placebo), equal to all randomized participants who received at least one dose. Adverse-event ascertainment runs through the safety follow-up period (up to 32 weeks), so outcome data are available for every randomized participant. The 15 participants (10 dulaglutide, 5 placebo) who did not complete the study are therefore not missing AE data for this Result.

The main article states that treatment allocation was masked from patients, investigators and sponsor staff involved in treatment or clinical evaluation, and the study drug was supplied in identical cartons with unmarked devices. The SAP restricts unblinding to emergency AE situations via IWRS. The AE assessors are masked investigators, so they were unaware of the assignment.

The same AE collection, MedDRA 24.1 coding and safety follow-up apply to both arms, and the masked design uses identical devices and dosing schedules. Nothing in the Sources describes an extra test, visit or diagnostic step for one arm. The registry AE table reports the same time frame and denominators for both groups.

The approved Result counts serious and non-serious gastrointestinal AEs, coded to MedDRA 24.1 with relationship to study treatment judged by the investigator, and the registry reports them in standard AE tables for all randomized participants through the safety follow-up. This is a standard, pre-specified safety method, not an instrument of doubtful validity. Whether AE collection could miss the outcome is a completeness question, addressed in Domain 3.

The per-PT AE counts are analysed in one pre-specified way: proportion of patients with the AE, compared with Fisher's exact test (SAP page 21, lines 27-31). The registry reports the same affected/at-risk statistic. No alternative analysis of these counts (adjusted, time-to-event or different denominator) appears in the Sources. Analyses of onset and duration are for other PTs and are not alternative analyses of the reported counts.

The GI AE domain is measured through one pre-specified method: AE incidence by MedDRA PT and SOC, with investigator-judged relationship (SAP 5.11.1, page 19; paper page 3). The registry reports per-PT affected/at-risk counts for all AEs. The reported component was selected by the researcher, not by the trial's reporting, so the reporting does not show selection among measurements. The SAP's onset, duration and severity analyses apply to diarrhoea, nausea, abdominal distension and vomiting (page 21, lines 34-39). These are additional measurements, but they cover a different PT set from the researcher's component and were not reported in the Sources as alternatives to the counts used.

SAP_001 section 5.11.1 (page 19) pre-specifies AE analysis by MedDRA PT and SOC, with per-group proportions of patients with AEs and Fisher's exact tests (page 21). The GI AE analysis includes a PT list for GIAEs (page 21, lines 34-39). The registry AE section reports per-PT affected/at-risk counts for the same ITT denominators (144 and 147). The registration pre-dates the study start (first posted 2020-10-19, start 2020-12-07). The SAP has a revision history (page 7) showing amendments, and no date stamp confirming finalization before unblinded data was available was located in the captured text. That gap keeps the answer at probably yes rather than yes.

Table 2 baseline pain 5.6 (1.8) vs 5.8 (1.8), n 138 each; Table 1 shows similar baseline age (44.7 vs 47.0 years), sex, and clinical characteristics, with 138 participants per group. The baseline pain and disability values for the analysed outcome show no imbalance suggesting a randomization problem.

Methods state: "Randomizations were sealed in opaque, sequentially numbered envelopes. Eligible participants were randomly assigned immediately after baseline assessment by opening the next numbered envelope, at which point they were considered enrolled." This matches the guidance example of opaque, sequentially numbered, sealed envelopes opened only after irreversible assignment.
Methods state: "A randomization sequence was generated using computer-generated block randomization (random block size range, 2-10)." Computer-generated block randomization includes a random element.

The statistical analysis analysed "participant data ... in the groups to which they were randomized, regardless of adherence", and the full analysis set "included all randomized participants who provided data at each time point analyzed". This is a modified intention-to-treat analysis that excludes only participants with missing outcome data, which the guidance treats as appropriate for this domain. The 52-week row uses the same linear mixed model with baseline adjustment.

Trial-context deviations were not reported. The protocol says the control therapist "will not provide advice about their low back pain" and participants "will not be required to stop any current treatment" in either arm, so co-interventions were not restricted by the trial context. Intervention fidelity was audited ("no concerns of treatment infidelity"), and control-arm attendance was median 12 of 12 sessions. Any deviations that did occur would be ordinary non-adherence rather than trial-context effects.

The protocol states "Patients will be blinded to group allocation and study hypothesis" and the control arm receives a sham/placebo program (sham tDCS, detuned devices, sham laser). The SAP states "Participants and outcome assessors are blinded to group allocation." No report of participants identifying their allocation or of intervention-specific unblinding was found in the read text.

The main report states "The trial clinicians were unblinded, but participants, researchers collecting outcome data, and researchers analyzing outcome data were masked to group identity." The protocol adds that "It is not possible for therapists to be blinded to the study hypothesis as the treating therapists are on the research team." The people delivering the interventions therefore knew the assigned intervention.

Figure 1 shows 128 of 138 (intervention) and 129 of 138 (control) provided pain data at 52 weeks, so 257 of 276 (93%) were analysed and 19 were missing (10 intervention, 9 control: lost to follow-up plus withdrawn). The guidance gives about 95% as often sufficient for continuous outcomes; 93% with unknown values for the 19 missing participants is short of that, and the 52-week effect (-0.5, 95% CI -1.1 to 0.1) is small enough that the missing values could plausibly change the conclusion.

The analysis uses a linear mixed model that includes repeated observations and baseline values and states that missing data were assumed missing at random. That assumption is stated only for the 18-week primary outcome, where missing data were judged trivial. No sensitivity analysis for missing 52-week pain data is reported, and the mixed model does not establish that missingness is unrelated to the 52-week value.

The proportions missing are almost equal (10 of 138 intervention versus 9 of 138 control, about 7% and 7%). No reported reasons for missing 52-week data differ between arms or suggest dependence on the outcome, and the mixed model uses repeated measures and baseline values, which partly accounts for participants with missing later data. These facts support a judgement that dependence is possible but not likely.

Loss to follow-up and withdrawal at 52 weeks could plausibly relate to a participant's current pain, as is usual in pain trials with self-reported 52-week follow-up. The reasons for the 19 missing outcomes are not reported in the read text, so the mechanism cannot be ruled out.

For a participant-reported outcome the assessor is the participant. The SAP states 'Participants and outcome assessors are blinded to group allocation', the protocol states 'Patients will be blinded to group allocation and study hypothesis', and the main article states that researchers collecting outcome data were masked to group identity. Participants received a matched sham program, which supports the participant remaining unaware. No report of unblinding was found.

Pain was collected by the same web-linked questionnaire at the same scheduled time points in both arms (the protocol says all questionnaires were sent to patients as web-links at baseline, 3 and 6 weeks, week 12, and 6, 3, 6 and 12 months). The control arm was matched to the intervention arm for time and therapist contact (sham program of 12 sessions), so the intervention arm did not get more opportunities to detect or record the outcome.

The outcome is mean pain intensity over the previous week on an 11-point NRS (0 = no pain, 10 = worst pain imaginable), the same measure as the protocol's primary pain outcome. The protocol names the NRS as the pain instrument, and the 1-point minimal clinically important difference it cites is on the same scale. Nothing read suggests the instrument cannot detect plausible effects or has poor validity.

The protocol plans one model for each outcome (linear mixed model, change from baseline by linear contrast), and the report presents the planned mixed model estimate for pain at 52 weeks. No alternative eligible analysis of the 52-week pain outcome (for example unadjusted final values) is reported or described in the plan.

Pain has one eligible instrument (the 11-point NRS) in both the protocol and SAP, and the report presents all of the planned pain time points (18, 26 and 52 weeks) in Table 2, so no time point was dropped from a set of eligible pain measurements. The 52-week result is not the only one reported, and its non-significance (P .09) makes selection on significance unlikely.

The protocol (version 5, dated 27 Nov 2015 in its header) specifies pain intensity (11-point NRS, average over the past week) at each follow-up time point, analysed with linear mixed models with random intercepts, adjusted for baseline and prognostic factors, with contrasts from baseline at each time point. The report analyses the 52-week pain outcome with a linear mixed model that accounts for baseline values, which matches the plan. The 52-week estimate is a non-significant secondary time point (P .09), not a result chosen for significance.

The report states that the baseline characteristics of the two groups were similar in age, disease severity, organ failures, and diagnosis on admission (Table 1), and that arterial blood gases and oxygen supply did not differ. No imbalance suggesting a randomization problem is reported. The numeric Table 1 values were not separately inspected, so this relies on the authors' statement.

Allocation used opaque, sealed, numbered envelopes prepared from a computer-generated random-number table, with sequential use. These are the envelope safeguards named in Box 4 for 1.2. The report does not state that envelopes were opened only after irreversible assignment or who held the envelopes, so Yes cannot be confirmed from the text. The methods do not suggest that enrolling investigators could see the next assignment, so Probably yes rather than No information.

The report states the investigators generated a random-number table on a computer and used it to prepare the allocation envelopes. A computer-generated random sequence is a random component under 1.1.

The analysed population was 26 control and 27 NIV patients, out of 57 consecutively enrolled. The four excluded patients (two per arm) were left out for lack of exhaustive data, which is a missing-data exclusion rather than exclusion by treatment received or by protocol adherence. No per-protocol or as-treated analysis is described. Whether this is a modified ITT analysis that excludes only missing-outcome participants is assessed under Domain 3.

The report acknowledges that investigators were part of the clinician teams and that the lack of blinding could not be fully avoided. It does not describe whether non-protocol co-interventions or deviations in preoxygenation or intubation occurred in either arm, so the report does not allow a judgement either way.
The limitations section states that 'our study could not be blinded', so participants knew their assigned preoxygenation method (usual bag-valve mask or NIV by face mask).

The same passage states the trial was not blinded and that study investigators were part of the primary clinician teams caring for participants, so those delivering the interventions knew the assignment.

57 consecutive patients were enrolled and none refused, but four patients (two per arm) were not analysed for lack of exhaustive data, so 53 of 57 (93%) were analysed for ICU mortality (Table 4 denominators 26 control and 27 NIV). The 7% exclusion is not clearly small enough that the outcomes of the four could make no important difference for a dichotomous outcome with 21 deaths in total. The report does not say whether their ICU mortality status was known.

The report describes no sensitivity analysis or imputation for the four patients excluded for lack of exhaustive data, so there is no evidence that results are robust to plausible values of their outcomes.

Missing data are equal in both arms (two per arm), so there is no difference in proportions between groups. No reasons for missingness by arm are reported, and no circumstance strongly suggests the outcome was likely missing because of death.

The exclusion reason, lack of exhaustive data, is not linked to a documented cause. In an ICU population in which deaths can interrupt data collection, missingness of the outcome could plausibly depend on whether the patient died. The trial was unblinded, which the guidance treats as a circumstance that may increase the likelihood of such dependence.
The study could not be blinded, and the investigators were part of the primary clinician teams who recorded outcomes. Assessors were therefore likely aware of the intervention received.

The count of deaths in the ICU is expected to be ascertained the same way in both arms. The report does not describe differing follow-up or extra contacts in the NIV arm that would create more opportunities to detect deaths, and the arms were otherwise managed in the same ICU.
ICU mortality is an observer-reported outcome that involves no judgement, so knowledge of the intervention could not plausibly influence the count of deaths.

ICU mortality is a count of deaths in the ICU, a simple observation that is not subject to a measurement instrument. Table 4 reports it as a count per arm. Nothing in the report suggests the method could not detect plausible differences in deaths.

The methods describe choosing between chi-square and Fisher's exact test as appropriate, and the report gives a single p value of 0.21. Both tests would be non-significant for this count difference, so the choice is unlikely to have been driven by the results. No adjusted or alternative analyses of ICU mortality are reported.

ICU mortality is a single count of deaths per arm. It has no alternative scales or time points within the report, and the reported row states no time window, so there is no alternative measurement from which this result could be selected.

The report's stated endpoints are the primary (mean drop in SpO2 during ETI) and secondary (PaO2 at 5 and 30 min). ICU mortality is not named among them, and no source dated before unblinded outcome data specifies it. The registry lookup found no record, and no protocol or SAP is in the dossier, so the analysis plan cannot be dated relative to outcome data.

The authors state that baseline characteristics were very similar between the two randomisation groups at admission, before preoxygenation, and during and after intubation (Tables 1 to 3). Table 1 contains only a few modest differences, with no reported P values and no evidence of a deviation from the 1:1 allocation ratio (group sizes 99 and 102). Under the guidance, a few apparent differences are compatible with chance, so no imbalance suggests a problem with the randomisation process.

Patients were assigned via an interactive voice response system at the central randomisation centre, in a 1:1 ratio. The authors also state they used the clinical research department's standard operating procedure to avoid knowledge of the randomisation list by trial participants. Remote, centrally administered allocation by an interactive voice response system that is independent of enrolment staff matches the Yes criterion for concealment.

The Results state that 201 patients were randomly assigned, and the registry describes random assignment to NIV or control. Neither source names the sequence-generation method (for example computer-generated numbers). The main report describes central interactive voice response randomisation in a 1:1 ratio stratified by centre and ventilation status, a design that normally uses a computer-generated random list. Given a multicentre trial run through a central randomisation service, a random sequence is probable but not directly confirmed, so the answer is Probably yes rather than Yes.

The Methods state that all analyses included the intention-to-treat population (all patients randomly assigned, analysed as randomised), which is the appropriate analysis for the effect of assignment. The analysed group sizes in Table 4 (99 NIV, 102 face mask) match the randomised numbers, so the analysed population appears to be the randomised population. The Results mention that six patients were excluded (Fig 1); the stage of that exclusion is not described in the text, but the analysed group sizes match the randomised numbers, so those exclusions do not appear to have removed randomised participants from the analysis.

The Methods describe the intended preoxygenation for each group (NIV with pressure support and PEEP 5 cmH2O versus a non-rebreathing bag-valve-mask), and the Results report 5 preoxygenation failures, all in the face mask group. However, the report gives no account of crossover between groups, non-protocol co-interventions, or how often the intended preoxygenation was delivered. It also does not say whether the 91 patients (45%) already receiving NIV before randomisation were managed differently after assignment. Without these details the report cannot show whether trial-context deviations occurred, so No information is the honest answer.

The abstract describes the trial as open-label, and the registry records masking as NONE. Participants were therefore aware of their assigned preoxygenation method (NIV via face mask or bag-valve-mask) during the trial.

The trial was open-label with no masking. The people delivering preoxygenation and intubation (NIV ventilator set-up versus non-rebreather bag-valve-mask) necessarily knew the assigned group. Central IVRS allocation concealed the assignment only until randomisation.

Table 4 reports the death outcome with denominators of 99 (NIV) and 102 (face mask), which equal the per-arm randomised numbers, and the Methods analyse all randomised patients (ITT). Deaths in ICU are directly observed events, so outcome ascertainment for this endpoint is expected to be near complete, and no missing deaths or lost-to-follow-up counts are reported for it. The text says six patients were excluded from the 201 randomised, but does not say in which arm or at what stage, and the reported per-arm denominators leave those six unaccounted for. Because the death percentages are based on 99 and 102 patients, the six excluded patients are at most about 3% of the randomised population. The probable answer is therefore Yes, not Probably yes, but the exclusion accounting is unresolved.

The trial was open-label with masking recorded as NONE in the registry. No source reports blinding of outcome assessors, so the outcome assessors (the ICU clinical team recording death) would have been aware of the assigned preoxygenation method.

The trial was run in ICUs with both groups managed in the same settings, and the Results report death as a single pre-specified endpoint in both groups. Death is documented in ICU records whichever preoxygenation method was used, so differences in detection between the two arms are unlikely. The text does not describe how deaths were ascertained, so this answer is probable rather than definite.

Death in the ICU within 28 days is an observer-reported outcome that involves no judgement. Knowledge of the assigned preoxygenation method is unlikely to influence whether a death is recorded, so influence is not possible in any meaningful sense for this outcome.

The outcome is death in the ICU within 28 days, defined in the Table 4 footnote as the percentage of death in intensive care unit within 28 days. Death is an unambiguous, objectively verified event, so the measurement method is not inappropriate for this outcome.

The paper states that binary outcomes were analysed by multivariate logistic regression on the intention-to-treat population, and Table 4 reports unadjusted percentages alongside the P value. The registry does not describe the analysis, and no statistical analysis plan was available. A binary death outcome could be analysed in more than one defensible way, for example unadjusted versus adjusted for baseline SOFA or strata, so whether the reported P value reflects a pre-specified analysis cannot be determined.

The registry lists a single mortality outcome among the registered secondary outcomes, and the paper reports one death outcome (Table 4 'Death'). No other ICU mortality measurement that could have been selected from was identified in the Sources, so there is no clear evidence of multiple eligible death measurements.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record (NCT00472160) lists 'Mortality' as a registered secondary outcome, and the registry was first submitted on 2007-05-10, before the trial start of 2007-06. The reported result is death in ICU, which matches that registered outcome in substance. The registry does not specify the analysis method, and no statistical analysis plan was found, so the pre-specification of the analysis itself is inferred rather than shown. No evidence of post-data changes to the outcome or analysis was found.

Table 2 of the main article (all 157 randomized patients, 78 vs 79) shows baseline characteristics well balanced. Two of roughly 30 comparisons reach P < .05 (age P = .02; haemoglobin P = .01), which is compatible with chance. No key prognostic factor shows P < .001, and the group sizes match the 1:1 intended allocation.

The same passage states that patients were randomly assigned using a web-based interactive response system. Remote allocation by an external system, performed after enrolment, meets the RoB 2 Box 4 (1.2) Yes criterion for central or remote randomization.

The 2022 AVATAR report (sh_695a701df7a7b784, p. 3) states that the assignment to each treatment group was computer-generated and stratified by centre using a permuted-block sequence with variable block size. A computer-generated random sequence is a random component under RoB 2 Box 4 (1.1).

The primary analysis of the reported HR 0.44 was intention-to-treat over all randomized patients (78 early surgery, 79 conservative), analysed in assigned groups with Kaplan-Meier, log-rank and Cox models. The sensitivity analysis excluding non-operated early-surgery patients is secondary and is not the reported Result.

Deviations are the 6 early-surgery patients who did not receive surgery (infection, death before surgery, declined surgery, lost contact) and the 25 conservative patients operated after protocol referral criteria were met. These are protocol-consistent clinical changes or patient choices consistent with what happens outside the trial, and no report attributes them to recruitment or engagement effects.

The 2022 supplement describes allocation between early surgery and conservative treatment with watchful waiting, where the conservative arm was referred for surgery on symptoms, LVEF below 50% or a Vmax rise above 0.3 m/s per year. Surgical versus non-surgical management is not blindable, so participants knew their assigned strategy.

Clinicians and surgeons delivering the strategies knew the assignment, since surgery was scheduled per arm and conservative patients were referred for surgery by the study team. The DSMB was explicitly not blinded to allocation during event review.

All 157 randomized patients (78 early surgery, 79 conservative) were included in the ITT analysis of all-cause death. The main report states that one early-surgery patient lost to follow-up was censored at last available information. With 40 deaths in total, one censored patient out of 157 cannot make an important difference to the HR 0.44, so outcome data are available for nearly all randomized participants.

The DSMB adjudicated events by consensus, and its members were not blinded to treatment allocation during the events review (2022 supplement p4). The outcome assessor for death is therefore aware of the assigned intervention, even though the event itself is objective.

Both arms were followed under the same protocol with the same 6-monthly in-person visits and the same medical-record review for events (2022 supplement p4). The early-surgery arm had additional hospital contact around valve surgery, which could in principle increase detection of deaths, but all-cause death is recorded from records and is unlikely to be missed differentially. The enrolment flowchart shows no crossover and a small number of post-randomisation exclusions (2022 report p3).

All-cause death involves no judgement by the assessor; it is an observer-reported event that the guidance treats as unlikely to be influenced by knowledge of allocation. The DSMB adjudication of death relies on registry and medical-record confirmation (2022 supplement p4).

The Result is all-cause death, ascertained at scheduled 6-monthly visits with medical records reviewed for any registered event (2022 supplement p4). Death is a discrete, unambiguous event, so the ascertainment method is suitable for this outcome. The main article's Table 4 reports the death counts used for the Result (13/78 vs 27/79).

The Result is the intention-to-treat Kaplan-Meier and Cox HR over all 157 randomised patients (main article p2 and p5). The 2022 report also presents sensitivity analyses that exclude early-surgery patients not operated on, and these address a different population rather than selecting a death analysis from several. No clear evidence in the captured sources shows that several eligible death analyses were run and only the favourable one reported.

The death domain has several eligible measurements: all-cause death within the 36-month and 5-year registered composites, and time to death over the full follow-up. The report presents the full follow-up death HR (0.44) and a 3-year restricted analysis for all-cause death (main article p5), so the eligible measurements appear to be reported together. The 2022 primary composite HR (0.42) and the HF hospitalisation HR (0.21) are reported alongside it, so no clear selection of one death measurement is visible.

The registry record (first submitted 2015-04-30, start 2015-06) lists the composite of all-cause death, MI, stroke and HF hospitalisation as primary outcomes at 36 months and 5 years, and lists all-cause death alone only as a component. No dated source captured in the dossier pre-specifies the standalone all-cause death measurement, its median 63-month window, or a Cox analysis of it. The registry was last updated 2022-01-12, so it cannot show what was fixed before unblinded data. The 2022 report's methods (main article p5) describe time to death as a secondary analysis, but that is a post-hoc publication, not a dated plan.

Table 1 shows substantial baseline imbalances between arms: 24-hour UPCR 1.97 (SD 0.82) placebo vs 1.55 (1.03) cemdisiran, median 24-hour urine protein 2.80 vs 2.00 g/24h, median eGFR 47 vs 68, male sex 33% vs 59%, and BMI 26.8 vs 30.4 (eh_e1c9c27090a7d268). Stratification was by baseline proteinuria only (eh_6b486227fed2e5b8), so these imbalances in eGFR and sex were not stratified. The imbalances are in prognostic factors and suggest the randomization may not have produced comparable groups, with a 22:9 allocation in a 31-patient trial.

Treatment assignments were maintained by the Interactive Response System, and cemdisiran and placebo were packaged identically with the syringe masked by a site pharmacist (eh_42203e211139b691). The SAP states randomization was carried out through the IRS upon confirmation of eligibility (eh_721bc5eb13475f2c). Central, electronic allocation by a system not controlled by recruiting investigators prevents investigators and patients from foreseeing the next assignment.

The main article states patients were randomly assigned 2:1 using permuted blocks of three (eh_7baf24c02b891123). The supplement and SAP describe permuted block randomization stratified by baseline proteinuria, with assignments kept in the Interactive Response System (eh_42203e211139b691; eh_721bc5eb13475f2c). No inspected passage states that the order of assignments within blocks was randomly generated, so the random sequence cannot be confirmed from the reported method.

Efficacy was analysed in the modified intent-to-treat population, defined as all patients who received any amount of study drug with baseline and at least one post-baseline 24-hour UPCR, grouped by assigned treatment at randomization (eh_916810d2feef3ceb). Figure 1 shows all 31 randomized patients (22 cemdisiran, 9 placebo) in the treatment arms, so the population excludes randomized patients only for missing post-baseline outcome data. Missing outcome data is assessed in Domain 3, and this analysis groups participants by randomized arm.

The main article describes a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design (eh_7baf24c02b891123). The supplement states that all site personnel and patients were blinded to study drug treatment during the efficacy period up to week 36, and that cemdisiran and placebo were packaged identically (eh_42203e211139b691). Participants were therefore not aware of their assignment during the double-blind period.

The supplement states that site personnel were blinded to study drug treatment during the efficacy period, that the syringe was masked by a site pharmacist before administration, and that treatment assignments were maintained by the Interactive Response System (eh_42203e211139b691). Concealment and masking support that carers and administering staff were not aware of assignment.

The registry reports 31 participants analysed at week 32 (9 placebo, 22 cemdisiran), matching the randomized allocation of 22:9, so the analysed set appears to include nearly all randomized participants. The main article's efficacy population is the mITT (any study drug plus at least one post-baseline 24-hour UPCR), and the primary analysis uses an MMRM with all data points from baseline to week 32, so the reported analysed counts do not separately show how many participants had an observed week-32 value. The main article (Figure 1, as recorded in the earlier read) reports 21 of 22 cemdisiran and 8 of 9 placebo patients completing the double-blind period, which means up to two randomized participants (about 6%) may lack week-32 data. Under the continuous-outcome 95% guidance, that is close to the threshold but the timing of those two discontinuations relative to week 32 is not stated, so 'probably yes' rather than 'yes' is the appropriate answer.

The supplement states that 'All site personnel and patients were blinded to study drug treatment during the efficacy period up to week 36', which covers site personnel and patients. It does not state whether the central laboratory staff who measured 24-hour UPCR were blinded to assignment. The outcome is an automated laboratory measurement, so the assessor is the laboratory, and its blinding status is not reported.

The same central laboratory and the same 24-hour UPCR method were used for both arms, and the endpoint was assessed at the same protocol time point (week 32) in each arm. The article reports no difference in visit schedule or measurement procedure between arms, and the primary outcome is pre-specified, so ascertainment is expected to be comparable across groups.

The primary outcome is a 24-hour urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio measured by a central laboratory. This is an observer-reported outcome that does not involve clinical judgement, and the guidance states such outcomes are unlikely to be influenced by knowledge of the intervention received, even when the assessor is aware.

The primary endpoint is pre-specified (main article p. 2: 'The primary end point was percentage change from baseline in urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) measured by 24-hour urine collection at week 32'), and 24-hour urine samples were analysed by a central laboratory. Measuring a urinary protein ratio on 24-hour collections is a standard, sensitive method for a proteinuria change of the size reported (-37.4%), so the measurement method is not inappropriate for this outcome.

The protocol specifies two analyses for the primary proteinuria endpoint, a linear model on log-transformed change with baseline covariate and stratification (primary) and MMRM using all urine protein assessments (sensitivity), and states that UPCR would be analysed similarly. The reported primary result for 24-hour UPCR comes from the MMRM approach (registry primary outcome description and the Figure 2A legend). The protocol-specified linear-model estimate for UPCR is not reported. Because the two reported estimates are of similar magnitude (-37.4% and -36.2%) and in the same direction, there is no clear evidence that the choice of MMRM was made on the basis of which estimate was most favourable, so the answer is probably no rather than probably yes.

The protocol names 24-hour UP as the primary proteinuria measurement and lists 24-hour UPCR, spot UPCR, percentage with partial remission, >50% reduction, and hematuria as secondary endpoints. The main article reports the primary 24-hour UPCR estimate (-37.4%), the 24-hour UP estimate (-36.2%, Supplemental Table 2, cited as a secondary end point) and spot UPCR (-45.8%) at week 32. The registry lists the primary outcome as 24-hour UPCR at week 32. The reported measures therefore cover the protocol's proteinuria measurements at week 32, and the reported set is not selected from a larger set of unreported measurements.

The protocol (original 10 Sep 2018, Amendment 1.0 26 Nov 2018) pre-specifies a primary endpoint of percentage reduction in 24-hour urine protein (UP) analysed as a linear model on log-transformed change with baseline covariate and randomization stratum, with MMRM as a sensitivity analysis. The reported primary result is the placebo-adjusted geometric mean change in 24-hour UPCR from an MMRM model. The SAP versions available (v1.0 dated 28 Feb 2020; Amendment 1 dated 29 Apr 2021; Amendment 2 dated 31 Mar 2022) and the registry primary outcome (UPCR, MMRM) describe the reported analysis. Whether the plan was finalised before unblinded data were available cannot be determined: the SAP says unblinding follows the interim database lock at last-patient week 36, the registry primary completion date is 17 Mar 2022, and no source gives the unblinding date or the date of each amendment relative to it.

Table 1 (page 4) reports baseline characteristics for 61 patients per arm in the intention-to-treat analysis. Age (61 (11) vs 64 (10) years), BMI (25.5 (5.4) vs 27.1 (4.9)), sex ratio (35:26 vs 42:19), stage IV disease (5 vs 3) and the other characteristics differ by amounts that are compatible with chance. The groups are equal in size (61 vs 61), consistent with the 1:1 allocation. There is no evidence of excessive similarity or of a substantial excess of significant differences.

The Methods (page 2) state that the schedule was 'sequentially numbered and placed in opaque, sealed envelopes that were opened by the investigator at the time of randomization'. Sequential numbering, opacity, sealing and opening after enrolment match the official criteria for envelopes. The report does not state a tamper-proof seal, and the enrolling investigator opened the envelopes, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes. No passage suggests that the enrolling investigator knew upcoming allocations.

The Methods (page 2) state that a 'computer-generated randomization schedule stratified by neoadjuvant treatment using random permuted blocks of 4 and 6' was used.
