A computer random number generator is a random component under the official guidance for signalling question 1.1, so the sequence was generated randomly.

The Statistical analysis section (page 3) describes an intention-to-treat analysis with 61 participants per arm. The Results (page 4) say that 'three patients (5 per cent) in each group were excluded' after randomization, and that 'two patients (3.3 per cent) in each group did not undergo the planned surgery', with one prehabilitation patient dying from 'a sudden cardiac arrest' before surgery. The complication outcome (Table 2, page 5) was analysed on 59 per arm, which removes these participants. Removing participants who had not received the planned surgery, including a death in the prehabilitation group, is not an analysis of all randomized participants in their allocated groups, so the analysis is not appropriate for the effect of assignment.

Participants and personnel were unblinded, so the question is active. Page 2 says the control group 'did not receive advice on prehabilitation-related interventions, apart from some who were recommended to use high-energy nutritional supplements for 10-14 days before surgery', and page 6 notes a 'risk of contamination in the control group'. The report does not say whether controls sought or received prehabilitation-type care because of the trial, nor how many did, and no adherence or co-intervention data were collected with an objective tool. The report therefore does not describe trial-context deviations well enough to judge them, which is 'no information' rather than evidence of a problem.

The study is described as an 'open-label RCT' (page 2), and the Discussion (page 6) states that 'Blinding of participants was not possible'. Participants knew their allocation, which is consistent with prehabilitation being a visible home-based programme.
Page 2 states that 'neither the participants nor personnel were blinded', so the people delivering the interventions and the carers knew the assigned group.

Up to two participants per arm (59 of 61 analysed) are missing from the complication analysis, plus three per arm excluded after randomization. The complication counts are 14/59 (prehabilitation) and 35/59 (control). Even if every excluded prehabilitation participant had a complication and every excluded control participant did not, the risk ratio would remain well below 1 (for example 16/61 vs 35/61 gives about 0.46), so the exclusions are unlikely to change the direction or the broad size of the effect. This is a judgement, since the reasons for the three exclusions per arm are not reported.

The approved Result covers all randomized participants (64 + 64 = 128). The primary outcome was analysed in 59 per arm (Table 2, page 5: 'Prehabilitation (n = 59)', 'Control (n = 59)'), so 10 of 128 randomized participants (7.8%) have no primary outcome data, with 5 missing in each arm. Page 4 states two patients per arm 'did not undergo the planned surgery', and the flow chart (page 3) records three per arm excluded after randomization (screening error, withdrawal of consent). Missing data are not 'nearly all' by the guidance: the number missing is well above 5% and, with 49 events among 118 analysed, the 10 unobserved participants could move the risk ratio (bounding by all-events and no-events extremes gives RR about 0.35 to 0.54). Page 6 says 'There were no missing data for the primary outcome', but the denominators contradict this for the Result's population.

The report describes sensitivity analyses but none addresses missing primary-outcome data. Page 4 states 'The listwise deletion method was used for missing data'. The sensitivity analysis (CCI score and mean number of complications, page 5) is still based on the same analysed participants and does not model the outcomes of the non-operated or excluded participants. No imputation or range of assumed outcomes for missing participants is reported, so the report gives no evidence that the result is robust to missingness.

Evidence that missingness is likely to depend on the true value would come from differing missingness proportions or differing reasons between arms. Both arms have 5 of 64 randomized participants without primary outcome data (7.8%), and the outcome-linked reasons are balanced: prehabilitation has one death before surgery and one unfit for surgery, while control has two unfit for surgery (page 4). The only asymmetry is the prehabilitation death, which is a single event. The report offers no adjustment for these participants. The balance of reasons and proportions makes differential dependence less likely, though it cannot be excluded.

Page 4 reports that in the prehabilitation group one patient died before surgery from sudden cardiac arrest and another was deemed unfit for surgery because of a decline in physical status, and that two patients per control arm were unfit for surgery. Unfitness for surgery and a death before surgery are plausibly linked to the true outcome (postoperative complications within 90 days cannot be measured without surgery, and a death before operation is a severe outcome). The non-operated participants are therefore probably missing for reasons related to their health status, which is the guidance's example of missingness that may depend on the true value. The screening errors and withdrawals of consent (page 3) are unlikely to depend on the outcome.

Page 2 states that 'the medical staff providing care for the patient were not actively informed about the allocation' and that 'Data collection and analyses were performed in a blinded manner with respect to the group allocation.' The registry record lists masking as SINGLE (OUTCOMES_ASSESSOR). Participants and personnel were not blinded (page 2, page 6), but complications are clinical events recorded by clinicians who were not informed, so the outcome assessor is probably not aware of the intervention received. Probably no, rather than no, because the study staff who conducted the prehabilitation telephone calls knew the allocation and their role in recording complications is not stated.

The method of recording complications (Clavien-Dindo classification from clinical care) was the same in both groups. The prehabilitation group had more contacts (supervised training sessions, physician and physiotherapist evaluation, routine telephone calls and interviews about adherence; page 2), which could in principle increase detection of minor events. Any such detection bias would push complication counts up in the prehabilitation group, which is the opposite of the observed direction. The observed minor-complication difference (Clavien-Dindo I-II, 6.8 versus 42.4 per cent; page 5) therefore is not explained by more opportunities to detect events in the intervention group.

The primary outcome is the number of patients with at least one complication within 90 days, with complications 'graded according to the Clavien-Dindo classification' (page 2, Outcomes). This is a pre-specified, standard clinical outcome recorded from routine postoperative care, with the same method in both groups. Nothing in the report suggests that the method is unlikely to detect plausible effects or has poor validity. The question does not judge whether the outcome itself is a sensible choice.

The primary analysis is an unadjusted comparison of the proportion of patients with at least one complication (14 of 59 versus 35 of 59, RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.66, P = 0.001), with the test stated in the Methods as chi-squared or Fisher's exact. Sensitivity analyses of the CCI and of the mean number of complications, and subgroup analyses, were reported and described as consistent with the primary result (p.4 and p.6), which the guidance treats as evidence against selection among analyses. There is an unexplained denominator issue: 59 per arm is analysed, against 61 per arm in the stated ITT analysis. Because both arms are reduced by the same number, the risk ratio is unchanged by the choice of common denominator (14/61 versus 35/61 also gives 0.40), so the denominator choice does not appear to have been made on the basis of the results.

The registry records one primary outcome measurement (Clavien-Dindo morbidity at 90 days), and the reported result is that measurement, in a form the registry names. The guidance restricts alternatives to eligible measurements, and here the eligible measurement is the proportion of patients with at least one complication within 90 days. The article's other complication measures (grouped minor and severe counts, the comprehensive complication index and the mean number of complications) are either the same measurement reported by grade or are described as sensitivity analyses. Table 2 reports the grade breakdown (Clavien-Dindo I, II, minor I-II, severe III+), so no grade-based alternative is withheld. There is no other registered time point for this measurement.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record (NCT04223401) was first submitted 2020-01-06 and the trial started 2020-02-06 (ACTUAL), so the entry predates enrolment. It names a single primary outcome, 'Postoperative morbidity rate by Clavien-Dindo' at 90 days postoperatively. The report analyses that measurement as its Methods describe: the primary outcome is the number of patients with at least one complication within 90 days, graded by Clavien-Dindo, analysed by intention to treat (p.2 'The primary outcome of the study was the number of patients with at least one complication within 90 days after surgery'; p.3 'The intention-to-treat method was used'). Under the guidance for 5.1, a pre-enrolment registry entry naming this measurement and time point, reported as its methods describe, supports Probably yes even without analysis detail. The analysis-plan date relative to unblinded data is not established by any captured source.

The baseline characteristics table (eh_c0408af84062a3ff) was read for this question, and it shows no baseline difference that the paper treats as a randomization problem. Under Box 4, signalling question 1.3, differences compatible with chance do not indicate a randomization problem. The sample is small (14 LGI and 12 control participants analysed, per Figure 1 eh_b416cc191ab46685), so some chance imbalance is expected and is not evidence of a flawed process.

The main report (eh_f285baedb6284450, eh_9d70034f70989d79) reports random assignment but no allocation concealment method, such as central or remote allocation, sequentially numbered opaque sealed envelopes, or sequentially numbered containers. The registry (eh_42c11827afa954d6) gives no concealment details either, so no evidence shows whether the enrolling staff could foresee assignments.

The main report (eh_f285baedb6284450) describes a randomized block design and the registry (eh_42c11827afa954d6) lists allocation as RANDOMIZED, but neither describes how the allocation sequence was generated. A blocked design without a statement that the order within blocks was random is answered No information under the official guidance (Box 4, signalling question 1.1; section 4.3.1.1). The journal word limit does not change this here, because the paper gives a block design and no random-component method.

The IVF-outcome analysis for oocytes retrieved is based on LGI n=9 and control n=12 (Figure 1, eh_b416cc191ab46685). The LGI group had 14 analysed, and 5 were excluded from IVF outcomes (3 spontaneous pregnancy, 2 IVF cycle cancellation), while none were excluded in the control group. These are post-randomization exclusions of randomized participants whose outcome could still have been assessed in their assigned group, which the official guidance (Box 6, signalling question 2.6) treats as inappropriate. The registry (eh_42c11827afa954d6) defines the oocyte outcome for all participants who underwent IVF, so the exclusions are not justified by that definition.

Figure 1 (eh_b416cc191ab46685) reports non-compliance as the reason for dropout (1 LGI and 3 control participants 'could not comply with the intervention'), with 2 personal reasons and 2 other health problems. This is ordinary non-adherence that would also occur outside a trial, not deviation caused by trial recruitment or engagement, and the report does not attribute any deviation to the trial context. Under Box 6, signalling question 2.3, such non-adherence supports probably no.

The methods (eh_f285baedb6284450) state that blinding was not possible in this diet trial. Participants on a low-GI diet, a conventional diet, or usual diet necessarily knew their assigned diet, so participants were aware of their assigned intervention. The registry (eh_42c11827afa954d6) records Masking: NONE.

The same methods passage (eh_f285baedb6284450) states that blinding was not possible, and the registry (eh_42c11827afa954d6) records Masking: NONE. Staff who delivered the diets and monitored participants therefore knew the assigned group.

Five of the 14 analysed LGI participants (36%) were excluded from the oocyte analysis, against none of the 12 control participants (Figure 1, eh_b416cc191ab46685). The excluded participants were excluded for reasons (spontaneous pregnancy and IVF cycle cancellation) that are plausibly linked to the diet and to the number of oocytes retrieved. The asymmetry and the size of the excluded fraction, relative to a group of 9 to 12 analysed participants, mean there is potential for a substantial impact on the result (Box 6, signalling question 2.7). The figure text is not OCR-verified, so the counts are read from the rendered image.

Figure 1 gives 35 randomised participants. The oocyte-retrieved analysis population is 21 (LGI 9 of 16 allocated; control 12 of 19 allocated), so 14 of 35 (40%) have no outcome data. This is far from 'nearly all'. Counts were read from the figure image, not OCR-verified, but the gap is large enough that the answer does not depend on the exact counts.

The oocyte comparison is a complete-case analysis restricted to participants with IVF outcomes. The sources read report no imputation and no sensitivity analysis about the outcomes of the 14 participants without oocyte data, so nothing shows the result is robust to plausible values for them.

Reported reasons for missing oocyte data differ between groups. In the LGI group, 3 participants were excluded for spontaneous pregnancy and 2 for medical cycle cancellation. In the control group, no participant was excluded from IVF outcomes, and its dropouts gave personal, non-compliance and other health reasons. Reasons that differ by group, and cancellation for medical reasons, make it likely that missingness depended on the true outcome, even though the proportions missing are similar (7 of 16 LGI and 7 of 19 control).

Figure 1 records two LGI participants excluded from IVF outcomes for IVF cycle cancellation for medical reasons. Cancellation for medical reasons plausibly reflects the ovarian response, which is the true oocyte count, so missingness could depend on the outcome's true value. Other exclusions and dropouts (personal reasons, could not comply, other health problems) are less clearly linked to oocyte number.

The trial was not masked. The report says blinding of the intervention was not possible, and the registry records masking as NONE. Assessors of the oocyte count were therefore aware of the assigned diet.

Both groups went through the same IVF stimulation and oocyte-retrieval procedure, and the count of retrieved oocytes does not depend on diagnostic testing or extra contacts that differ by group. The diet arms involved more contact, but that contact does not change how oocytes are counted.
The oocyte count is an observer-recorded number with little judgement. Knowing the diet is unlikely to change how many oocytes are counted or recorded at retrieval.

The outcome is the number of oocytes retrieved at the IVF oocyte-retrieval procedure, a direct count of a pre-specified, clinically standard endpoint. The registry records it as a secondary outcome measured during the IVF cycle (between 12 and 16 weeks), and it is the endpoint the report analyses. Nothing in the sources suggests the method is insensitive or invalid.

The report gives the oocyte comparison as a single complete-case analysis (LGI n=9, control n=12). Several analyses were possible, for example an all-randomised analysis or one that handles the excluded participants differently, but no pre-specified analysis plan is available to show which was intended. Whether the reported analysis was chosen on the results cannot be judged from the Sources.

The registry lists the number of oocytes retrieved as one secondary outcome, measured once during the IVF cycle, and the report analyses that single count. The registry does not list other eligible oocyte measurements or time points that were left unreported, so there is no evident choice among measurements of this outcome.

No protocol or SAP is captured: the companion capture lists no linked documents. The only pre-specification is the ClinicalTrials.gov record, first submitted 2015-04-07, after the study started (2012-01) and completed (2013-12). Under the guidance, a registry entry submitted after enrolment began, with no earlier protocol or SAP, cannot show what was fixed before outcome data were available. The report does not describe a dated analysis plan for the oocyte comparison.

Baseline data are reported for age (33.8 +/- 3.7 vs 33.6 +/- 2.8 years, page 1 lines 87-89), indications for IVF (page 1 lines 90-96), and weight at the start of the cycle, which 'did not differ significantly' between groups (page 3, lines 43-44). Systolic and diastolic blood pressure differences on the day of oocyte retrieval were also 'not significant' (page 3, lines 56-62). Group sizes were 10 and 8, which does not indicate a substantial departure from an intended allocation ratio. No excess of significant baseline differences is reported, so the imbalances appear compatible with chance.

The Methods describe how groups were assigned only as 'randomly divided into two groups' and give no mechanism for delivering or protecting the sequence from enrolling staff (page 1, lines 79-83). Nothing describes remote allocation, sealed envelopes or numbered containers. Without these details, neither a probable yes nor a probable no is reasonable.

The Methods state only that 'Patients were randomly divided into two groups' (page 1, lines 79-80). The report contains a bare randomization statement and no description of the sequence generation method. The only Source is the main article, and a search for 'randomly' returned only these two page-1 passages. The study is a small single-centre pilot (18 women), so the circumstances do not support a probable answer. The Result itself does not depend on this item.

One randomized normal-sodium woman was excluded after randomization because her IVF cycle was cancelled for inadequate ovarian response; this is a post-randomization exclusion of an eligible participant, so the analysis is probably not an appropriate intention-to-treat analysis.
The Source does not report any deviation from the assigned diet or stimulation protocol, so whether any deviation arose from the trial context cannot be determined.

The sodium-restricted diet (10-20 mmol Na+/day) versus ad libitum normal sodium intake was given to participants, who were monitored with urinary sodium:creatinine checks; no placebo or sham blinding is described, so participants were probably aware of their assigned diet.
Diet instructions and compliance monitoring were delivered by study staff, and no blinding of personnel is described, so personnel were probably aware of the assigned diet.
One of 10 randomized women in the normal sodium group (10%) was excluded after randomization; in a sample this small, that exclusion could substantially change the normal-sodium weight estimate.

Randomized women were 10 normal sodium and 8 low sodium; one normal-sodium woman (10% of that arm) was not included because her IVF cycle was cancelled, so outcome data are missing for 1 of 18 randomized women and for 1 of 10 in the normal sodium arm. For a continuous outcome the 95% benchmark is usually required, and the one-arm loss of 10% falls below it.
No sensitivity analysis, imputation or other missing-data correction is reported for the day-of-oocyte-retrieval weights, so there is no evidence that the result is robust to the one missing woman.

The only reported reason is cancellation for inadequate ovarian response, which is a cycle-level event rather than a measured weight; the reasons differ by one participant between arms, which by itself is not evidence that missingness depended on the outcome. The trial circumstances do not make weight-dependent dropout widely expected.

The documented reason for the missing weight is cancellation of the IVF cycle for inadequate ovarian response; ovarian response is linked to body weight in IVF populations, so the missingness could depend on the true (unmeasured) weight.

The study compared two dietary regimens that participants followed and that study staff monitored, and no masking of the staff who weighed participants or recorded blood pressure is described; awareness is therefore assumed.

Body weight was measured on the same occasions (start of cycle and days -4, 0, +3, +6, +9, +12) with the same scale and procedure in both groups, so measurement or ascertainment would not be expected to differ between diet groups.
Body weight is an objective measure recorded on a calibrated scale with no judgement involved, so knowledge of the diet group could not plausibly change the recorded value.

Body weight was measured in kg to one decimal place on a SECA-alpha scale with the patient clothed but without shoes, and blood pressure with an automatic device averaged over three readings; these are standard, valid methods for the outcome.

The report gives only group means and SDs for day-of-retrieval weight (eh_6b92be49f02fc4f5). It does not state the analysis used for the weight comparison, nor whether a change-from-baseline, adjusted or final-value analysis was also run, and no between-group test is reported for weight. Several analyses were possible, and no intention source shows which was planned.

Body weight was measured at several time points: start of cycle, days -4, 0, +3, +6, +9 and +12 (eh_291ee44fcce77795). The report gives numerical group values only for the start of study and day of oocyte retrieval (eh_6b92be49f02fc4f5), and the normal-sodium start-of-stimulation value is not given. Without intentions, it cannot be determined whether day-of-retrieval weight was one of several eligible measurements chosen on the basis of its results.

No captured Source is a protocol, SAP, or registry entry dated before unblinded outcome data were available. The only Source-level mention of 'protocol' (eh_862999307971fbfd) refers to the ovarian stimulation flare-up protocol, not a trial protocol. The report (eh_291ee44fcce77795, eh_6b92be49f02fc4f5) describes the weight measurements and their analysis only in summary, with no statement that the weight analysis was pre-specified or when it was fixed.

Table 2 (page 4) reports baseline age, infertility duration, and state and trait anxiety by diet group for all 119 randomized women (57 restricted, 62 normal). The diet comparisons give p = 0.46, 0.55, 0.39 and 0.09, none of which indicates an imbalance beyond chance. Group sizes (57 vs 62) are close to the intended 1:1 allocation. The baseline data cover all randomized participants, not only the analysed 69.

No passage in the main article or the registry capture describes how allocations were concealed from enrolling staff or participants (no central service, envelopes, or containers). A zero-hit search for 'allocation concealment' returned no matches. The absence of text does not establish that concealment failed, so the answer is No information rather than No.

The only description of allocation is 'assigned ... by a restricted randomization method', citing an external reference (page 2, Randomization). The text does not state whether a random component (random numbers, tables, permuted blocks) generated the sequence or how the block order was produced. Per the RoB 2 guidance, a statement that the study was randomized, or that blocked allocation was used without stated random order, gives No information. The search for 'restricted randomization' returned only this passage, and the registry capture contains no design detail.

The reported pregnancy result was analysed in the 69 women who completed their cycle with adequate compliance to the assigned diet (page 4). That excludes 50 of 119 randomized women (42%), including women excluded for non-compliance and cycle cancellation. Excluding participants based on adherence to the assigned diet is a per-protocol-type analysis, and excluding eligible participants after randomization is inappropriate under RoB 2. The analysis was not by assignment to all randomized participants.

Table 1 (page 3) lists the reasons for leaving the analysis: follicle-count cancellations under the IVF-ET protocol, failed fertilization, cycle disturbances, personal reasons, non-compliance with diet (6) and unknown compliance (4). Non-compliance is ordinary non-adherence that would also occur outside a trial, and the cancellation criteria were set in the IVF-ET protocol. The report does not describe any trial-context cause of deviation, such as trial staff undermining the diet or recruitment activities inducing non-protocol behaviour. Page 6 notes that only a small proportion of drop-outs were due to non-compliance.

The diet was a prescribed, visible behaviour: the sodium-restricted group was given an advised intake of 20 mmol Na+ per day, with dietary instructions from professional dieticians (page 2), and the compliance check was built on the assigned diet. Participants were not told the hypothesis about coping (page 3), but they knew their diet. No blinding of participants is described, so participants were probably aware of their assigned diet during the cycle.

Dietary instructions were given by professional dieticians, who delivered different diets to the two groups, so the people delivering the interventions were aware of each participant's assigned diet. No blinding of carers or dietitians is described, and the allocation concealment method is unknown, so the dietitians probably knew the assignment.

Under the inappropriate analysis, 50 of 119 randomized women (42%) were excluded, and the pregnancy events were reported only in the 69 analysed women (13 pregnancies in total). The text states that dropouts had higher baseline state anxiety, which may predispose to cancellation (page 6), so the exclusions are related to prognosis. The excluded women's pregnancy outcomes are not reported, so a substantial impact on the pregnancy estimate is possible.

Of 119 randomized women, 50 (42.0%) were excluded and their pregnancy outcome is not reported (eh_bb88e60b56af21ca, Table 1; eh_7298e685c3c803ed, p. 2: 'The data of 50 of these women could not be used'). The pregnancy outcome is reported only for the 69 analysed women (36 restricted, 33 normal; eh_92ffd795c61b9908). The missing outcomes are far too many to be 'nearly all'. The arm-level exclusion proportions differ (21/57, 36.8%, restricted vs 29/62, 46.8%, normal). With 13 pregnancies among the 69 analysed women, the 50 unobserved outcomes could change the estimate substantially.

The only analysis reported is complete-case: pregnancy rates in the 69 women who completed their cycle with adequate compliance (eh_92ffd795c61b9908; eh_bb88e60b56af21ca). No imputation, weighting, or sensitivity analysis for the 50 excluded women is reported in the inspected passages. The authors' statement that dropout occurred in 'similar proportions' is not a sensitivity analysis and does not address whether the excluded women's pregnancy outcomes could differ from the analysed women's.

The reasons for missing outcomes are mainly cycle cancellation for follicle response and failed fertilization, which the trial circumstances make likely to affect pregnancy chances (eh_bb88e60b56af21ca). The counts differ between arms: fewer than 4 follicles 5 restricted vs 10 normal; cancellations in total 21 restricted vs 29 normal (eh_bb88e60b56af21ca). The excluded women also had higher baseline state anxiety, which the authors link to cancellation (eh_92ffd795c61b9908). This fits reason 4 of the RoB 2 guidance: dropout from IVF cycles for poor response is widely understood to be linked to the chance of conception. The analysis did not adjust for the characteristics that would explain this; no model of dropout or cancellation risk is reported.

Excluded women were mainly those with cycle cancellation for poor follicle response (fewer than 4 or more than 20 preovulatory follicles, 25 of 50), failed fertilization (6), or cycle disturbances (7) (eh_bb88e60b56af21ca, Table 1). These reasons are plausibly linked to the chance of pregnancy, so missingness of the pregnancy outcome could depend on its true value. Dropouts also had higher baseline state anxiety (eh_92ffd795c61b9908), and the authors state this 'may predispose to cancellation' (page 6 of the main article). Dependence is possible, although the pregnancy-specific mechanism is not directly reported.

The inspected passages do not say who determined pregnancy (laboratory, clinician or participant) or whether that person was masked to diet. The statement that 'patients were not informed about the possible role of dietary sodium restriction' (eh_bb88e60b56af21ca) concerns participants and the STAI questionnaires, not outcome assessors. No double-blinding statement is reported. Under the FAQ, absence of information leads to assuming awareness or recording NI; this is recorded as NI.

The same end-of-cycle pregnancy test is described for the whole sample (eh_7298e685c3c803ed), and no arm-specific extra visits, scans or testing are reported. Dietary instruction was given by dieticians to participants in the restricted group, which could add contacts, but the report does not say whether extra contacts or testing differed between arms. Differential exclusion of cycles before the test is treated under Domains 3 and 5.

Pregnancy is determined by a test, which is an observer-reported outcome that involves no clinical judgement, and the guidance states such outcomes are usually not influenced by knowledge of the intervention (eh_7298e685c3c803ed for the test). A positive test is not a matter of interpretation. The residual concern is the clinician-level cycle decisions, which the protocol criteria govern (eh_bb88e60b56af21ca), and these are assessed under Domain 3 rather than here.

The report states that the diet continued 'until the end of the IVF-ET cycle (pregnancy test or menstruation)' (eh_7298e685c3c803ed, p. 2). A pregnancy test is a standard, sensitive method for this outcome, and nothing in the inspected passages suggests it was unsuitable. The assay type, threshold and whether pregnancy was confirmed clinically are not reported.

The report gives one analysis of pregnancy: the 69 women who completed the cycle with adequate compliance (eh_92ffd795c61b9908; eh_bb88e60b56af21ca). The 50 of 119 randomized women excluded by cancellation, failed fertilization and non-compliance are not analysed for pregnancy in the report. Several analyses were possible (for example randomized-population versus compliant-population analysis), and the captured text does not say whether any was pre-specified or whether the compliant-population analysis was chosen on the results. Analysis intentions are not available, so this cannot be assessed beyond no information.

The report measures one pregnancy outcome. Pregnancy could be defined in more than one way (for example clinical versus biochemical pregnancy, which the report does not specify; eh_92ffd795c61b9908), so the outcome domain could have been measured in several eligible ways. Without an intention source, it cannot be shown whether other pregnancy measures were collected or reported. The STAI anxiety measures are a separate outcome domain and are not alternatives for pregnancy.

No protocol, SAP or dated analysis plan is among the captured Sources. The registry capture returned not_found (sh_cda9e7d41a79e720), so it gives no registered outcome or dates. The methods section (eh_bb88e60b56af21ca) describes the STAI measures and the ANOVA models but says nothing about a pregnancy analysis plan, and the pregnancy result is reported only for the 69 analysed women (eh_92ffd795c61b9908). Without a source dated before unblinded data were available, a pre-specified plan cannot be confirmed or excluded.

Table 1 and the baseline text report baseline values only for patients 'who eventually returned for follow-up at 4 months' (n = 45 treated, 49 control). The guidance gives 'no useful baseline information' for studies that report baseline characteristics only for analysed participants. The text's statement of 'no significant differences' therefore cannot be checked against all randomized patients.

The report does not say who ran the minimization or how assignments were delivered. It does state that the physician who saw patients at the initial examination 'did not know which group each patient was in' (p4 lines 13-16), and assignment followed that examination (p2 lines 120-127), so the enrolling physician appears not to have known the forthcoming allocation. Detail is sparse, so this is a judgement rather than a confirmed Yes.

The Methods state that after an initial medical examination patients 'were randomly assigned to a treatment group or a control group according to the minimization principle'. The guidance treats minimization as generally including a random element, so the sequence is answered Yes.

The result analyses patients who returned for 4-month follow-up: 45 treated and 49 control, grouped by assigned arm (p5 lines 85-88). The 2 patients who never started and the 7 who dropped out were excluded; only two of these nine could be contacted and were excluded from the analysis (p6 lines 83-94). Excluding randomized patients for missing outcome data is a modified ITT analysis, which the guidance accepts for this domain; the consequences of that missingness belong to Domain 3. The analysis is by assigned group, with no per-protocol or as-treated grouping.

The report describes no deviations from the protocol that arose from the trial context. Dropouts left the programme for patient-level reasons (addiction, smoking restriction, difficulty, neurological disease, increased pain), not because of trial recruitment or staff actions (p4 lines 1-12). Control patients 'could go anywhere else for treatment' (p4 lines 104-109), which is consistent with the usual-care comparator, not a deviation from the intended intervention. Treated patients' post-graduation training was part of the programme (p4 lines 100-103; p7 lines 23-25).

The comparator is an 'untreated control group' (p1 lines 14-17), with no sham or placebo described, so control participants knew they were not in the programme. The report also says blinding 'was broken in about 10% of the cases ... when patients disclosed this information during the follow-up examination' (p4 lines 17-21), confirming that participants knew their group.

The treated group received a 3-week programme delivered by the study team at the Copenhagen Back Center (p4 lines 22-35, 90-103), so those delivering the intervention knew which patients were in the programme. Only the physician doing the initial and 4-month examinations is described as blinded to group (p4 lines 13-16). Delivery staff were therefore not blinded.

Of 106 randomized, 94 (89%) returned for the 4-month visit (p1 lines 18-19). The analysed numbers are 45 of 55 treated and 49 of 51 control (p1 lines 14-20), so 10 treated (18%) and 2 control (4%) have no outcome data. Twelve participants, 11% of those randomized, are missing, which is above the 5% the guidance treats as small, and the missingness is unevenly distributed. Nine of the treated missing participants are the 2 who never started and 7 who dropped out, and only two of those nine could be contacted (p3 lines 101-104; p6 lines 83-94). The Figure 1 flow counts are not legible in the extracted text, so the arm-level split of the remaining missing participants is uncertain. Because 43 observed events do not greatly outnumber the 12 missing participants, the bias cannot be shown to be necessarily small, so the answer is probably no.

The report analyses only the patients who returned for follow-up (45 treated, 49 control) with a comparison of counts (p5 lines 66-79; p5 lines 85-88). It reports no imputation, no multiple imputation, no last-observation-carried-forward, no weighting, and no sensitivity analysis for the 12 participants without outcome data. The statistical methods are limited to Mann-Whitney tests and a Fisher-Irwin test for baseline work status (p5 lines 66-79). Without any missing-data method or sensitivity analysis, there is no evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data.

Three of the five reasons for a yes apply. First, the proportions of missing outcome data differ between arms, 10 of 55 (18%) treated against 2 of 51 (4%) control (p1 lines 14-20; p3 lines 101-104), a difference of eight participants, well beyond the one or two the guidance says is not by itself evidence. Second, several reported reasons among the treated dropouts relate to the outcome: increased back pain they could not accept, neurological disease, and difficulty of the programme (p4 lines 1-12). Third, reasons for missingness are reported only for the treated arm, so they cannot be compared across arms. The reasons for two never-started patients (a disk herniation while waiting and one who never appeared) are plausibly unrelated to the outcome and do not themselves establish dependence. On balance the answer is probably yes, which places the domain at High risk.

The reasons for missing outcome data given for treated participants who left the programme include strong addiction to morphine, the programme's smoking restriction, difficulty of the programme, neurological disease, and three with increased back pain they could not accept (p4 lines 1-12). Several of these could be related to the health status that the outcome, ability to work, measures. The guidance notes that loss to follow-up is usually related to health status, so dependence on the true value could not be excluded.

The physician who conducted the initial and 4-month examinations was blinded to group, and blinding was broken in about 10% of cases, equally distributed between the groups, when patients disclosed their group at follow-up (p4 lines 13-21). Work status is largely self-reported by the participant, who is the assessor for a participant-reported outcome, and participants were not blinded: the control group was untreated, so control patients knew they were not receiving the programme (p1 lines 14-17). Under the guidance, an unblinded participant makes the outcome assessor aware of the intervention received, so the answer is probably yes. The blinded examiner is a mitigating factor.

Both arms were assessed at the same 4-month follow-up examination. The control group was matched at randomization to a treated patient so that the interval from initial examination to follow-up was identical (p5 lines 73-79). The same physician saw all patients in both groups at the initial and follow-up examinations (p4 lines 13-17). Nothing suggests the arms received different numbers of opportunities to detect the outcome, so measurement is probably comparable between groups.

The guidance treats influence as more likely when there are strong beliefs about benefit or harm, when the comparator is no treatment, and when the outcome is recorded soon after treatment. Here the comparator is untreated, which raises the chance of expectation effects. However, the outcome is an employment status (full-time work, school, or seeking work) recorded about four months after a three-week programme, which the guidance notes is less likely to be influenced. The examining physician was blinded, and no report of strong expectations or belief-driven reporting is given. On balance, influence is possible but not likely, so the answer is probably no. This domain therefore gives some concerns through this question rather than high risk.

Ability to work at follow-up is largely a participant-reported status, which the guidance lists among outcomes that knowledge of the intervention received could influence. Because participants were not blinded to their group, and the outcome includes judgement categories such as 'seeking work', there is a possibility that knowledge of assignment shaped how patients reported their work status.

The outcome is ability to work at the 4-month follow-up examination, defined as having a job, being in school, or seeking work (p5 lines 80-83). That is a conventional measure of return to work that the report applies to both arms, and nothing in the report suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity. The report does not say whether this definition was pre-specified, and it does not describe the instrument used to elicit work status, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

Analysis intentions are unavailable, and more than one analysis of the same measurement was possible. The article reports unadjusted group proportions and a P value (P < .001) without stating a pre-specified primary analysis (eh_d3226c69f15d79b1). Baseline ability to work differed between groups (27% treated vs 16% control; eh_58aead5379893e48), and the article reports no baseline-adjusted analysis, although adjusted analyses of the same measurement were possible. The article states that the Fisher-Irwin test was used for the within-group change. Without the analysis intentions, the guidance answer is 'No information'.

Analysis intentions are unavailable, and the outcome domain could plausibly have been measured in more than one eligible way. The article defines workability as 'having a job, being in school, or seeking work' (eh_d3226c69f15d79b1), which is a broad composite. The same data also allow a narrower measure: the article gives full-time job counts (17 of 29 treated, 10 of 14 control; eh_d3226c69f15d79b1), so a full-time employment outcome could have been reported instead. The article does not say whether the broad definition was chosen before the data were seen. Because the intentions cannot be read and alternative measurements are possible, the guidance answer is 'No information'.

The only captured Source is the 1996 journal article. No protocol, statistical analysis plan, registry record or other dated analysis intention is among the captured Sources, so no source dated before unblinded outcome data were available can be compared with the reported analysis. The Methods describe a Mann-Whitney test and a Fisher-Irwin test on the baseline and 4-month values (eh_5c95d4185e6bc8fa), but these are described in the article itself and cannot be dated as pre-specified. Under the guidance, 'No information' applies when no source dated before outcome data could be seen specifies this measurement.

Table 1 (page 3) reports no baseline difference at P below 0.05 across the fourteen tests listed (ages, sex, work capability, days off, back pain, leg pain, ADL), with P values from 0.06 to 0.99. The text says the groups were 'largely comparable', with work capability tending to be better in the FR group. This is compatible with chance and is not evidence of a problem with randomization.

The inspected text describes minimization and the enrolment statement, but says nothing about who held the allocation sequence or how assignments were concealed from the enrolling staff (page 2, lines 65-83). Concealment cannot be judged from the report, and the guidance treats minimization as needing this information to protect against prediction.

The report states that allocation was 'randomization, or rather stratification by minimization' across the two treatments (page 2, lines 65-71). The guidance says minimization is generally implemented with a random element and should generally be considered random. The report does not say explicitly whether a random element was used when scores were equal, so 'probably yes' rather than 'yes'.

The Result is taken from the graduates analysis: Table 3 gives FR n 48 and OIT n 50, and the report states that the main conclusions were drawn from graduates who completed treatment and attended 1-year follow-up (page 2, lines 60-64; page 4). This excludes non-starters and dropouts, which is a per-protocol-type restriction on the intervention received and completed. The guidance treats such analyses as inappropriate for the effect of assignment. The report says that several intention-to-treat analyses were performed (page 4, lines 101-111), but their results are not presented for this Result, so the reported analysis cannot be treated as ITT.

The only departures reported from the protocol are the 5 FR and 6 OIT participants who did not start treatment. Reasons given were a job offer during the wait, not attending, and disc herniation in two patients (page 2, lines 84-89). These are consistent with what could happen outside the trial, not with trial-context effects such as staff or participants being steered to the other programme. The consent statement may have affected engagement, but the report gives no evidence that it changed the interventions received.

The programmes were visibly different: a full-day 3-week functional restoration programme versus 1.5-hour outpatient sessions three times a week for 8 weeks (page 2; page 4). Participants were told at inclusion that FR was not known to be more effective and that they had to accept the randomization result (page 2, lines 74-83). No placebo, sham or masking of participants is described, so participants were probably aware of their assigned programme.

Both programmes were delivered by the same staff, and the programmes differ in content and schedule (page 4, lines 67-74 of the page-4 window). No blinding of the people delivering the interventions is described. Allocation concealment is unresolved (Domain 1), so carers and staff were probably aware of assignment.

The analysis excluded about a quarter of those randomized to FR (16 of 64 derived from 59 starters plus 5 non-starters) and about a third of those randomized to OIT (24 of 74 derived from 68 plus 6). The excluded participants are reported to have worse outcomes than graduates (page 5, lines 14-20), and back pain is a subjective continuous outcome. Excluding participants whose outcome is likely to be prognostically different can substantially change the estimate, so the potential impact is probably substantial.

The Result is based on graduates who completed treatment and attended 1-year follow-up: FR n 48 and OIT n 50 (Table 3). Randomized numbers, derived from the text, are 64 FR (59 starters plus 5 non-starters) and 74 OIT (68 plus 6), so 16 of 64 (25%) FR and 24 of 74 (32%) OIT participants have no outcome in the Result. The text gives a 94% follow-up rate for graduates and a 92% overall follow-up rate for all starters (page 3, lines 16-21). Under either reading, the outcome is not available for nearly all randomized participants, which is well below the 95% that the guidance uses as a rough threshold for continuous outcomes.

The article states that several intention-to-treat analyses were performed to account for dropouts (page 4, Statistical Methods), and that the dropout analysis gave no indication of bias (page 6, lines 1-3). Neither a sensitivity analysis nor the results of the ITT analyses are presented for the Result. The statement that there was no indication of bias is not supported by reported data, so there is no evidence that the Result was unbiased by missing outcome data.

The authors report that participants who dropped out had worse outcomes than graduates (page 5, lines 14-20), which indicates that missingness is related to the outcome itself. Missing data proportions also differ between arms, 25% in FR and 32% in OIT, derived from the randomized counts and the graduate numbers (page 2, lines 84-89; Table 3), and the dropout rates during treatment differ (14% versus 19%, page 3). In a chronic low back pain population, continuing symptoms plausibly drive dropout, and the guidance lists this as a circumstance that makes dependence likely. The analysis that could have corrected for this (ITT or sensitivity analysis) is not reported.

Dropouts are described as having outcomes worse than those of the graduates (page 5, lines 14-20), and the 1-year back pain outcome is a symptom measure that is plausibly related to whether participants stay in and complete follow-up. Dropout during treatment was 14% for FR and 19% for OIT (page 3, lines 18-19). Loss to follow-up in a chronic pain population is probably related to health status, so missingness could depend on the outcome's true value.

The assessor of back pain is the participant, because it is a participant-reported outcome (section 7.1; Box 10 4.3). The physician who was blinded to treatment (about 80% successfully) discussed only a few queries and was not the source of the pain rating (page 4, Outcome Evaluation). The article does not state that participants were blinded to their program. The two programs were fundamentally different (full-day 3-week FR versus 1.5-hour OIT sessions), with no sham described, so participants were probably aware of the intervention they received.

The 1-year outcome was collected the same way for both groups: a questionnaire sent in advance and completed before a meeting at the Back Center, with a few queries discussed with a physician (page 4, Outcome Evaluation). The Source does not describe different questionnaires, thresholds or timing by arm. The FR group had more contact during treatment, but the outcome was collected at the same follow-up visit in both groups, so there is no sign of more opportunities for detection in one arm.

The guidance asks whether influence was likely, not merely possible (Box 10 4.5). The participants were told that it was not known whether FR is more effective than outpatient training, which is a neutral, equipoise message rather than a strong expectation of benefit (page 2, lines 74-80). The comparator is an active program, not no treatment, which the guidance says lowers the likelihood of influence. The outcome was rated at 1 year, well after the 3-week FR program and its follow-up days, which also makes influence less likely (section 7.3). The investigators' prior enthusiasm for FR is a possible source of expectation, but it is not documented as shaping participants' ratings.

Back pain is a participant-reported outcome, which the guidance lists as one that knowledge of the intervention received could influence (Box 10 4.4). Participants who knew they had attended a full-day intensive program, or the less intensive outpatient program, could rate their pain differently. The outcome is a subjective self-rating, so it is susceptible to expectation.

Back pain was measured on an 11-point box scale (0 = no pain, 10 = worst possible pain), averaged over the preceding 2 weeks (page 3, lines 1-6). This is a standard, pre-specified-type pain intensity scale with a range wide enough to detect a plausible difference between programs, so the method is unlikely to be insensitive to effects. The article does not validate this specific box scale, but it is a widely used format and nothing in the Source indicates poor validity.

The article states that 'several intention-to-treat analyses were performed to account for dropouts' (page 4, Statistical Methods), but Table 3 reports only the graduate analysis for back pain (page 5). The dropout analysis is described as showing no indication of bias, with 'the data not presented' (page 6, lines 1-3). Several analyses of this back-pain measurement were therefore calculated and only one reported. Whether the graduate-only analysis was chosen because of its results cannot be determined from the Source, and no analysis intentions are available. The approved target uses all randomized participants, so the population choice is an issue for Domains 2 and 3 and is not counted again here.

The back pain outcome was measured on the 11-point box scale averaged over the preceding 2 weeks (page 3, lines 1-6). The randomization covariate Manniche's rating scale (page 2) also reflects pain as one component, so the outcome domain of back pain could plausibly have been measured in more than one eligible way, and no intention document is available to show which measures were eligible or intended. Without those intentions, whether the reported 1-year box-scale result was chosen from several measures on the basis of its results cannot be determined.

No protocol, statistical analysis plan or registry record for this trial is among the captured Sources, so no dated document shows that the analysis of back pain was fixed before unblinded outcome data were available. The article says the graduate analysis was used because 'the main conclusions were drawn from these patients' (page 2), and it describes the statistical methods (page 4) without dating them. The Source therefore cannot confirm or refute a pre-specified analysis.

The report states: 'There was no significant difference between baseline variables (Table 3)' (p.6 lines 19-34). The reported baseline comparison therefore shows no imbalance suggesting a randomization problem. Table 3 itself was not separately inspected in this pass; the answer relies on the textual statement.

Allocation was made by a remote web-based service 'externally provided by the Institute of Health of Aarhus University' (p.2 lines 33-43), which is an external allocation process controlled by a unit independent of the enrolling staff. The report states 'the staff and investigators were blinded to the process' (p.2 lines 33-43). Together these meet the guidance description of a remote, centrally administered allocation (Box 4, signalling question 1.2) and support 'Yes'.

The only sequence-generation statement is that patients 'underwent a two-, four- or six-block web-based block randomization, externally provided by the Institute of Health of Aarhus University' (p.2 lines 33-43). Block randomization is described, but the report does not say that the order of allocation within the blocks was random. Per the guidance (section 4.3.1.1), blocked allocation without an explicit statement of random within-block order should generally be answered 'No information'. The trial is not a large trial reported under strict word limits that would justify a 'probably yes' inference from circumstances alone.

The analysis was 'performed using an intention-to-treat approach' (p.6 lines 19-34), and the primary LOS comparison reports the surgery-intention-to-treat population of 107 patients (50 intervention, 57 standard). A per-protocol analysis (n=100) is reported as a sensitivity check and gives the same result (p = 0.6), so the primary analysis is not per-protocol. The 22 patients rediagnosed or who reconsidered their treatment after randomization are excluded from the 107. Their missing outcome data are a Domain 3 concern rather than an inappropriate exclusion in this domain, but the reason for exclusion is not fully explained, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.

Because 2.1 (probably yes) and 2.2 (yes) are answered yes, this question is active. The main report describes standardised discharge criteria (p.4 lines 25-40) and an intention-to-treat analysis, but does not report deviations from the intended intervention arising from the trial context, such as non-protocol co-interventions or contamination, nor describe delivery and adherence in enough detail to judge them. Absence of such reporting does not establish that none occurred.

The intervention is a multiprofessional exercise-based prehabilitation and enhanced mobilisation programme (p.2 lines 9-13 design; intervention description). Such a programme cannot plausibly be delivered without the participant knowing they are receiving it, so participants were probably aware of their assigned intervention. The report does not state participant blinding explicitly.

The report states: 'Owing to the nature of multiprofessional interventions in clinical practice, the staff were not blinded to the allocation' (p.4 lines 21-24). The people delivering the intervention and the discharge decisions were therefore aware of assignment.

Of 129 randomized participants, 107 (83%) are in the surgery-intention-to-treat analysis that reports LOS; 22 (17%) were rediagnosed or reconsidered after randomization and have no reported LOS (p.2 lines 33-43; flowchart p.2 lines 49-54 and 60-91). The reported result therefore does not cover nearly all randomized participants, and the Result's intended population is all randomized participants.

The report gives no missing-data sensitivity analysis or imputation for the 22 excluded participants. A search for 'sensitivity analysis' returned only statistical wording and no missing-outcome analysis (sr_b84b750f5d807f16). The adjusted analysis (median 7 days, p=0.94) adjusts for discharge criteria, not for the excluded participants, and the per-protocol analysis (p=0.6) also excludes participants.

Three of the five reasons for Yes apply. Proportions excluded after randomization differ by arm: 15 of 65 (23%) intervention versus 7 of 64 (11%) standard (flowchart p.2 lines 49-54 and 60-91). Reported reasons differ by arm, with advanced disease recorded only in the intervention arm (8 versus none). Advanced disease and withdrawal are reasons plausibly related to the true outcome. Both arms' exclusions are pre-surgery, so it is not established that the LOS was missing for reasons unrelated to outcome.

The reasons recorded for the 22 post-randomization exclusions include advanced disease (8, intervention arm), conservative treatment (1 intervention, 2 standard), withdrawal (3 intervention, 2 standard) and reconsidered patient choice (3 in each arm) (flowchart p.2 lines 60-91). Advanced disease is a health-status reason that could plausibly relate to the postoperative LOS, so missingness of the outcome could depend on its true value.

The staff were not blinded to allocation: 'Owing to the nature of multiprofessional interventions in clinical practice, the staff were not blinded to the allocation' (p.4 lines 21-24). The discharge decision is made by the care team, so the assessor is aware of the assigned intervention. The blinding of 'staff and investigators' on p.2 lines 40-41 refers only to the randomization process.

The same discharge criteria and outcome definition were applied to both groups (p.4 lines 25-40, 53-56). The intervention arm had additional contacts (study nurse, diaries, programme documentation; p.4 lines 8-24), which could in principle add opportunities to document discharge-relevant criteria, but the report gives no sign that discharge recording or ascertainment differed between arms.

The report gives no evidence that clinicians' expectations about the intervention drove discharge decisions. The discharge criteria were standardized across both arms and recorded delays (p.4 lines 25-40). The primary result was null (median 8 days in both arms, p=0.68), and the timely-LOS analysis showed the same reduction in both groups (p.7 and p.6), which does not suggest differential influence on discharge.

Discharge is an intervention-provider decision, which the guidance lists as usually influenced by knowledge of intervention when the provider is aware (section 7.1, item 4). Staff were aware of allocation (p.4 lines 21-24), and discharge depended partly on criteria that the intervention targeted (activity achievement and PADL; p.4 lines 25-40).

The primary endpoint is postoperative days from surgery until discharge, measured with a predefined discharge checklist (PADL, nutrition, activity goals, oral medication, bowel function) and with delays recorded (p.4 lines 53-56 and 25-40). Days to discharge is a standard, appropriate measure of this outcome; the report does not suggest it is insensitive to plausible effects.

The article reports three analyses of LOS: the ITT median of 8 in both groups (p=0.68), a per-protocol analysis (p=0.6), and an analysis adjusting for discharge criteria with a median of 7 days (p=0.94) (p.6 lines 19-34). All three are reported, which is consistent with no selection, but that does not establish which analyses were intended. Without a protocol or SAP, the report does not show which analysis was pre-specified as primary. More than one analysis was possible, so the answer is no information.

The methods name the number of postoperative days from surgery to discharge as the primary endpoint (p.4 lines 53-56). They also define a second LOS measure, timely LOS, as days until the discharge criteria were met. Both measures are reported in the article: actual LOS in Table 4 and the ITT results (p.6), and timely LOS and its adjusted median of 7 days (p.6 line 34, p.7). The reported result therefore covers both eligible LOS measurements, and the result reported as primary is the one named as primary in the methods. No clear protocol or SAP is available to confirm eligibility, so this rests on the inference route in section 8.3.2 rather than on a dated plan.

No source dated before unblinded outcome data were available was captured. The only captured source is the article. The registry is cited as ClinicalTrials.gov M20100122 (p.2 lines 9-13), but the registry record, protocol and SAP are not captured, and the registration context lists no registered outcomes. The methods name LOS as the primary endpoint (p.4 lines 53-56), but nothing dates that plan before unblinded data. The discussion frames the discharge-criteria analysis as 'Auditing the present results' (p.7), which suggests it was done after the data were seen. This is not evidence of a pre-specified analysis, so the answer is no information rather than probably yes.

Table 1 (eh_af6b69bf92679ee4) shows broadly similar arms: mean age 30.5 vs 30.7 years (women) and 34.2 vs 33.9 years (men), similar BMI categories and ethnicity. The largest contrasts are smoking among women (14 (13%) vs 7 (7%)) and alcohol intake among women (19 (18%) vs 29 (27%)). These are compatible with chance and give no evidence of a randomisation problem, consistent with the guidance that a few differences are compatible with chance.

Allocation was made through an online password-protected randomisation programme after eligibility check and informed consent (eh_783832621c41d8df; eh_298098ff4c080e58). This is an internet-based allocation service that the enrolling nurse cannot see in advance, matching the guidance example of Yes for remote or internet-based randomisation. The protocol states randomisation follows consent and eligibility check.

The main report states couples were block randomized (stratified by clinic) by an online password-protected programme (eh_783832621c41d8df). The protocol describes a computer-generated randomisation scheme, 1:1 by arm and stratified by centre (eh_298098ff4c080e58). Guidance treats a computer-generated list as a random component, but also says blocked allocation without an explicit statement that order within blocks was random should generally be No information. The protocol does not state the within-block order, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.

The protocol states that couples are analysed by randomized arm, including withdrawals, which is an intention-to-treat approach (protocol p14). The main report's time-to-event analysis is a Fine and Gray model with censoring at 12 months or the Covid-19 stop (hoad036 p4), and it does not exclude randomized couples post-randomization. The Table 2 counts for the gestational-sac row are reported per arm (hoad036 p7).

The main report gives 91.5% compliance and lower app use, especially among male partners (hoad036 p6). These are non-adherence patterns that could occur outside a trial. The supplement reports Covid-19 changes that stopped the trial early and censored 80 couples (supplement p1), but it does not link any deviation from the protocol interventions to the trial context. No source reports deviations caused by consent or recruitment processes.

The main report states that after written consent couples were block randomized by an online password-protected programme and that the study was open-label, with only the statistician blinded (hoad036 p3). Participants were therefore aware of their assigned programme.

The protocol states that study nurses and the PhD student were aware of allocations (protocol p6), and the main report states the trial was open-label with only the statistician blinded (hoad036 p3). Carers and people delivering the intervention therefore knew the assigned intervention.

The Table 2 counts for the gestational-sac row (52 of 105 control, 52 of 106 intervention) are events only; no observed or unavailable count is printed for this endpoint (hoad036 p7). The supplement reports that 80 couples were censored because the study stopped for Covid-19 on 13 March 2020, and that only 51 couples completed as planned (supplement p1). Couples censored without a confirmed gestational sac lack an observed outcome for this row, so up to 80 of 211 randomized couples (about 38%) may have missing outcome data. That is more than the number of events, so the extent of missing data is large and cannot be shown to be small.

No sensitivity analysis or bias-correcting analysis for missing outcome data is reported in the passages read. The main analysis for the pregnancy outcome is a Fine and Gray model that censors couples at 12 months or at the Covid-19 stop (hoad036 p4). That approach assumes censoring is not related to the outcome, and the report gives no assumption about couples who were censored and might have become pregnant.

The discontinuation counts are balanced between arms overall (12 of 105 and 12 of 106 for IVF clinic discontinuation; Table 2), and the only notable difference is psychosocial reasons (5 control versus 3 intervention), which is small. The Covid-19 stop is an administrative date applied to all couples. Reported censoring reasons do not link missingness to pregnancy status in either arm. No differing reasons for missing outcome data between arms are reported, so missingness is not clearly likely to depend on the outcome.

Couples could leave observation for reasons linked to whether they conceived. IVF clinic discontinuation is a competing event (12 of 105 control and 12 of 106 intervention, Table 2), and psychosocial discontinuation differs slightly (5 control and 3 intervention). Couples who do not conceive may be more likely to stop IVF treatment and be lost to outcome follow-up (hoad036 p4, p7). The Covid-19 stop censored 80 couples (supplement p1), and censoring is not explicitly described as unrelated to pregnancy status.

The study was open-label; only the statistician was blinded (main report p3). The study nurses and the PhD student were aware of allocations (protocol p6). The sources do not state who confirmed the gestational sac by ultrasound, so the assessor cannot be shown to have been blinded. Following the FAQ, where the assessor's awareness is not established the answer is probably yes.

Pregnancy confirmation by ultrasound is part of routine IVF care in both arms, and the same definition applies to both arms (protocol p13; Table 2 reports both arms on the same row). The intervention added app tracking and coaching contacts (protocol p9), which could create more opportunities to detect pregnancy, but the sources do not indicate that gestational-sac confirmation was prompted by those contacts. This is likely comparable across groups.

Confirmation of an intrauterine gestational sac by ultrasound is a largely objective observer record and involves little judgement, which the guidance identifies as unlikely to be influenced by knowledge of the intervention received. The outcome is recorded at a visit that occurs in routine IVF care in both arms. The sources do not describe judgement-based assessment for this endpoint.

The approved endpoint is clinical pregnancy defined as an intrauterine gestational sac confirmed by ultrasound. The registry defines secondary outcome 7 in the same terms (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03790449), and the protocol's data definitions use the gestational sac as the implantation and clinical pregnancy marker (protocol p13). This is a standard, pre-specified clinical measure, and the sources give no reason to think ultrasound confirmation is insensitive to the effect of interest.

The reported row is a per-arm count of one binary definition. Table 2 gives no alternative analysis of this count (no adjusted, sensitivity or differently defined version), and the protocol specifies one analysis type for binary secondary outcomes (eh_aa65eb18e0866749). Nothing in the Sources suggests the count was chosen from several analyses.

The clinical-pregnancy definitions the protocol and registry describe (gestational sac, fetal heartbeat, ongoing pregnancy at 12 weeks) are all reported in Table 2 for both arms (eh_df6df6661c40d73c, eh_83a94b2495b4011a). No eligible measurement of this outcome in the report appears to have been left out. The registry's 13 registered outcomes include COPR as the primary outcome, which the report says was evaluable only in a subset (n=51) after the change to time-to-event (eh_f8bc560fcca62efb). That change is linked to the Covid-19 stop, not to results.

The protocol (p14, eh_aa65eb18e0866749) lists implantation and clinical pregnancy as binary secondary outcomes analysed like the primary outcome. The registry (eh_caf4b4939572e347, Secondary outcome 7: number of clinical pregnancies, defined as evidence of a gestational sac confirmed by ultrasound, 12 months) names this exact measurement. The registry was first submitted 2018-11-12 and the study started 2019-01-02 (eh_3eba89fe2910fcdd), so the measurement was dated before enrolment and before outcome data accrued. The report presents this row as a descriptive count consistent with that plan. The change of primary outcome from COPR to time-to-event followed the Covid-19 stop (eh_f8bc560fcca62efb), a result-independent reason that does not concern this row.

The authors state that baseline characteristics were similar between arms (their Table 1). The randomised numbers by arm (control 124, RIF35HZE 64, RIFQHZ 60, RIF20QHZ 57, RIF20MHZ 63) are close to the intended 2:1:1:1:1 ratio, with no sign of a substantial allocation-ratio imbalance. No passage reports a baseline imbalance beyond chance. A probable answer is justified by the author statement, but the table itself was not in the captured text, so 'No' is not firm.

Allocation was controlled by an external, centrally operated computerised system maintained by the MRC Clinical Trials Unit, independent of enrolling personnel. This meets the Box 4 criterion for central, remote allocation. Open-label status affects masking of participants and clinicians, which is assessed in Domain 2, not sequence concealment.

The main article states that patients were assigned centrally by a web-based computerised algorithm with a random element of 80% for minimisation, stratified on site, baseline bacterial load and HIV status. The registry record describes a probabilistic minimisation algorithm on the same strata. Minimisation with a random element is treated as random sequence generation under the Box 4 guidance.

The outcome is patients with at least one grade 3, 4, or 5 AE, and the non-protocol interruptions were for grade 2 events in 2 of 63 patients (3%) in one arm. Stopping drug for a grade 2 transaminase rise does not, by itself, determine whether a patient has a grade 3-5 AE, so the deviations are unlikely to have changed this outcome. Overall grade 3-5 AE proportions are similar across arms (11-14%, Table 4), and the direction of any effect would be uncertain.

Table 4 reports adverse events by assignment group, with denominators for the safety analysis of 123, 63, 59, 57, and 63 (total 365). The trial profile shows 124, 64, 60, 57, and 63 randomised, with 3 patients randomised in error and never started on treatment. The only exclusions are these randomised-in-error patients, which were not assignment-related and are not eligibility exclusions after randomisation, so the safety analysis is effectively an intention-to-treat analysis by assignment. The AE result is not drawn from a per-protocol or as-treated analysis.

Two patients in arm RIF35HZE had treatment interrupted for grade 2 elevated transaminases, although the protocol interruption criteria were not met (Table 4: 'Treatment changed due to hepatic AE-not fulfilling protocol criteria and not being symptomatic' 2 (3%) in RIF35HZE, 0 elsewhere). The Discussion attributes this to the unblinded design: "since clinicians were not blinded to treatment allocation this might have influenced the decision to stop treatment". Protocol-inconsistent interruptions occurring only in the arm whose clinicians knew allocation, and named by the authors as possibly allocation-influenced, support a probable answer of Yes. The authors hedge this, so the answer is not Yes.

The article states: "Because of the orange discoloration of body fluids with higher doses of rifampicin it was not possible to mask patients and clinicians to treatment allocation." Participants were therefore aware of their assigned regimen, and rifampicin-specific discoloration and side effects would make allocation apparent.

The same passage states that clinicians were not masked to allocation, and the Discussion says "clinicians were not blinded to treatment allocation". Carers and intervention providers were therefore aware of assignment. Laboratory assessments were blinded, but that concerns outcome assessment (Domain 4), not this question.

Table 4 reports the adverse event counts for a safety analysis of 365 patients: 123, 63, 59, 57 and 63 by arm. The trial profile (eh_b00d7cef0f8805d3) shows 368 randomised (124, 64, 60, 57, 63), so 3 randomised patients are absent from the safety denominator (1 control, 1 RIF35HZE, 1 RIFQHZ). The earlier Domain 2 reasoning recorded these as randomised in error and never started on treatment, so they had no adverse event exposure to record. Missing AE data is therefore at most 3 of 368 (0.8%), and an outcome count of 45 events is unlikely to change materially even if all 3 had a grade 3-5 AE. The main article states that adverse events were registered by CTCAE 4.03 with telephone follow-up at 3 and 6 months after end of treatment. The authors do not state the AE data completeness per arm, so this answer is probably yes rather than yes.

The article states: "it was not possible to mask patients and clinicians to treatment allocation. However, all laboratory assessments were done blind to treatment allocation." Laboratory-graded AEs were therefore assessed blind, but clinical events and clinician-assigned severity grades were recorded by unblinded clinicians. The Discussion confirms that "clinicians were not blinded to treatment allocation". Most grade 3-5 AEs in a trial like this would be recorded by the treating clinicians, so the assessor was probably aware of the intervention received.

All arms were registered with the same CTCAE 4.03 system and followed up in the same way: "Follow-up was done at 3 months and 6 months after end of treatment by telephone, and patients were invited to attend the clinic for assessment if feeling unwell." The arms differ in drug regimen, but the captured text does not describe different AE ascertainment or visit schedules by arm. Diagnostic detection bias would require an arm-specific reason to test more, and none is reported in the captured text.

Guidance Box 10 (4.5) says influence is likely when there are strong beliefs in beneficial or harmful effects. Here the comparator is standard active treatment, not no treatment, and the captured text reports no strong, widely held expectation that the experimental regimens would cause more grade 3-5 AEs. Much of the outcome is objective (laboratory-graded hepatic events and deaths), and it is recorded systematically through a defined CTCAE scheme with telephone and clinic follow-up. The unblinded influence described in the Discussion concerns treatment interruption for grade 2 transaminase rises, not the grade 3-5 count, so awareness is unlikely to have materially changed this outcome.

The outcome includes clinician-assigned severity grades and clinical events such as hospital admission, which involve judgement and can be influenced by knowledge of the intervention (guidance Box 10, 4.4). The Discussion notes that because "clinicians were not blinded to treatment allocation this might have influenced the decision to stop treatment". This shows that unblinded clinician decisions were a concern for this trial's safety reporting, so influence on the outcome is possible.

The main article states: "Adverse events were registered according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events 4.03 (CTCAE)." CTCAE is a standard, graded system that defines the severity scale used for the outcome (grade 3, 4 or 5). Table 4 reports patients with at least one grade 3-5 AE using this scale, and serious AE and death are separately defined. Nothing in the captured text suggests the instrument is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity, so the method is probably appropriate for a pre-specified safety outcome.

Per-arm AE counts can be analysed at several severity or category thresholds: any AE, drug-related AE, SAE, and grade 3-5 AE. The posted results report any-AE and SAE counts per arm (registry lines 525-545, eh_b3617aaafbfc5ecd). The article reports the grade 3-5 patient count as its safety Result (eh_be7bc6be7888a211) and describes the planned safety analysis as proportions of all AEs and of probably or definitely related AEs (main p6 lines 54-58, eh_498bbc69b50fa1ac). The Result is a severity-threshold analysis that differs from both the described analysis and the posted any-AE analysis, and the report gives no justification for the threshold. The grade 3-5 counts are close across arms (11% control versus 12-14% experimental), so the selection concern is one of direction and unexplained change rather than a large numerical advantage.

The registered AE measure is eligible in more than one framing: all AEs and AEs considered drug-related, both coded with standard dictionaries (registry lines 185-189, eh_555ddd5573e0b2a1). The posted results give per-arm counts of patients with at least one AE and with at least one SAE (registry lines 525-545, eh_b3617aaafbfc5ecd). The article's Table 4 reports only the grade 3-5 patient count for the AE domain (eh_be7bc6be7888a211), without all-AE or drug-related AE proportions. The posted all-AE proportions are 53/63 (84%) for RIF35HZE, 49/58 (84%) for RIFQHZ, 42/56 (75%) for RIF20QHZ, 49/63 (78%) for RIF20MHZ and 92/123 (75%) for control. Omitting the all-AE framing from the article removes the experimental-arm excess shown in the posted data, while the article concludes that experimental arms had 'similar safety profiles' (main p9, eh_33c6983116384838). That pattern is consistent with selection on the basis of the result, which is the concern in this domain.

The reported Result is patients with at least one grade 3, 4 or 5 AE (Table 4, main p8).
