The only pre-specified description of AE analysis in the captured sources does not describe that grade-threshold count. The registry registers 'Frequency of Adverse Events' over 0-12 weeks, covering all AEs and drug-related AEs, with no grade threshold (registry lines 185-189, eh_555ddd5573e0b2a1). The article Methods state that safety was presented as 'the proportion of adverse events and the proportion of adverse events assessed by the investigators as probably related or related to treatment' (main p6 lines 54-58, eh_498bbc69b50fa1ac). The grade 3-5 patient count is therefore not the analysis described in either pre-specified source, and the report gives no reason for the difference. AEs were classified by CTCAE 4.03 (main p5, eh_1b81c6242fb8aba1), which supports a standard grade basis for the threshold but does not show it was pre-specified as the analysed result.

Baseline Table 1 shows similar sex, smoking, complications, medication and age, height, weight, blood pressure and heart rate between arms (for example female 19% vs 19%, age 62.4 vs 62.9 years). Among the baseline Table 2 variables, only VWF differed at P = 0.01 unadjusted, and it became P = 0.07 after adjustment. A single significant baseline difference is compatible with chance and is not evidence of a randomization problem.

The report says only that patients were randomly allocated and that the trial was double-blind with central laboratory analysis. It does not describe who held the allocation sequence, how assignments were delivered, or whether they were concealed until enrolment. Bounded lexical searches for allocation and central-allocation wording returned only the same Methods text and the phrase central laboratory analysis, so the circumstances support neither probably_yes nor probably_no.

Methods state patients were randomly allocated using a "randomized permuted block allocation rule". Permuted blocks imply a random order within blocks, but the report does not name the generator (computer, table, etc.), so probably_yes rather than yes.

The Methods state analyses were on an intention-to-treat basis, but the eight warfarin users were excluded from all thrombotic and CRP comparisons. Those eight were randomized and eligible, and the exclusion is post-randomization and based on a co-intervention, not on missing outcome data. The analysed numbers (85 aspirin and 91 clopidogrel of 184) show the remaining randomized participants were kept in the analysis.

The report describes protocol-inconsistent use of the other drug: eight clopidogrel patients (9%) took aspirin, mostly for short periods (median 2 days), and one aspirin patient took clopidogrel for 15 days. Aspirin was given to all on admission. No cause is reported that suggests the trial context drove these changes, and the authors state there was very little cross-contamination. These look like ordinary non-adherence or usual clinical care outside the trial context.

The summary and Methods describe a randomized, double-blind trial, so participants were presumably unaware of their assignment. The report does not describe placebo matching and does not say whether any side effects were known to be specific to one drug.

The report says the trial was double-blind but does not say who was masked (carers or people delivering the interventions) or how. Allocation concealment is not described either (see the randomization Domain), so carer awareness cannot be judged from the report.

Eight of 184 randomized participants (4%) were excluded, five aspirin and three clopidogrel, a near balance. The stated reason is warfarin's interference with laboratory assays rather than a prognostic or outcome-related factor. A substantial impact on the 6-month fibrinogen comparison therefore seems unlikely.

Figure 1 and the Results text give 184 randomized and 151 (82%) completing 6 months (aspirin 72 of 90; clopidogrel 79 of 94), so 33 randomized participants (18%) did not complete, including 8 deaths and 25 discontinuations. That is far from 'nearly all' for a continuous outcome, where about 95% is the usual threshold. The 6-month analysis used 85 aspirin and 91 clopidogrel participants, which exceeds the non-warfarin completers (about 150). The source does not say how many analysed participants had a 6-month sample, so the observed-outcome count cannot be confirmed.

The report gives no sensitivity analysis and no imputation or model-based handling of the missing 6-month outcomes. Analyses are described as intention-to-treat with exclusion of warfarin users, which is complete-case-like for missing outcomes. Two bounded searches found no matching text, but a no-hit receipt does not establish absence; the Methods and Results sections were read in full and state no such analysis.

Non-completion is similar by arm (aspirin 18 of 90, 20%; clopidogrel 15 of 94, 16%), and the reported reasons are not split by arm, so reason 3 cannot be assessed. Deaths and adverse events are health-related, but nothing in the report links missingness to the fibrinogen value itself, and no circumstance of this trial makes fibrinogen-driven dropout likely. Of the five reasons in the guidance, none is clearly met.

Reasons for not completing 6 months include adverse events (14), death (8) and consent withdrawn or lost to follow-up. These reflect participants' health and treatment tolerance, so missingness could depend on the true value of the 6-month fibrinogen, the acute-phase marker that this trial measured after MI.

The report says 'double-blind' and 'central laboratory analysis' but does not say whether the laboratory staff or any outcome assessor were masked to treatment. The guidance says to answer No information (or assume awareness) when nothing states who was masked.

All samples were analysed at one central laboratory using the same assays, with plasma stored locally at -40 C and transferred to Glasgow within 3 months. Measurement methods and timing were therefore comparable across arms, so no differential detection is apparent.

Every outcome here is a laboratory assay that produces a numerical value with no clinical judgement involved. Knowledge of assignment is unlikely to influence such an assay even if the laboratory staff were aware of the treatment.

Clauss clotting-rate fibrinogen, immunonephelometric assays, ELISAs for D-dimer, t-PA and VWF, a one-stage FVIII assay and high-sensitivity immunonephelometry for CRP are standard, pre-specified laboratory methods. The report gives no sign that these methods are insensitive to plausible effects or lack validity for the outcome.

The Methods describe unadjusted t-tests and general linear models adjusted for age, sex, weight, height, blood pressure, smoking, month of infarct and time from infarct, with transformations. Table 2 reports both unadjusted (column 1) and adjusted (column 2) P-values, and reports both final values and baseline-to-final differences. The reported Clauss result therefore sits alongside the other analyses the Methods describe, and the report contains no sign of a subset of analyses chosen for their results.

The Methods say the thrombotic variables and CRP were measured, including fibrinogen by both Clauss and immunonephelometric methods, D-dimer, VWF, FVIII, t-PA and CRP. Table 2 reports baseline, final and difference values with P-values for every one of these, plus plasma viscosity. The abstract states no between-group difference for any variable at 6 months. Under the section 8.3.2 inference approach, the reported Clauss result is not one subset selected from a larger set of reported measurements, and the trial's null findings across all measurements argue against selection on significance.

Only the main article is captured. The Methods (eh_f173d20a01257bef) describe the power calculation for Clauss fibrinogen, the t-tests and general linear models, the transformations, and the warfarin exclusion, but give no date and no statement that a plan was finalized before unblinded outcome data were available. No protocol, SAP or registry record is captured, so no source dated before outcome data could be seen specifies this measurement and analysis.

Table 1 reports baseline characteristics for all 10,142 randomized participants, with closely matched means and proportions between canagliflozin (N=5795) and placebo (N=4347) across age, sex, race, cardiovascular history, eGFR, HbA1c, blood pressure and albuminuria. The main text states baseline characteristics were balanced. Group sizes are consistent with the intended allocation ratios (1:1:1 in CANVAS and 1:1 in CANVAS-R) when the two trials are combined, so there is no sign of a substantial deviation from intended allocation. No imbalance is apparent that would indicate a problem with the randomization process.

Allocation was made centrally through an interactive web-based response system (main article), and the protocol states that the randomization code linking randomization numbers to treatment groups was maintained within the IVRS/IWRS and not provided to investigators except for emergency unblinding. Study drugs were identical in appearance and packaging. This is remote, centrally administered allocation controlled by a unit independent of enrolment staff, which meets the minimal criteria for adequate concealment.

The main article states that randomization used a computer-generated randomization schedule with randomly permuted blocks, prepared by the trial sponsor and delivered through a central interactive web-based response system. A computer-generated random component with permuted blocks meets the RoB 2 criterion for a random sequence.

The main article states that the primary hypothesis test used the full integrated data set of all participants who underwent randomization, with the intention-to-treat approach. The intention-to-treat analysis set counts one participant who was randomized at two sites only once, at the first randomization.

The main article states that participants and all trial staff were unaware of individual treatment assignments until completion of the trial. The protocol describes identical study drug and identical containers and packaging, so the blinding was designed to hide allocation from participants.

The same passage states that all trial staff were unaware of individual treatment assignments until completion of the trial. Protocol passages describe IWRS-controlled randomization codes withheld from investigators except for emergency unblinding, and identical study drug, supporting blinding of carers and personnel.

The main article reports that 9,734 of 10,142 randomized participants (96.0%) completed the trial, meaning they were alive and assessed for safety and efficacy outcomes during the final follow-up window or died before it, and that vital status was confirmed for 10,100 (99.6%). The primary outcome was analysed as a time-to-event composite using all available follow-up in the full integrated data set, so participants lost to follow-up contribute follow-up until censoring rather than being dropped. The proportion without complete follow-up (about 4%) is small relative to the total randomized population, supporting that nearly all participants had outcome data.

The protocol states that blinding to treatment allocation is maintained for subjects, investigators, the Endpoint Adjudication Committee and sponsor site monitoring personnel throughout the study, and that the committee is composed of external specialists blinded to treatment. The main article states that participants and all trial staff were unaware of individual treatment assignments until trial completion. Outcome assessors for this composite (the adjudication committee and the blinded investigators) were therefore unaware of assignment.

The protocol describes a single independent, externally staffed Endpoint Adjudication Committee that classifies events in both arms using the same charter-defined endpoint definitions, while blinded to treatment. Because the same adjudication applies to both groups, differential ascertainment by method or threshold is unlikely. The main article describes the outcome as pre-specified with identical definitions across arms.

The approved outcome is a pre-specified composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI and nonfatal stroke. The protocol states that the Endpoint Adjudication Committee classifies only prespecified endpoint events using a charter-defined methodology, so the measurement method is a standard, pre-specified endpoint ascertainment process. Nothing in the inspected passages suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity.

The primary intention-to-treat analysis is the reported result; the imputation sensitivity analysis gives the same conclusion (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.97), and the testing sequence is prespecified. Integrated analyses are reported as separate exploratory analyses.

The inspected passages show one protocol-defined primary composite (MACE) with the primary endpoint unchanged, and other composites are presented as secondary or exploratory outcomes rather than alternative definitions of the same primary outcome.

The reported composite (MACE) was the CANVAS primary endpoint and the protocol-stated primary endpoint, which the integrated SAP states was not changed. The sponsor's later integrated SAP revision added mortality endpoints, so the approval date of the integrated SAP relative to unblinded data is not confirmed.

Page 5 (Analysis) states that 'the treatment groups were well matched with respect to age, sex, race, and cardiovascular risk factors'. Table 4 (page 4) shows near-equal group sizes (9599 clopidogrel vs 9586 aspirin) and similar baseline characteristics across all patients and subgroups. The visible differences (for example in the MI and PAD subgroups) are small and compatible with chance; no imbalance in key prognostic factors large enough to suggest a randomization failure is reported.

Page 4 (Assignment and Blinding) reports that the randomisation code was restricted to the Independent Statistical Centre, the chairman of the External Safety and Efficacy Monitoring Committee and two drug-preparing companies, and that a copy of the scheme was deposited with a public notary. Study drugs were supplied in blister packs that were 'indistinguishable from one another', packaged 'in a predetermined order in a carton that contained supplies for four patients', with a sealed treatment code label retained at the centre. These features make it unlikely that enrolling staff could know the forthcoming assignment, but the report does not state that allocation was remote or centrally administered at enrolment, that containers were sequentially numbered, or that cartons were opened only after irreversible assignment. Full Yes criteria cannot be confirmed from the text, so Probably yes is the best-supported answer.

Page 4 (Assignment) states the Independent Statistical Centre provided 'computer-generated balanced blocks of four treatments with random allocation to clopidogrel or aspirin, stratified by clinical centre and the three disease subgroups.' A computer-generated random allocation with a random element satisfies the Yes criterion.

Page 3 (Analysis plan) states that the primary analysis was 'an intention-to-treat analysis in which all patients randomised were considered at risk to their planned end of study, irrespective of their compliance with study protocol'. Page 5 reports the primary result on 'all patients randomised' with 19185 patients analysed intention-to-treat, and states that the 42 lost to follow-up were included with follow-up censored at last contact and that 4059 early permanent discontinuations were not censored. Sixteen patients found not to have the qualifying disease were also kept in the analyses as randomised. This is an intention-to-treat analysis in the assigned groups, which the guidance treats as appropriate.

Page 4 (Blinding) describes study drug supplied as 'blister packs containing either 75 mg tablets of clopidogrel plus aspirin placebo tablets or 325 mg aspirin tablets plus clopidogrel placebo tablets, such blister packs being indistinguishable from one another', so each arm received matched placebo for the other drug. Page 8 states 'the blinding was well maintained'. Participants were therefore probably not aware of their assignment. The report does not state whether participants were asked or could recognise their treatment from side effects, which could partly unblind them (page 7 reports rash and diarrhoea differences), so Probably no rather than No.

Page 4 (Blinding) reports identical, indistinguishable blister packs supplied from a predetermined order, with a sealed treatment code retained at the centre for emergency use only, and 21 (0.11%) code breaks during the study. Page 8 states that 'the blinding was well maintained' and that code breaks at the clinical centres were small in number. Carers and people delivering the interventions were therefore not expected to know assignments, and nothing in the report suggests that blinding of personnel failed.

Figure 2 (participant progress, eh_26e09897ca20eafd) reports 42 patients lost to follow-up in total (22 clopidogrel, 20 aspirin) against 19185 randomized, with 9577 and 9566 completing the trial. The abstract (eh_65d7678deabd0d40) reports 1960 first events in the outcome cluster. Missing outcome participants (42) are far fewer than observed events (1960), so their outcomes could have made no important difference to the estimate (RoB 2 guidance section 6.1.4 and Box 8, 3.1). The 4059 early permanent discontinuations were not censored in the ITT analysis, so they are counted as observed outcome data under the ITT population. Only the Results statement and Figure 2 are used; the per-arm censoring timing is not separately reported.

Outcome events were assessed by the Central Validation Committee, which was separate from treating investigators: each event was reviewed independently by two members, and only the secretariat communicated with the reporting investigator (page 3, lines 88-104). The report states that blinding was well maintained (page 8, lines 26-28), and the active comparator was delivered in identical blister packs (page 4, eh_86be71f6694dd69d). The passages do not explicitly state that the Central Validation Committee reviewers were unaware of assignment, so this answer relies on the general blinding statement and the independence of the adjudication process.

Follow-up visits were scheduled identically in both arms (monthly for the first 4 months, then every 4 months; page 2, lines 59-63), and every reported non-fatal event was validated by the same Central Validation Committee under the same process (page 3, lines 88-104). No passage reports differing ascertainment, extra visits or diagnostic testing in one arm, so measurement or detection is unlikely to have differed between groups.

The outcome is a pre-specified composite of centrally validated ischaemic stroke, MI and vascular death, with fatal events classified by the Central Validation Committee (page 3, lines 88-104; page 5 Results). Nothing in the inspected passages suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity, so the screening question is answered No/Probably no, consistent with RoB 2 guidance for pre-specified outcomes.

The report presents several analyses of the primary cluster: the primary unadjusted ITT analysis with Cox relative-risk reduction of 8.7% (page 5, lines 49-59), an adjusted analysis for prognostic baseline variables that gave estimates virtually unchanged (page 5, lines 68-70), and an on-treatment analysis giving 9.4% (abstract, page 1). All are reported, and the adjusted analysis agrees with the primary result, which is evidence against selection among analyses. The requested result is the ITT primary analysis, which the report designates as primary.

The requested outcome is the primary ischaemic stroke, MI or vascular death cluster. Table 6 (page 5, lines 76-151) reports this primary cluster together with the four predefined secondary clusters, including amputation-containing, vascular-death, any stroke/MI/death, and all-cause death. The report presents all these clusters without any visible omission, and the text says the secondary clusters were predefined (page 5, lines 62-67). Reporting every stated cluster is evidence against selection of the primary cluster from several outcome definitions, but it is not confirmed against a dated plan.

The Sources contain only the 1996 Lancet report. The report states the primary analysis was intention-to-treat (page 5, lines 49-52) and refers to four predefined secondary outcome clusters (page 5, lines 62-63), but no protocol, SAP, registry entry or other dated document is among the Sources. Under the guidance, no source dated before unblinded outcome data were available specifies this measurement and analysis, so the plan's finalization cannot be dated.

Table 2 (p4) compares the 61 BTB and 60 BTB-LET knees at inclusion. Group sizes are close to the intended 1:1 ratio. Every reported baseline P value is at or above .30: age at inclusion .84, age at last follow-up .39, posterior tibial slope .30, sex .32, sports participation .96, medial meniscal tear .31, lateral meniscal tear .51. This is consistent with chance, and no excess of significant differences or key prognostic imbalance is reported.

No passage describes how assignments were delivered or protected from enrolling staff. The text says only 'Unblinded block randomization at inclusion' (p2, lines 76-77). Searches for 'envelope' and 'concealed' returned no hits, and 'allocation' returned only the same sentence. RoB 2 guidance (section 4.3.2) expects a judgement when details are rarely reported, but the article gives no basis for a probable answer: nothing indicates central or remote allocation, sealed or numbered envelopes, or drug containers. With unblinded block allocation and no stated block size, last-allocation predictability cannot be excluded.

The only methods statement on allocation is 'Unblinded block randomization at inclusion of the 121 knees' (p2, lines 76-77). It names blocked allocation and a randomization label but does not say how the sequence was generated or that the order within blocks was random. RoB 2 guidance section 4.3.1.1 says blocked allocation without an explicit statement of random order should generally be answered No information. The searches for 'random' hit only the title, abstract, this sentence and the discussion, and none describes a generator, table or permuted-block procedure. The circumstances (single-centre trial, 1998-1999, unblinded) do not support a probable answer.

The analysis compares BTB with BTB-LET by assigned group (Table 4, p5), which is a group-based comparison. However, the analysed population is 80 knees with patient-reported outcome data, excluding 40 knees lost to follow-up (p4, Table 3) and one patient who had a total knee replacement at 18 years and 'was excluded from the analysis' (p4, lines 3-12). Excluding missing outcome data is a modified-ITT approach that Domain 3 assesses. Excluding a randomized, post-randomization participant whose outcome could have been measured, without reporting that the outcome was unmeasurable, is inappropriate under RoB 2 section 5.3, and the report does not say the knee's IKDC was unavailable. So the exclusion is not a clean ITT-type analysis.

The report describes the surgical technique (p2-p3) and the outcome schedule but does not describe postoperative rehabilitation, co-interventions, adherence to the assigned graft or tenodesis, or crossover between groups. Searches for 'rehabilitation' and 'crossover' and 'intention' returned no hits. Nothing in the captured text shows whether deviations arose from the trial context, and the report does not describe delivery and co-interventions well enough to judge whether such deviations occurred.

The trial was unblinded: the randomization is described as 'Unblinded block randomization at inclusion' (p2, lines 76-77). The two groups differ visibly in surgery (isolated intra-articular BTB ACLR versus BTB plus an extra-articular gracilis tenodesis with an incision extended to Gerdy tubercle, p3). Participants undergoing a different operation would be aware of their assigned intervention.

The same unblinded design (p2, lines 76-77) means surgeons and the people delivering the interventions were not masked to the assigned group. The procedures differ in their operative steps (p3: an extra-articular tenodesis was added in the BTB-LET group), so the surgical team could not be blinded to which operation was performed. No blinding of carers or surgeons is described.

Only one post-randomization exclusion (one TKA patient) is reported, out of 121 randomized knees (1 of 81 with follow-up). Its effect on the between-group comparison of subjective IKDC is small relative to the 10-point minimum clinically important difference the trial itself used (p3). A single knee cannot plausibly shift the group means or the P value to a substantial degree, although the direction is unknown.

The approved Result is the Table 4 subjective IKDC comparison at 19.4 years (n = 80). The randomized denominator is 121 knees (61 BTB, 60 BTB-LET). p4 states that 41 patients (34%) were lost to follow-up, and only 79 patients (80 knees) completed the PRO questionnaire. Table 3 gives 80 available and 40 lost. Roughly one third of randomized knees lack the outcome, which is far from 'nearly all' for a continuous outcome (guidance threshold about 95%). The sources disagree by one patient (40 vs 41 lost) and on 80 patients vs 79 completing PRO, but either count leaves about a third missing.

No sensitivity analysis, imputation, weighting or other missing-data correction is reported for the IKDC comparison. The analysis is a complete-case comparison of 80 patients by group (Table 4). The bounded searches for 'sensitivity analysis' and 'imputation' returned no hits, and the Statistics section describes Fisher, t and Mann-Whitney tests with no missing-data method. The paper gives no assumptions about the outcomes of participants who were lost, so there is no evidence that the result was robust to missing data.

Of the five reasons for a Yes answer, none is directly established. Reason 1: the arm-level proportions missing can only be approximated (about 31% BTB versus 37% BTB-LET, from mixed denominators of knees and patients), and the difference is small and not tested by the authors. Reasons 2 and 3: no reasons for missingness are reported, so they cannot differ between arms. Reason 4: the circumstances do not clearly make dependence likely. Reason 5: the PRO outcome is not a time-to-event analysis. Table 3 shows no significant baseline differences between patients available and lost. These findings support a 'could' rather than a 'likely' dependence, so the answer is probably no, with uncertainty.

Loss to follow-up in a 19-year cohort with a patient-completed questionnaire could plausibly relate to health status. The authors describe 'the extensive loss to follow-up' (p3) and report that patients returned for on-site evaluation only if willing (p3), and 34% were lost (p4). Patients with graft failure had lower subjective IKDC scores (p4), so missingness among patients with poor knee function is a plausible mechanism. The reasons for loss to follow-up are not reported in the captured text.

For a patient-completed questionnaire the participant is the outcome assessor (Full guidance section 7.1). The article states that the trial was unblinded at randomization, and the LET arm involved a visibly different operation (gracilis harvest and an extended femoral incision, eh_10c8ea5acb46dae4), so participants probably knew their assigned group. The article does not state whether the independent examiner who recorded the scores was blinded to group, and no blinding statement was found.

All patients completed the same subjective IKDC questionnaire at the same 19-year follow-up, administered by an examiner independent of the surgeon (eh_10c8ea5acb46dae4, p3). No difference in measurement method, threshold or timing between the BTB and BTB-LET groups is reported, and the LET arm's extra surgery does not create extra opportunities to record a questionnaire score.

Influence is likely only when there are strong beliefs about benefit or harm (Box 10, question 4.5). The comparator is an active intervention (isolated BTB), not usual care or no treatment, and the questionnaire was completed about 19 years after surgery, when the effect of the procedure is unlikely to be salient to participants. The article reports no strong expectation about LET and no evidence of participant belief. Awareness alone does not make influence likely. This supports 'could but no reason to believe it did' (Some concerns).

Participant-reported outcomes such as the subjective IKDC can be influenced by knowledge of the intervention received (Full guidance Box 10, question 4.4). Because the participant completed the questionnaire and was probably aware of the assigned group (see 4.3), influence on the score is possible.

The approved Result uses the subjective IKDC, a patient-completed questionnaire that the authors pre-specified as the primary outcome (eh_10c8ea5acb46dae4, p3). The same instrument was used for both groups at the same time point, and the source does not describe any problem with its validity or sensitivity for this comparison.

The Statistics section describes a conditional choice of test: Student t tests or Mann-Whitney tests depending on normality, Fisher exact tests for categorical data and a log-rank test for survival (eh_10c8ea5acb46dae4). The article reports one unadjusted between-group P value for subjective IKDC (P = .7, eh_438daef10f05cb8d). It does not state which test produced that P value, or whether adjusted, change-score or alternative analyses were run. Several eligible analyses of this measurement were plausible, and the analysis intentions are not captured, so the question cannot be answered from a plan.

The methods name subjective IKDC as the primary outcome and Lysholm, forgotten knee score, graft failure and osteoarthritis as secondary outcomes (eh_10c8ea5acb46dae4). Table 4 reports subjective IKDC, Lysholm and forgotten knee scores for all 80 patients in the two groups with P values (eh_438daef10f05cb8d), and the text states that none of the three differed significantly between groups (eh_0504885fdf114acc). So every eligible patient-reported measure in the outcome domain is fully reported, and the reported subjective IKDC is the one stated as primary. The approved target is the 19-year time point. The earlier 2-month to 2-year follow-ups fall outside it and were not published (eh_10c8ea5acb46dae4), so they cannot be a selection among eligible 19-year measurements.

The article calls subjective IKDC the primary outcome and reports a power analysis for it, but these statements are in the undated methods of the report (eh_10c8ea5acb46dae4). No protocol, SAP or registry record is among the captured Sources. The searches for 'registered' and 'statistical analysis plan' returned zero hits. The short- and medium-term follow-ups were presented only as meeting communications, so an earlier plan may exist, but none is captured. No source dated before unblinded outcome data were available specifies this measurement and analysis.

Table 1 reports baseline characteristics and P values for the 18 participants analysed at 6 months (9 per group). The footnote and the sex counts (6/3 and 5/4) confirm that the baseline data cover only analysed participants. No baseline data are reported for the 20 randomized participants, so the randomization process cannot be checked against group sizes or baseline balance in the full cohort. Among the reported comparisons, no P value is below .147, which is compatible with chance.

Randomization was performed by selecting and opening a sealed envelope containing the assigned procedure just after the surgeon arthroscopically diagnosed the ACL tear (p2). Registry record states final randomization occurred after intraoperative grading, so assignment followed eligibility confirmation and consent. Sealed envelopes opened after eligibility are a concealment safeguard, but the article does not state whether envelopes were opaque or sequentially numbered, and the surgeons who enrolled participants also introduced the allocation sequence.

The article states that patients were randomly assigned and that surgeons introduced 'the random allocation sequence' (p2). The registry record also states that participants were randomly assigned. Neither source describes the sequence-generation method (for example computer-generated numbers or blocks), so a random element is stated but not specified. The reporting team is an experienced academic surgical group, which makes a random sequence probable rather than merely unknown.

The abstract states that all participants were randomly assigned, and the statistical comparison of SSD values between groups was a Mann-Whitney U test. The analysed sample at 6 months was 9 per group (18 total), and the two patients who withdrew before 6 months account for the difference from the 20 enrolled. This is consistent with a modified intention-to-treat analysis that excludes participants with missing outcome data, which the guidance treats as appropriate. The article does not report the number randomized per group, so the analysed set cannot be confirmed against the full randomized set.

Because surgeons and participants were probably not blinded, the question is active. The passages read so far do not report any non-protocol intervention, co-intervention, or rehabilitation difference between the arms, and do not state whether any deviation arose from the trial context. The Discussion limitation about rehabilitation has not been located in the passages read.

The registry record lists masking as NONE, and the article describes allocation being opened in the operating room after the tear was diagnosed, with the procedure then assigned. Because the LET adds a separate tenodesis to the ACLR, participants in the two arms were likely able to tell which procedure they had received. The article does not explicitly state whether participants were blinded, so this is an inference from the design and the registry record.

The article states that surgeons and their clinical team introduced the allocation sequence, enrolled participants and assigned them to interventions, and that allocation was revealed by opening a sealed envelope during surgery. The surgeons who performed the procedures therefore knew the assigned intervention. The registry record lists masking as NONE.

Methods state that 20 patients were included and that 2 patients withdrew before 6 months; 18 (9 per group) completed 6-month kinematic testing, so 10% of enrolled participants lack the 6-month outcome. For a continuous outcome the guidance regards data from about 95% of participants as often sufficient, so 90% availability does not establish 'nearly all'. The per-arm randomized counts are not reported, so the arm-specific proportions cannot be checked.

The passages read describe a complete-case analysis of the 18 participants who completed 6-month testing (Mann-Whitney U test of SSD values). No sensitivity analysis, imputation, or weighting for the two withdrawals is described, so there is no evidence that the result is robust to plausible values of the missing outcomes.

The article reports that two patients withdrew before 6 months, but gives neither the reasons for withdrawal nor the arm in which each withdrawal occurred. Without reasons or arm-specific counts, the proportions and reasons cannot be compared between groups, and the circumstances do not establish a likely dependence. The answer is No information, not a finding of dependence or independence.

The two withdrawals before 6 months are unexplained in the article. Withdrawal from a post-operative knee kinematics study could plausibly relate to knee function, symptoms or the patient's recovery, so missingness could depend on the true value of the outcome. The guidance notes this is usually the case for loss to follow-up.
The article describes the kinematic testing and tracking procedure but gives no statement on whether the people collecting or registering the data were blinded to allocation.
Both groups underwent identical kinematic testing at the same laboratory, at the same time points and with the same protocol, so measurement is not described as differing by group.

The outcome is a kinematic variable computed from biplane radiographs by an automated model-based tracking technique, which involves little clinical judgement and is unlikely to be influenced by knowledge of allocation.

Kinematics were measured by dynamic biplane radiography with a validated volumetric model-based tracking technique, stated accuracy better than 0.7 mm, so the method is sensitive to the ATT differences reported.

The Methods describe the SSD at each 10% gait-cycle instant, compared between groups by Mann-Whitney U tests, with repeated-measures ANOVA across instants. The Results report only the 0% instant as significant at 6 months, and the Methods report no adjustment for multiple comparisons across instants and time points. This suggests the reported analysis may have been selected from several eligible analyses of the same measurement on the basis of its significance.

The Methods define the primary kinematic variables as ATT and TR over the initial 40% of the gait cycle and state that SSDs were calculated at each 10% increment, at 6 and 12 months. The Results and Abstract report a single instant, 0% at 6 months, as significant, and the Conclusion rests on it. Other instants and time points are reported as non-significant or are not highlighted. This pattern of one reported instant among many eligible ones suggests selection on the results, but no protocol or SAP is available to confirm it.

The only pre-specified source is the ClinicalTrials.gov record, which was first submitted on 2016-09-16 with a start date of 2016-01, so it was filed after enrolment began and cannot show what was fixed before unblinded data were available. No protocol or SAP is among the Sources, and the report's Methods do not cite a dated analysis plan.

Group sizes (97 intervention, 93 control) are close to the intended 1:1 allocation. Baseline characteristics are reported for all 190 randomised participants. Several differences are visible in Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1, for example intracranial haemorrhage 35.1% vs 24.7%, septic shock 6.2% vs 14.0%, ischaemic heart disease 15.5% vs 26.9%, and male sex 60.8% vs 69.9%. With about 95 per group, differences of this size are compatible with chance, and no baseline P values are reported that would indicate a substantial excess of significant imbalances or an imbalance in a key prognostic factor unlikely to be due to chance.

The main article states that allocation was made through a web-based randomisation service generated by an independent statistician and that allocation concealment was maintained until completion of randomisation. A remote, centrally administered allocation service independent of enrolment staff meets the guidance's criteria for Yes. The protocol states that allocation concealment will be maintained until registration and randomisation is completed, which is consistent with the report.

Methods state that subjects were randomised 1:1 with variable blocks of 4 and 6, stratified by site, via a web-based randomisation service generated by an independent statistician. A statistician-generated web randomisation sequence implies a computer-generated random component, so Probably yes rather than Yes. The passage does not explicitly say that the order within blocks was random.

The analysis is described as intention-to-treat, which is the appropriate approach. However, two randomised control patients were excluded after randomisation (one DNR order and one intubated in the operating room), and the mortality percentages imply a control denominator of 88, not 93. Excluding randomised participants whose death could still be measured is not consistent with a full ITT analysis, so the analysis cannot be confirmed as appropriate for this outcome.

The report gives no description of protocol deviations arising from the trial context. Table 3 records that most patients continued with their allocated oxygenation (15/97 and 13/93 reported as continued with allocated group, with one change to other oxygenation in the intervention arm), which is consistent with ordinary clinical management rather than context-driven non-adherence.
The Methods describe an open-label randomised trial and state that blinding of the ED team and patient was not possible because of the intervention, so participants knew their allocation.
The ED team that delivered the preoxygenation and apnoeic oxygenation intervention was not blinded, so they knew participants' allocation. Blinding applied only to the admitting ICU clinicians.

Two randomised control patients were excluded, one with a DNR order and one intubated in the operating room, and the mortality denominator implies a further shortfall. The DNR exclusion is strongly prognostic for death, and the control arm has only 21 deaths, so excluding two patients (and possibly five more) could substantially change the mortality estimate.

The report says all 97 intervention and 93 control patients were included in the ITT population. However, the mortality percentages imply a control denominator of 88 (21/88 = 23.9%), so about five control patients appear to lack mortality data. Mortality events total 45 across both arms, so five missing control patients is not a trivial number relative to the events, and the missingness is unexplained.

The analysis is described as intention-to-treat, adjusted for study site with a van Elteren test. No sensitivity analysis or missing-data method for the mortality outcome is reported in the inspected main-report passages, so there is no evidence the result was protected against missing-outcome bias.

Missingness is likely to depend on the outcome. The reported exclusion of a control patient with a DNR order after randomisation is a reason strongly related to death. The implied shortfall of control denominators (93 to 88) appears only in the control arm, so missingness is likely differential between the groups.

The outcome is death. Missingness for a mortality outcome can plausibly depend on the outcome itself: deaths in the ED and ICU, and patients with DNR orders, are the kind of patients most likely to be lost from a mortality count. The report records a DNR order and an operating-room intubation among excluded control patients, and Table 3 shows deaths in the ED and before discharge.

The main report states that blinding of the ED team and the patient was not possible, and that only clinicians in the admitting ICUs were blinded. Death on discharge is recorded by treating clinicians, so the assessors were at least partly aware of allocation.

Table 3 reports discharge deaths for both arms in the same ITT framework, with no indication that ascertainment differed by arm. The protocol describes electronic follow-up for the trial, which applies to both groups, though it is not confirmed as the discharge-mortality source.

Knowledge of allocation is unlikely to influence a recorded death before discharge, which involves no judgement by the observer, consistent with the guidance that all-cause mortality is unlikely to be influenced.

Mortality on discharge is an all-cause, observer-recorded clinical outcome that does not involve judgement, so a standard measurement method is unlikely to be unsuitable for it. The main report and registry give no sign of a measurement instrument with poor validity or insensitivity to plausible effects.

Table 3 contains two discharge-death rows with different counts: 'Died on discharge' 23 (24.7) vs 17 (19.3), and 'Mortality on discharge' 24 (25.8) vs 21 (23.9), reported with the adjusted RR 1.08. The protocol gives no analysis for mortality, and no SAP is available. The denominators do not reconcile, so it cannot be determined whether these are alternative eligible analyses or different populations or definitions.

Table 3 reports mortality at several time points (died in ED, mortality in ICU, and mortality on discharge), so no time point was omitted from the report. All-cause mortality on discharge is a single outcome measure with no alternative scales, and the protocol names only that measure as the secondary endpoint.

The protocol names in-hospital mortality on discharge as a secondary endpoint, and it predates enrolment. Its statistical section, however, describes only a t-test or non-parametric comparison for lowest SpO2, Fisher's exact test for categorical data, and regression only if important imbalances arise. It does not specify the site-stratified van Elteren test or the adjusted risk ratio used for mortality in Table 3. The registry, first submitted 2018-01-01, does not list mortality at all. The reported analysis therefore departs from the dated plan without a stated reason.

Table II reports baseline characteristics with group sizes of 98 and 104, consistent with the intended 1:1 allocation. Most variables are similar between groups (gestational age 25.9 vs 25.7 weeks, birth weight 809 vs 790 g, intubation at enrollment 48% vs 51%, RSS at enrollment 2.00 vs 1.96). Among roughly 30 comparisons, only a few differences are flagged: multiple gestation and early-onset bacteremia (P<.05) and diabetes (P≤.10). A small number of differences at P<.05 is compatible with chance and does not indicate a randomization problem under the guidance.

Allocation was delivered from sequentially assigned sealed envelopes, with the randomization code held by a site pharmacist not involved in enrolment (CONSORT item 9 and 10; main article p.2 and protocol p.1). This matches the Box 4 pattern for a central or independent assignment mechanism, but the reports do not state that the envelopes were opaque, sequentially numbered, or opened only after irreversible assignment. The Cochrane guidance expects a judgement where detail is rarely reported, so Probably yes is the best-supported answer rather than Yes.

The CONSORT checklist supplement states the random allocation sequence was obtained from a random number generator for each site (item 8a), and that blocks of 2 were used (item 8b). The main article states block randomization in blocks of two at each site for each gestational age group with a 1:1 allocation ratio. A random component is therefore reported for sequence generation.

The statistical analysis section states that all analyses were based on infants' group randomization assignments. Table IV reports the primary outcome for all randomized infants (ERT n=104; CT n=98), with no post-randomization exclusions reported for this row. This is an analysis by assignment, not a per-protocol or as-treated analysis.

The protocol and report describe the rescue rules for each arm, and the rescue treatment reported is protocol-consistent. Table IV, however, shows an unexplained imbalance in dopamine use (25% CT vs 13% ERT, P<.05) and corticosteroid use, and the report does not say whether these co-interventions were non-protocol or arose from the trial context. The report therefore does not describe deviation delivery well enough to answer probably_no or probably_yes.

The main report states that randomization was blinded but treatment allocation was not (p.5 limitations). The protocol says the trial was not blinded for treatment, because blinding would have required unnecessary IV lines, therapy and blood tests in the Conservative group. The registry lists masking as SINGLE with only the outcomes assessor masked, so participants were not masked. Early routine drug treatment versus no drug treatment makes assignment likely to be known to participants.

Treatment allocation was not blinded (main report p.5; protocol p.2). The protocol states that treatment blinding would have required unnecessary intravenous lines and therapy in the Conservative group. The registry masks only the outcomes assessor, so carers and people delivering the interventions were not masked to allocation.

Table IV reports the primary outcome (ligation or outpatient PDA follow-up) with denominators equal to all randomized infants (ERT n=104, CT n=98), and the statistics section states that all analyses used group randomization assignments. The Figure 2 flow diagram caption indicates exclusions occurred before enrolment, so no post-randomization exclusions are reported for this outcome. Data availability for nearly all randomized participants is therefore supported, but the article does not state explicitly that outcome status was ascertained for every randomized infant, and deaths before discharge are not clearly classified within the primary outcome. The answer is probably_yes rather than yes for that reason.

The main article states that treatment allocation was not blinded, and the protocol states that treatment blinding was not used because it would have required unnecessary intravenous lines. Ligation and cardiology follow-up decisions were therefore made by clinicians who knew the assigned arm. The registry lists the outcomes assessor as masked, which conflicts with the article and protocol; the masking may refer to a limited outcome-adjudication role that is not described.

The primary outcome is a pre-specified composite of ligation and outpatient PDA follow-up, and the protocol applies the same definition to both arms. The inspected passages do not describe arm-specific detection procedures, extra visits, or different thresholds for the outcome. However, the ERT arm received scheduled drug treatment that may have involved more echocardiographic monitoring, which was not verified.

The main article reports that 18% of eligible infants were not enrolled because the medical team wished to treat them outside the trial and 3% because the team did not want to treat them, which indicates that clinicians held strong preferences about early treatment. Those preferences make it plausible that unblinded ligation and follow-up decisions were influenced by arm knowledge. This is a host judgement from indirect evidence; no outcome data directly show influence.

The primary outcome includes ligation and referral to outpatient cardiology follow-up, which are therapeutic decisions by the care team. Such decisions can be influenced by knowledge of the assigned arm, and the team knew the assignment because treatment allocation was not blinded.

The protocol (eh_5c17bae4fb30295d) defines the primary outcome as ligation or the presence of an open PDA needing cardiology follow-up, which is a clinically standard way to determine ductal status. The main article reports it as a pre-specified primary outcome. Nothing in the inspected passages suggests the method was insensitive or invalid for the outcome. The question concerns the method rather than whether the outcome is a sensible surrogate.

The protocol prespecifies two analysis families for neonatal outcomes: univariate logistic regression for risk ratio and risk difference, and adjusted GEE models that add gestational age, multiple birth, early-onset bacteremia and treatment assignment. Table IV reports only the univariate estimates and says so in its footnote. No adjusted estimate for the primary outcome is reported in the sources read. There is no evidence that the choice of univariate reporting was driven by the direction or significance of the result, and the univariate method is the one prespecified for the primary outcome.

The registry and protocol prespecify a single primary measurement for this outcome: need for in-hospital ligation or open ductus at discharge. The reported result is that measurement. The other PDA-related measure (moderate-to-large PDA at 10 days after randomisation) is a separate prespecified secondary outcome at a different time point, so it is not an alternative measurement of the same outcome domain.

The registry (first posted 2013, before the trial started in 2013-12) and the protocol both prespecify the same primary outcome (need for in-hospital ligation or open ductus at discharge needing outpatient cardiology follow-up, through hospital discharge). The reported primary row in Table IV matches that outcome. The protocol prespecifies logistic regression for risk ratio and risk difference, which is the method used in Table IV. The registry record was last updated 2018-11-30, after the data were analysed.

Table 1 shows closely matched baseline characteristics for 2373 dapagliflozin and 2371 placebo patients (for example age 66.2 vs 66.5 years, female sex 23.8% vs 23.0%, LVEF 31.2% vs 30.9%). The primary analysis is intention-to-treat on the full analysis set of all 4744 randomized patients, analysed by randomized group, with no per-protocol or as-treated primary analysis reported.

The protocol describes a double-blind design with identical dapagliflozin and placebo tablets, and the main report describes matching placebo, so participants were not aware of their assigned intervention.

The protocol states that no member of the AZ study team, site personnel, or CRO will have access to the randomization scheme, and the tablets are identical, so carers and people delivering the intervention were not aware of assignment.

Figure 1 reports that 14 dapagliflozin and 20 placebo patients had incomplete follow-up for the primary outcome, and 2 placebo patients had unknown vital status (0 dapagliflozin). All outcomes were adjudicated by a clinical-events committee that was unaware of trial-group assignments, under prespecified criteria (p.4, lines 14-18). The Methods describe one evaluation schedule for all randomized patients: 14 days, 60 days, 4 months, then 4-month intervals (p.3). No inspected passage reports more visits or testing in one arm for the outcome.

The requested outcome is the pre-specified primary composite: unplanned hospitalization or an urgent visit with IV therapy for heart failure, or cardiovascular death. The main article defines it (p.3) and reports it as adjudicated events (p.4-5). Nothing in the inspected passages reports a poor-validity instrument or a method insensitive to plausible effects. The outcome is clinical events, not a surrogate, so the screening question is answered probably no.

The reported hazard ratio (0.74) comes from the pre-specified Cox model, stratified by diabetes and adjusted for HF hospitalization history, on the full randomized (ITT) analysis set (protocol p.8; main article p.4, lines 60-67). The report's Kaplan-Meier and Cox results agree with the registry primary.

The requested outcome is the single primary composite (worsening HF or CV death). The registry registers one primary outcome with one time frame, and the report uses the same composite, so no alternative primary measurement of this outcome domain was available for selection (registry lines 109-113). The components (HF hospitalization, urgent IV visit, CV death) and the secondary composites are separately reported with their own estimates (main article p.5, Table 2), so no measurement of this domain was left unreported.

The SAP edition 1.0 is dated 31 January 2017 and specifies the primary time-to-event analysis: a hazard-ratio hypothesis, closed testing, and the Kaplan-Meier and Cox presentation (protocol p.210). The registry record was first submitted 26 January 2017, before enrollment started on 8 February 2017, and names the same composite primary outcome with time frame 'Up to 27.8 months' (registry lines 25-42 and 109-113). The later SAP edition 3.0 is dated 23 July 2019, after the primary completion date of 17 July 2019, so it cannot be shown to pre-date unblinded data. No source shows a change to the primary analysis.

Table I and Table II show comparable baseline groups (n=35 vs 37; most P values .2 to .9). The text states 'Variables at randomization were comparable in the 2 groups.'

Methods state the list was held by the pharmacy and 'each new recruit was allocated at random by research staff using sealed envelopes' to NSAID or equal-volume saline. Central custody of the list plus sealed envelopes supports probably yes. Opacity, sequential numbering and opening only after irreversible assignment are not reported, so the answer is not 'yes'.

Methods state: 'A random number was generated with a variable block size for each site using Prism 8 (GraphPad Software).' A computer-generated random list with random block sizes is a random component under RoB 2 Box 4 (1.1).

The main report states that data were analysed on an intention-to-treat basis, and the analysed groups are the randomized groups (NSAID n=35, placebo n=37, total 72). No naive per-protocol or as-treated analysis is reported for this outcome.

Only 2 infants (3%) received open-label NSAID, one in each arm, and the report states the protocol was closely adhered to. Open-label NSAID treatment was not permitted by protocol. Nothing in the report attributes these two treatments to the trial context, and open-label NSAID use for a PDA is consistent with usual care outside a trial. The changes are therefore consistent with what could occur outside the trial context.

The main report states that the pilot had a weakness of lacking double blinding of the study drug, and that only the assessor of the primary outcome was truly blinded. Participants (parents) therefore were probably aware of assignment, although the report does not state explicitly what participants were told.

The report states the study drug was not double blinded and that only the primary outcome assessor was blinded. Clinicians who prescribed and gave the NSAID or saline were therefore aware of allocation, and allocation was drawn by research staff from sealed envelopes held with pharmacy.

The analysed denominators for the CLD or death row are the full randomized groups (NSAID n=35, placebo n=37; 72 infants in total), and the report analyses all 72 on an intention-to-treat basis without listing post-randomization exclusions for this outcome. The composite counts are reported for every randomized infant, which indicates that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. The main report does not explicitly state that every infant was assessed at 36 weeks; this is inferred from the denominators.

The Methods describe a blinded research nurse performing the oxygen challenge (eh_d012c80cecc1495f), which supports probably_no. The Discussion, however, states that the study was only partially blinded, with only the primary-outcome assessor truly blinded (eh_a42c9be475578a17). This conflict is recorded as counterevidence. Because the secondary composite was ascertained by the same nurse role described as blinded, the conflict does not establish that the assessor was aware of allocation, but it prevents a firmer answer.

The Methods state that medical staff performing cardiac ultrasound and pathology staff were blinded to allocation, and that a blinded research nurse performed the 36-week oxygen challenge (eh_d012c80cecc1495f). Nothing in the source indicates that outcome ascertainment differed between arms.

The composite outcome is defined in the Methods as death or CLD, with CLD defined as oxygen dependency determined by an oxygen challenge test at 36 weeks postconceptual age (eh_d012c80cecc1495f). This is a standard, clinically recognised measure of CLD and applies the same method to all randomised infants, so the measurement method is appropriate for the approved Result.

The reported result is a single unadjusted between-group comparison of counts, with the test stated in the Methods as chi-square or Fisher exact (eh_6c22a185e2fcf8c8). The Methods describe no alternative analysis of this outcome, and the report contains no adjusted analysis that was performed but left unreported. The P value and the components reported in Table III are consistent with a single analysis.

The approved target is one outcome measurement, death or CLD with CLD defined by oxygen challenge at 36 weeks postconceptual age. The Methods list that same measurement as a secondary outcome (eh_d012c80cecc1495f). Table III reports the composite together with its components, death and CLD, and reports the other secondary outcomes listed in the Methods (eh_6c22a185e2fcf8c8). Nothing in the report suggests a second eligible measurement of this outcome that was omitted, so selection among measurements is unlikely.

The report states that the protocol was not changed after trial commencement and that the secondary outcomes included death or CLD defined by oxygen challenge at 36 weeks (eh_d012c80cecc1495f). It does not give the date or content of the protocol, and no dated protocol, SAP, or registry record for this trial is among the captured Sources. The only registry source captured, NCT01630278, is the TRIOCAPI trial and cannot show what was prespecified for de-waal-2021. The Methods cite ACTRN12616000195459 for this trial, but that record was not captured. Without a dated source that specifies this measurement and analysis before unblinded outcome data were available, the answer is No information.

Table 1 reports baseline characteristics for 8582 dapagliflozin and 8578 placebo participants. The table footnote states there were no significant differences between groups, and the displayed values differ by small amounts (for example, age 63.9 vs 64.0 years, female sex 36.9% vs 37.9%, and HbA1c 8.3% in both groups). No imbalance suggests a problem with randomization.

Allocation is made centrally by IVRS/IWRS after the investigator has assigned a unique enrolment number and the participant has been determined eligible at Visit 2. The allocation sequence is held by the central system, not by enrolling personnel, so enrolling investigators cannot foresee the next assignment.

The registry-linked protocol (Prot_000, pp. 40-41) states that allocation is through an IVRS/IWRS using randomization codes that are computer generated by AstraZeneca R&D using the GRAND system, in balanced blocks, with stratification by CV risk category and baseline hematuria. Computer-generated codes carry a random component, so the sequence is random.

The main article states that the primary cardiovascular analyses were performed on an intention-to-treat basis, with data from 17,160 randomized patients, excluding 30 participants from one site. The exclusion was made because of Good Clinical Practice violations in another trial, not because of treatment received or outcome, so it is a post-randomization exclusion unrelated to assignment.

The trial was double-blind, with matching placebo and identical active and placebo tablets (protocol p. 42, Section 5.4.1), and the main article describes randomization to dapagliflozin or matching placebo in a double-blind fashion. Nothing in the captured text reports that participants were unblinded through intervention-specific effects.

The protocol states that no member of the study delivery team, study center personnel, or CRO handling data has access to the randomization scheme during the study, apart from named AZ and IVRS/IWRS personnel. Investigators can unblind only in emergencies. The main article describes the trial as double-blind.

The primary analyses used 17,160 randomized patients (eh_e0dc32a70bf82ed0). The article reports 30 patients lost to follow-up (rate <0.1% per year), with no difference between groups, and 224 withdrawals of consent (eh_2eb2be8664c23545). Missing outcome data therefore affect at most about 254 of 17,160 participants (about 1.5%), against roughly 1,560 MACE events. The MACE definition is time-to-first-event with adjudicated events; the article does not say whether vital status and MACE were ascertained for the 224 participants who withdrew consent, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes. The 30 participants excluded from one site for GCP reasons are handled under Domain 2 and are not counted here.

The main article states the trial was double-blind with matching placebo, and the protocol describes a blinded independent CEC that adjudicates the MACE components (p. 85). The protocol's single-dummy technique (p. 42) describes blinding of the study delivery team to the randomization scheme. The outcome assessor for MACE components is the CEC, which the protocol describes as blinded, so probably no. The Sources do not confirm that the CEC was in fact blinded in execution, so I answer probably no rather than no.

The same follow-up schedule applied to both groups (in-person visits every 6 months, telephone contact every 3 months), and the same CEC adjudication process applied to all primary CV events. The Sources describe no intervention-specific visits or testing that would create more opportunities to detect MACE in the dapagliflozin group.

MACE is a pre-specified composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or ischemic stroke, and the main article states the clinical-events committee adjudicated all components of the primary outcomes. The protocol (p. 85) says an independent CEC adjudicates all primary and secondary CV endpoints using investigator-reported events and source documentation. Nothing in the Sources suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity. The question does not judge whether MACE is a sensible outcome.

The SAP pre-specifies one primary analysis of MACE: a stratified Cox model on the FAS with CEC-adjudicated events (eh_c8a7865674e2bf6c). The report uses that analysis. The incomplete-follow-up checks in SAP section 4.4.1.3 (eh_6d2d7c255081f1d7) are diagnostics for informative censoring, not alternative estimates of the MACE effect. No alternative adjusted, unadjusted or differently defined MACE analysis appears in the read passages, so the reported HR is the pre-specified one.

For the requested construct (MACE, a composite of CV death, MI or ischaemic stroke), the registry, SAP and report define a single composite as time to first event (eh_c8a7865674e2bf6c; eh_e722f0b0d75e8e22). No alternative eligible MACE definition, scale or time point appears in the read passages, so the reported MACE is the only eligible measurement. The component analyses in SAP section 4.4.1.2 are analyses of components, not alternative measures of MACE.

The SAP (Edition 8, dated 31 May 2018; eh_4e47e04d6c9b46bb, p.37) pre-specifies the MACE hypothesis as a noninferiority test (HR < 1.30), and section 4.4.1.2 (p.38, eh_c8a7865674e2bf6c) pre-specifies the primary analysis: time to first CV death, MI or ischaemic stroke, FAS, events adjudicated and confirmed by the CEC, stratified Cox model. The report analyses MACE in that way (eh_5ded4369260d1e8f). The registry record was first submitted 2012-11-15, before start on 2013-04-25 (eh_dd748fcad6d2cff3), and registers the same composite as Primary outcome 1, up to 5.2 years (eh_e722f0b0d75e8e22). The report states the alpha-split decision was made without any comparative MACE data (eh_2dbd06ece1454646). Probably yes rather than yes because the SAP's own date (31 May 2018) is not shown to precede any unblinded MACE data reaching investigators. The current registry record cannot show earlier wording, and the protocol and SAP postdate enrolment.

Table 1 shows closely matched groups (3131 vs 3132 randomized; age 71.8 vs 71.5; female 43.6% vs 44.2%; type 2 diabetes 44.7% vs 44.9%; LVEF distribution 34.1/36.2/29.7% vs 33.5/35.9/30.7%; eGFR 61 vs 61). Protocol section 6.3 states that all patients were centrally assigned to randomised IP through an interactive voice/web response system (IxRS), operated remotely from enrolling staff. Kit identification numbers were allocated by the IxRS at dispensing, and treatment codes were held in the IxRS, not by site staff before assignment. This is a remote, centrally administered allocation method, which the guidance treats as adequate concealment.

Protocol section 6.3 states that randomisation codes were computer generated and that assignment was performed in balanced blocks (1:1). Computer-generated codes are a random component, so the sequence was random. The appendix Supplementary Methods (Trial Procedures) also describes randomization in balanced blocks stratified by T2DM status.

The Statistical Analysis section states that all analyses were performed according to the intention-to-treat principle, and the Results report all 6263 randomized patients (3131 dapagliflozin, 3132 placebo) analysed in the overall population, consistent with an ITT analysis.

The main article describes the trial as double-blind, with patients receiving dapagliflozin or matching placebo in addition to usual therapy, so participants were not aware of their assigned intervention.
The same double-blind design with matching placebo indicates that carers and people delivering the interventions were also blinded to assignment.

The main article reports that vital status was known at the end of the trial in all but 2 patients in the dapagliflozin group and 2 in the placebo group, out of 3131 and 3132 randomized, so the time-to-event outcome data were available for nearly all randomized participants. Discontinuation of study drug (14.2% and 14.1%) is reported separately and is not itself described as censoring of outcome follow-up.
The events committee adjudicating the outcome was unaware of trial-group assignments, and the trial was double-blind with matching placebo.
All potential worsening heart failure events and all deaths were adjudicated by the same committee using the same prespecified criteria in both arms, so ascertainment was comparable across groups.

The primary composite (worsening heart failure events and cardiovascular death) was measured by adjudication of potential events against prespecified criteria by an independent clinical events committee, a method suited to the outcome.

The planned stratified Cox analysis (appendix p.22) is the reported analysis. The main report also presents the sensitivity analyses (censoring at COVID-19 diagnosis and a competing-risk model) and the rate-ratio analysis of total events, so alternative analyses are visible and not selectively withheld.

The reported primary composite is the single defined composite, and both its full-population and LVEF<60% versions are reported. The secondary composite of total worsening HF events and CV death is also reported, so no eligible outcome measurement appears to be left unreported.

The appendix protocol text (p.22) prespecifies the composite primary outcome and a stratified Cox analysis by T2DM status, and the report follows it. A dual primary analysis (full population and LVEF<60%) was added by amendment on 4 Nov 2020, during enrolment and before the final analysis. Only the DMC's independent statisticians were unblinded for the interim analysis, so the amendment appears to predate investigator-level unblinding. The composite itself is unchanged.

Table 1 (p.4) shows baseline characteristics with P values mostly above 0.05 (sex 0.343, age 0.976, weight 0.491, HIV 0.261, protein 0.057). The only P 0.001 is rifampin mg/kg, which reflects the assigned dose rather than a randomization problem. The text says the groups were 'equally balanced across the groups' apart from chance differences (p.2, lines 33-37). Differences compatible with chance do not indicate a randomization problem.

Allocation used 'matching placebo tablets' manufactured for the trial (p.10, lines 16-19), so the arms were indistinguishable, and a separate list holder is named (p.11, lines 9-10). The trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled with identical tablets, which supports a central or independently held allocation, but the text read does not describe how assignments were released or whether containers were sequentially numbered.

The main report states the randomization used 'variable block sizes and was stratified by BMRC grade' (p.9, lines 54-58) and acknowledges 'Lika Apriani as the random list holder' (p.11, lines 9-10), so a generated list existed. The generation method (for example computer-generated numbers) and the within-block ordering are not described in the text read. Random permuted blocks with a separate list holder in a double-blind trial by an experienced unit makes a random sequence probable, though the method itself is not stated.

The report states 'The data for safety/tolerability and survival were analyzed by the intention-to-treat principle' (p.10, lines 63-64). Safety was analysed in all 60 randomized participants (20 per arm), as the Table 3 denominators show (p.7, lines 33-45). No per-protocol or as-treated analysis is reported for the safety outcome, and no randomized participant is excluded from the Table 3 counts.

The report describes the study as 'a double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled phase II trial' (p.9, lines 54-58) and says the oral doses were made with 'matching placebo tablets' (p.10, lines 16-19): the standard dose had one active and two placebo tablets, the double dose two active and one placebo. Participants were therefore unable to tell which dose they received from appearance. Nothing in the text read says blinding failed. Side effects specific to one arm could in principle reveal allocation, but the report does not describe participant guesses or unblinding.

The report calls the trial double-blinded (p.9, lines 54-58), and the registry record lists QUADRUPLE masking of participant, care provider, investigator and outcomes assessor. Matching placebo tablets (p.10, lines 16-19) and separate random list holder (p.11, lines 9-10) make it unlikely that delivery staff knew the allocation. Concealment was probably_yes in Domain 1, so the pattern of blinding is consistent. Side-effect unblinding of staff is not described in the text read.

The safety analysis covered all 60 randomized participants, 20 per arm, on an intention-to-treat basis (p.10, lines 63-64), and Table 3 gives 20 per arm as the denominators (p.7, lines 33-45). Two participants withdrew early, but the report says they were kept in the analysis: 'the two withdrawn patients were considered survivors in our explorative analysis of efficacy' (p.5, lines 1-8). For a dichotomous outcome with 15 events, missing data from two participants are unlikely to change the conclusion. The report does not give the per-arm withdrawal counts or say how 30-day AE status was ascertained for them, so 'Probably yes' rather than 'Yes'.

The report calls the trial 'a double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled phase II trial' (p.9, lines 54-58), and the ClinicalTrials.gov record lists masking of participant, care provider, investigator and outcomes assessor (sh_b29012ecac824bfb, registry record, read in full). Blinded assessors make awareness of allocation unlikely for the graded AEs. The record does not describe how the assessors' blinding was maintained, so this is 'Probably no' rather than 'No'.

The same CTCAE v4.03 grading applied to all arms (p.7, line 144), and the AE definition and 30-day window are the same for all groups (p.10, lines 39-42; p.3, lines 19-20). Equal opportunity for detection is expected in a placebo-controlled trial where all arms had the same monitoring schedule. The report does not describe differences in visit frequency or testing between arms, although the report does not state the monitoring schedule explicitly.

The outcome is Grade III-IV adverse events graded with CTCAE v4.03 (p.7, line 144), a standard instrument for this purpose, and the 30-day window is stated (p.3, lines 19-20). The safety assessment was defined before analysis as events 'possibly/probably related to their treatment (hematological, gastrointestinal, and skin disorders)' (p.10, lines 39-42). The method is therefore suitable for detecting drug toxicity, and the report does not suggest the grading was insensitive or invalid.

The Methods state that adverse events 'were presented descriptively for all patients and by study group' (p.10 lines 59-60), and that safety data were analysed by intention-to-treat (p.10 lines 63-64). The Methods describe a single analysis of safety data: counts per group. No adjusted, transformed or alternative-definition analyses of AE counts are described, so there is no evidence of multiple eligible analyses from which one was selected. The test behind P 0.503 is not named; the only named test in the Methods is chi-square for mortality (p.10 lines 64-65).

The registry names an AE outcome measured over 60 days, and the report uses a 30-day window, so the outcome domain was measured in more than one eligible time frame (p.1 lines 174-177). There is no clear evidence that the 30-day result was chosen on the basis of its results. The 30-day window matches the 30-day course of study drugs (p.9 lines 54-58) and the window stated in the Methods (p.3 lines 19-20). The report's safety definition (p.10 lines 39-42) is also restricted, while Table 3 reports all grade III-IV AEs, including hepatotoxicity (p.7 lines 87-91); these are inconsistencies between sections, but the direction of selection is not clear. The registered serious-AE outcome is not reported at all. That is selective non-reporting, which is outside this Domain (RoB 2 section 8.1).

The registry record (sh_b29012ecac824bfb) lists a secondary outcome 'Grade 3 and 4 and serious adverse events', time frame 'within 60 days', with monitoring at days 3, 7, 10, 14, 30, 45 and 60 (p.1 lines 174-177). The report analyses grade III-IV AEs over 30 days after the start of study drugs (p.3 lines 19-20; Table 3, p.7 lines 33-45), so the reported time frame differs from the registered one. The first submission date (2014-06-15, p.1 line 30) precedes enrolment, but the retrieved record was last updated 2017-06-01 (p.1 line 23), after primary completion on 2016-11-05 (p.1 line 26). ClinicalTrials.gov returns only the current version, so the 60-day time frame cannot be confirmed as present when the study was first registered. No protocol or SAP is linked to the record (sh_bd089379aed782bc, read: no documents). A dated plan for this analysis therefore cannot be shown, so the answer is No information rather than Probably no. The report gives no reason for the difference in time frame.

Baseline characteristics were reported as similar across groups (HbA1c 9.3% in all arms; similar group sizes). The article notes fewer women in the exenatide group and fewer Hispanic patients in the dapagliflozin group. These differences are not described as statistically significant and are not in prognostic factors for gastrointestinal adverse events; they are compatible with chance.

Allocation was performed centrally by an interactive voice and web-response system, which is a remote, externally controlled method independent of enrolling investigators. Matched placebo tablets and injections were used, and patients, investigators and data analysts were masked to assignment.

The main article states that patients were randomly assigned centrally (1:1:1) via an interactive voice and web-response system, stratified by baseline HbA1c. The article does not name the sequence-generation method. Per the RoB 2 guidance for a large phase 3 trial reported in a word-limited journal, absence of method detail supports probably_yes rather than no_information.

The adverse-event summary (Table 3) uses the safety analysis set, which is all randomly assigned patients who received at least one dose of study drug, grouped by arm (231 exenatide plus dapagliflozin, 233 dapagliflozin).
