The intervention was a visible behaviour-change programme with community health promoter contacts and an app, and the control group received standard clinic care with a reminder call. Participants therefore knew their assigned arm.

Carers and intervention deliverers were not blinded: the trial is described as non-blinded, the registry records Masking: NONE, and the community health promoters delivered the intervention arm's contact points. Enrolling study nurses also worked from clinic ID lists carrying randomisation codes, so they could see allocation.

The abstract reports 549 participants and 305 completers (eh_08c1dcb7ba5822f6). Page 4 reports 548 randomised, 305 analysed (55.6%), and pregnancy as the main reason for loss (eh_d503a49cf3cee332). The Table 2 analysis uses 145 intervention and 160 control participants (eh_b223a1370e65dede). Roughly 44% of randomised participants therefore lack the primary outcome, far from 'nearly all'.

The pages read (abstract, pages 4-5) describe a complete-case analysis of 145 and 160 participants, with bootstrapping used only to adjust for age group (eh_b223a1370e65dede, eh_d503a49cf3cee332). No imputation, sensitivity analysis or bias-correcting method for missing endpoint data is reported in those pages.

The analysis adjusts only for age group by bootstrapping (eh_b223a1370e65dede). It does not adjust for pregnancy or other characteristics that would plausibly explain loss related to waist-circumference change. Loss is dominated by pregnancy (eh_d503a49cf3cee332), which makes it likely that missingness depends on the outcome's true value.

Pregnancy before endpoint is the main reported reason for loss (eh_d503a49cf3cee332). Pregnancy plausibly changes waist circumference, so missingness is plausibly related to the true value of the outcome. The article does not report reasons for loss by arm, so the relation cannot be confirmed.

The trial was non-blinded (eh_08c1dcb7ba5822f6) and the registry records Masking: NONE (eh_a3e9032b8a41bac9). Assessors were study nurses who were part of the intervention team, so they were aware of the intervention received in at least some cases. Blinding of the outcome assessor is not reported.

The same measurement method and procedure (WHO STEPS, eh_5764ff7d4b854207) applied to both arms at baseline and endpoint. Waist circumference is a directly measured quantity, so extra CHP contacts create no additional opportunity to detect it, unlike passively detected events. The control arm's endpoint reminder call does not change how the outcome is measured.

Influence would be likely only with strong beliefs about the intervention's effect or high-judgement assessment. The primary outcome is a physical measurement under a standardised WHO STEPS protocol, with limited room for judgement. The article reports no evidence that measurers held strong expectations about the intervention effect. Some concern remains because data collectors belonged to the intervention team.

Waist circumference is a manual measurement made by a nurse at a landmark, which involves some measurer judgement. Knowledge of group allocation could therefore influence the reading (eh_5764ff7d4b854207 describes data collectors as part of the intervention team; eh_08c1dcb7ba5822f6 confirms the trial was non-blinded).

Waist circumference was measured with standardised WHO STEPS procedures in both groups, expressed as change from baseline (eh_5764ff7d4b854207, page 3). This is a standard, sensitive measure for a continuous outcome, so the method is not inappropriate for the Result.

The report gives only one analysis of the primary outcome: change in waist circumference in 145 and 160 completers, age-adjusted by bootstrapping, with P = 0.811 (eh_b223a1370e65dede, eh_d503a49cf3cee332). Several analyses were possible (adjusted versus unadjusted, completer versus all-randomised), but the analysis intentions are not captured, so it cannot be determined whether other analyses were run and omitted. The report also does not state an unadjusted result or an intention-to-treat analysis.

The registry specifies one primary waist-circumference measurement over months 0-8 (eh_a3e9032b8a41bac9), and the report presents that same measurement (eh_b223a1370e65dede). No other waist-circumference measurement or time point is registered or reported as eligible and omitted. The other registered outcomes are separate outcome domains (BMI, weight, lipids and so on) and are not alternative measurements of waist circumference.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record registers the primary outcome as 'Difference in waist circumference' over months 0-8 (eh_a3e9032b8a41bac9). Its first submission and start dates (2015-11-18 and 2015-11-23) are before enrolment and outcome data. The report analyses the same primary outcome, change in waist circumference from baseline to 33 weeks, over the same window (eh_b223a1370e65dede). The registry gives no analysis detail, so the registry entry fixes the measurement but not the analysis.

Table 1 (main report p5) reports baseline characteristics for 4731 albiglutide and 4732 placebo participants, matching the intended 1:1 allocation. Age (64.1 vs 64.2 years), sex (30% vs 31% female), region, medical history, glucose-lowering and cardiovascular medications, BMI, HbA1c and eGFR are closely similar, with no imbalance in key prognostic factors suggesting a randomization problem.

Main report p3 lines 21-22: 'Investigators used an interactive voice or web response system to obtain treatment assignment.' Protocol p35 (lines 5-8): 'Randomised treatment assignment will be done via the Interactive Voice Response System (IVRS) ... based on a sequestered fixed randomisation schedule. Study centre personnel will call the IVRS once a subject has met all prerequisites for randomization; the IVRS will assign treatment.' SAP p12 lines 24-26: 'Centralized randomization via PPD Interactive Response Technology (IRT) system will be used for treatment allocation.' Allocation was controlled by a remote system independent of enrolling staff, and the schedule was sequestered until assignment, which meets the Box 4 criteria for Yes.

Main report p3 lines 18-20: 'according to a sequestered, fixed, computer-generated randomisation code that used balanced permuted blocks of treatment group allocations, without stratification.' A computer-generated random component was used, so the sequence was random.

Main report p3 lines 98-108 sets the statistical analysis of the composite in an intention-to-treat population. Main report p4 states that the Cox analyses 'included all patients who had been randomly assigned to study treatment, whether this treatment had been taken or not', and the trial profile reports all 9463 randomized participants (albiglutide 4731, placebo 4732). SAP p14 defines the ITT population as all randomized subjects excluding those who did not consent, based on the treatment to which the subject was randomized, and SAP p13 sets the primary MACE hypothesis for that population. The reported result is an effect of assignment, not a per-protocol or as-treated estimate.

Main report p1 lines 18-19: 'patients and all study investigators were masked to their treatment allocation'; p3 lines 14-24: placebo with 'matched administration device, diluent, and volume injected', and 'All investigators and patients involved in the trial were masked to treatment group.' Participants were blinded by a matched placebo. The report does not describe unblinding through side effects or ascertainment; GLP-1 receptor agonist gastrointestinal effects could in principle hint at allocation, but no passage says participants recognised their assignment, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

Main report p3 lines 21-24: 'Investigators used an interactive voice or web response system to obtain treatment assignment. All investigators and patients involved in the trial were masked to treatment group.' Protocol p175 states the IVRS assigns treatment after study-centre personnel call it, so site staff did not select allocation. Carers and people delivering the intervention were therefore blinded to group; the outcome committee was also blinded (main report p3 lines 84-89).

Main report trial profile (p.4, eh_4efa4578dab2aab5, eh_5e340b00f789def5): of 4731 albiglutide patients, 4619 (97.6%) had a complete assessment of cardiovascular events at the end of the study and 112 had incomplete assessment; of 4732 placebo patients, 4577 (96.7%) had a complete assessment and 155 had incomplete assessment. Vital status was unknown for 30 albiglutide and 31 placebo patients (p.8, eh_107ce33dd288dd8a). Analysis was of all 9463 randomized patients (ITT). Outcome data are available for about 97% of randomized patients in each arm, and the 338 and 428 observed primary events exceed the number of incomplete assessments in each arm, so the missing data are unlikely to make an important difference to the effect estimate. Judged as probably yes rather than yes because the trial reports incomplete-assessment counts but not the proportion of missing data per arm within the time-to-event analysis, and withdrawals were censored rather than analysed as events.

Patients and all study investigators were masked to treatment allocation (main p.1, eh_56509de03a0ece88; main p.3, eh_d0f0217f154d865a: 'All investigators and patients involved in the trial were masked to treatment group'). The events were adjudicated by a clinical events committee blinded to treatment (main p.3, eh_d0f0217f154d865a). Guidance says to answer No when outcome assessors were blinded, so the assessors had no knowledge of the intervention received.

The same event definition and adjudication process applied in both arms of this double-blind trial (main p.1 and p.3, eh_56509de03a0ece88, eh_d0f0217f154d865a), so measurement and ascertainment should not differ by intervention group. Guidance flags differential detection only for passive collection or extra healthcare contacts in one arm; the passages read describe neither. Not confirmed: whether unscheduled visits or hospital record review differed between arms, since the reported trial profile does not break that down.

The primary composite (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke, first occurrence) is a standard, pre-specified clinical event outcome, classified by an independent clinical events committee using prespecified criteria (main p.3, eh_d0f0217f154d865a). Guidance says the answer is usually No or Probably no for pre-specified outcomes; no passage read suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or lacks a defined event system.

The SAP (p.14) defines the primary population as ITT, and the registry and main report use Cox PH with treatment as the only covariate in the ITT population. The reported estimate (HR 0.78) is that registered primary analysis, not an alternative selected for its direction or significance. Pre-specified per-protocol and on-treatment sensitivity analyses (SAP p.26) are not reported in the main article, but the reported primary is the one the registry and SAP specify.

The registry lists one primary outcome measurement, the CEC-adjudicated MACE composite over the CV follow-up period. The SAP (p.12) plans one composite event outcome with a 611-event target and adjudicated events. The components (CV death, MI, stroke) and the MACE-or-urgent-revascularization composite are registered as secondary outcomes and reported as secondaries in the results, so the primary composite was not chosen from alternative measurements of the same domain.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record was first submitted on 2015-06-04, before the actual start on 2015-07-01, and registers as primary outcome 'Time to First Occurrence of MACE During CV Follow-up', adjudicated CV death, MI or stroke, analysed by Cox PH with treatment as the only covariate in the ITT population. The SAP planned analysis (p.12) and hypothesis (p.13) use the same MACE definition, a 1.3 non-inferiority margin and the ITT population (p.14). The reported result (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.68-0.90, ITT) is the registered analysis. The RAP was approved 14-30 Nov 2017, after the 8 Nov 2017 event determination, so the date stamp rests on the 2015 registry entry rather than the RAP. The SAP population table (p.15) labels the primary endpoint as assessed using the per-protocol analysis, which conflicts with the registered ITT primary, so the answer is not Yes.

Main report Table 1 footnote: among the characteristics tested, only sodium concentration (P = 0.004), previous tuberculosis (P = 0.045), total CSF white-cell count (P = 0.006) and CSF lymphocyte percentage (P = 0.01) differed significantly (eh_a5f74a7de5a3db10). Group sizes were 409 and 408. Key prognostic factors were balanced: MRC grade 1 38.7-39.1%, grade 2 43.5-43.9%, grade 3 17.4% in both arms, and HIV infection 42.5% vs 42.9%. A handful of differences at these P values is compatible with chance and no key prognostic factor shows a very small P value.

Protocol section 8.3: enrolment logs assign each patient to the next available sequential number within strata; that number corresponds to two coded, sealed, pre-packaged bottles prepared centrally by a study pharmacist, and only two central pharmacists hold the master list (eh_314d35fb1b7757b1). Main report: the study pharmacist 'prepared visually matched pills in identical, sequentially numbered treatment packs according to the randomization list for dispensation in sequential order as patients were recruited', and enrolling physicians and investigators remained unaware of assignments until the last patient completed follow-up (eh_0fc0a8d739d67d15). This matches the minimal criteria for a central or independent pharmacy with sequentially numbered identical containers.

Main report: patients 'were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio ... according to a computer-generated randomization list, with randomization in variable block sizes of 4 and 6' (eh_0fc0a8d739d67d15). The protocol's section 8.3 describes block randomization with variable block size within strata (eh_314d35fb1b7757b1). A computer-generated random list is an explicit random component.

The main report's statistical analysis states that the primary analysis population was the intention-to-treat population, which included all randomized patients (eh_fb223bde56999a84). The protocol's analysis section specifies that adverse-event analysis uses all randomized patients (intention-to-treat) (eh_faca37367ee5ce15). The Table 3 denominators are 409 and 408, matching all randomized patients.

Protocol section 6.1 describes 'a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial' (eh_514d7a2728e6a5cd). The main report states that the study pharmacist prepared 'visually matched pills in identical, sequentially numbered treatment packs' and that participants, enrolling physicians and investigators were unaware of assignments until the last patient completed follow-up (eh_0fc0a8d739d67d15). Placebo matching supports participant blinding.

The main report states that enrolling physicians and investigators were unaware of assignments until the last patient completed follow-up (eh_0fc0a8d739d67d15). The protocol states that drug appearance and administration schedules were identical to maintain blinding among attending physicians and nurses, and that the master list was held only by two central pharmacists (eh_314d35fb1b7757b1). Carers and people delivering interventions were therefore blinded.

Figure 1 of the main report gives, in the ITT population, 22 lost to follow-up, 5 withdrawals and 1 patient who went home to die and could not be contacted in the standard arm (28), and 21 lost to follow-up and 2 withdrawals after treatment assignment in the intensified arm (23, plus 2 withdrawn before treatment). The text reports 53 non-death non-completers (28 standard, 25 intensified; eh_fb223bde56999a84). This is about 6.5% of 817 randomized patients, and the 9-month outcome is not available for these participants. Per-arm missingness (about 7% and 6%) is not so small that any missing outcomes could make no important difference, because a worst-case assignment of missing events moves the between-arm difference across the null.

The protocol's AE analysis summarizes grade 3 and 4 AEs in patients with an event using Fisher's exact test on the observed data, with no missing-data adjustment or sensitivity analysis (eh_d1307c41110343a2). The protocol's only pre-specified missing-data handling (last recorded disability status and multiple imputation) applies to the disability outcome (eh_f3a3a4485b395e11). The appendix's sensitivity analyses (Table S6 footnote) also concern disability, not AEs (eh_74897c6383bfe364). No analysis shows the AE result is robust to the 53 missing participants.

The proportions missing are similar across arms (28 of 409 standard vs 25 of 408 intensified), and the reported categories (lost to follow-up, withdrawal) are not stated to relate to the AE outcome. The one death-related loss (went home to die, unreachable) is a plausible health-related missingness mechanism in the standard arm, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

Figure 1 records losses to follow-up, withdrawals and one patient who went home to die and could not be contacted (eh_d9fc5ffde1125c97). In patients with tuberculous meningitis, loss or withdrawal from follow-up can plausibly relate to health status, including deterioration or adverse experiences, so missingness could depend on the outcome.

The trial was described as double-blind and placebo-controlled, with identical drug appearance and administration schedules maintained to keep the attending physicians and nurses blind (protocol p.24, eh_514d7a2728e6a5cd; protocol p.26, eh_314d35fb1b7757b1). The main report states that participants, enrolling physicians and investigators remained unaware of treatment assignment until the last patient completed follow-up (main report p.3, eh_0fc0a8d739d67d15). The clinicians who recorded grade 3/4 AEs were therefore described as blinded. The Sources do not describe a separate blinded adjudicator, and it is not stated how the blind was checked for AE grading, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

Both arms were monitored on the same schedule: daily review of inpatients until discharge, then monthly clinical and laboratory visits to 9 months (main report p.4, eh_fb223bde56999a84), and both arms were recorded on the same CLINEVE/NEREVE forms (protocol p.138, eh_a4754d284da81bdc). Nothing in the Sources indicates that the intensified arm received additional clinical encounters or investigations that could have increased detection of grade 3/4 events.

The outcome is the count of patients with at least one clinical grade 3 or 4 adverse event, recorded on the clinical event (CLINEVE) and neurological event (NEREVE) forms during daily inpatient review and monthly visits (main report p.4, eh_fb223bde56999a84). Grade 3/4 clinical events are a standard clinical recording method, and nothing in the Sources suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or poorly validated. The protocol confirms that only grade 3 or 4 AEs were systematically collected and that a missing grade counts as grade 3 or 4 (protocol p.138, eh_a4754d284da81bdc), which is a conservative ascertainment rule rather than a measurement defect.

The protocol prespecified a stratified CMH test for this AE comparison, and the report presents Fisher's exact test (P 0.44) instead (protocol p.139, eh_840baaace6974474; prespecified outcome eh_514d7a2728e6a5cd; Table 3, eh_aec3fb2e424d6494). Two eligible analyses of the same count therefore exist, and only the substituted one is reported. The authors give a methodological reason for the change, and nothing in the Sources shows that the choice was driven by the result. The answer is probably no, but the unreported CMH result is an open question.

The protocol prespecifies one clinical AE measure in this category, 'Any grade 3 or 4 adverse event' (protocol p.24, eh_514d7a2728e6a5cd), with the AE derivation given in protocol p.138 (eh_a4754d284da81bdc). The reported Table 3 row 'Any event' (229 (56.0) vs 240 (58.8), P 0.44; eh_aec3fb2e424d6494) is that same prespecified measure, so the reported measurement is the intended one, not one chosen from several.

The protocol (dated 24 Feb 2011, before enrolment began in April 2011) prespecifies the outcome 'Any grade 3 or 4 adverse event' (protocol p.24, eh_514d7a2728e6a5cd). The analysis plan for this outcome states that the protocol specified a generalized Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test stratified by HIV status and TBM severity, and that the authors instead used Fisher's exact test, 'directly reproducible based on the presented summary data' and 'descriptive statistics only' (protocol p.139, eh_840baaace6974474). The reported P = 0.44 comes from the substituted test. The departure is documented, and the stated reason is methodological rather than result-driven. However, the Sources contain no date-stamp showing that the analysis plan was finalised before unblinded outcome data were available, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

Table 1 of the main article reports baseline p values of 0.154 (age, the only continuous characteristic with a visible difference: 24.4 vs 28.9 years) and 0.915 or higher for every other characteristic, with group sizes of 10 and 8. The registry baseline table, with 'Analysed' counts equal to the randomized numbers (10, 8, 16, 18), shows phase 2 group sizes of 16 and 18 and phase 1 baseline marijuana inhales per day of 50.1 vs 27.1 (SD 43.8 and 13.2). These differences are compatible with chance and nowhere near the P < 0.001 level the guidance uses for problems. No baseline pattern suggests failure of randomization.

The main article states that the McLean Research Pharmacy prepared capsules containing either nabilone or placebo, with riboflavin in both, and that participants received blister packs of identical-appearing study medication. The protocol states that study staff presented prescriptions to the McLean pharmacy and participants received blister packs. The registry records quadruple masking. These describe a delivery mechanism in which identical study medication was prepared by a pharmacy and supplied without the enrolling staff choosing the arm. The official guidance expects a judgement for Probably yes in this situation, where identical study drug is supplied centrally. Unknown: the sequence-holder, whether containers were sequentially numbered, and whether assignment was irreversible before dispensing.

The main article describes the study as a randomized prospective pilot and says participants were randomized to placebo or nabilone, but does not name a sequence-generation method. The protocol (section 8.2.1.c) describes stratification by self-reported daily versus non-daily cannabis use, with the aim of preventing one arm being overrepresented by daily users, but does not state whether a random element was used to generate the sequence. The registry records allocation as RANDOMIZED without method. The official guidance treats a bare statement of randomization as No information unless the circumstances support a probable answer; this is a small single-site pilot (18 randomized), so the circumstances do not support one.

The main article states that the primary hypothesis concerned adverse events during study treatment and that an intent-to-treat approach including all randomized participants was used. The adverse-event counts are reported per arm, with no per-protocol or as-treated analysis reported. The adverse-event analysis population and denominator are not stated explicitly, so this is a judgement rather than a firm answer. No post-randomization exclusions are reported.

The main article describes placebo capsules prepared by the McLean Research Pharmacy, with riboflavin 25 mg in both arms to confirm adherence, and 7-day blister packs. The registry records masking as QUADRUPLE. The adverse-event profile is similar in both arms: nausea was reported by one participant in each group and sedation by one in each group, with vomiting only in placebo. Nausea and sedation are not nabilone-specific here, so side effects give no clear sign of unblinding. The report does not say whether participants were asked to guess their group, so this is a judgement rather than a firm answer.

The registry records masking as QUADRUPLE, which implies masking of more than the participant. The main article states that the McLean Research Pharmacy prepared the capsules and riboflavin was used in both arms, and the protocol states that study staff presented prescriptions to the pharmacy and that participants received blister packs. Nothing reported indicates that the staff delivering the medication could see which arm a participant was in. The report does not state who could see the allocation during dispensing or pill counts, so this is a judgement rather than a firm answer.

18 participants were randomized. Six did not complete the 10-week treatment: the report states that 12 completed treatment, and the registry flow for the phase 1 arms shows 6 of 10 nabilone and 6 of 8 placebo completing. The report includes 'all available data on those lost to follow-up' in the ITT analysis, but it does not state AE ascertainment or AE denominators for those participants. Roughly one third of randomized participants without stated AE outcome data is not nearly all, so the answer is probably no.

The analysis is described as intention-to-treat using 'all available data' for participants lost to follow-up. No sensitivity analysis or assumption about the AE experience of participants with missing data is reported, and an ITT approach of this kind does not correct for bias from missing outcome data.

Most documented reasons (time constraints, moving, pregnancy) are unrelated to AE occurrence, and the report does not link any withdrawal to adverse events. The AEs were all mild or moderate and no participant discontinued because of an AE beyond those listed. The arm difference in non-completion (4 of 10 versus 2 of 8) is a concern, but with small numbers and unreported reasons by arm, it does not establish likely dependence.

The reasons for non-completion include three withdrawals for time constraints or moving, two participants withdrawn by staff for repeated missed visits (participants were withdrawn after more than 4 days without medication), and one participant removed after a positive pregnancy test. The report does not give reasons by arm. The nabilone arm had 4 non-completers versus 2 on placebo, and the medication-gap rule could plausibly reflect the tolerability problems (nausea, sedation) that are the outcome being measured. So missingness could depend on the true AE experience.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record lists quadruple masking, including the participant, care provider, investigator and outcomes assessor. The protocol describes a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, with matched placebo capsules containing riboflavin in both arms. The main report does not say that blinding was broken, so assessors were probably unaware of assignment. The record is not independently confirmed by the report, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

Both arms had weekly medical management visits with a study physician, and the protocol applies the same side-effect checklist and the same low threshold for additional workup to all participants. No extra visits or testing are specified for the nabilone arm, so ascertainment was probably comparable across groups.

The protocol specifies that side effects are obtained through a standard Adverse Events Checklist and the Frequency and Intensity of Side Effects Rating at each medical management visit. The main report describes adverse events as ascertained by an open-ended clinician interview and review of clinical measurements. These are established methods for pre-specified adverse events and are not unsuited to detecting plausible effects, so the answer is probably no.

The report gives group totals of adverse events (eh_c7fdee5ef90859c3, eh_9d29e7f1b45b3721) with no effect estimate, test or stated analysis method. Adverse-event counts can be analysed in more than one eligible way, for example by participants with at least one event, by number of events, or by rate, and the protocol statistical section (eh_85ded6624e074db3) does not state which analysis was planned for adverse events. The planned analysis intentions are therefore not detailed enough to judge whether the analysis was selected.

The protocol plans two adverse-event instruments: a standard Adverse Events Checklist and a Frequency and Intensity of Side Effects rating (eh_a34b2b44b94f2056). The report gives only event counts from an open-ended interview and review of clinical measurements (eh_9d29e7f1b45b3721) and does not report the side-effect burden rating. The reason for that omission is not stated. Nothing in the sources shows that the omitted rating was measured and dropped because of its results, so selection on the basis of results is not established, and a probably-no answer is given.

The report states that enrolment began in September 2010 and was completed in April 2013 (eh_a68e44424483b669). The ClinicalTrials.gov record was first submitted on 2011-04-26 and lists a start date of 2010-06 (eh_08e894d2a499878e), so the registry entry was not finalised before unblinded data existed. The registered outcomes (eh_5324ce9ac2f32d18) include cannabis use, inhales and neuropsychological measures but no adverse-event outcome. The protocol statistical section (eh_85ded6624e074db3) covers cannabis use and ASI scores only. No date-stamped analysis plan for the adverse-event result was found, so the pre-specification cannot be confirmed.

The report states that the two groups were well balanced for demographic, clinical and procedural characteristics. The randomised groups were 2710 and 2728 (near 1:1), so no substantial imbalance in group size is present. No imbalance is reported that suggests a problem with randomisation.

Allocation was made by a web-based IWRS run by the MRCC, which is external to the enrolling sites. The allocation was made after eligibility was confirmed and recorded, so enrolling personnel could not foresee the assignment. This meets the guidance criteria for a remote, centrally administered method.

The report states patients were randomly assigned by a web-based application (MRCC IWRS) in consecutive order, 1:1, without blocking or stratification. It does not name the random number generation method. The guidance gives this situation as the example for Probably yes: a large trial run by an experienced clinical trials unit, with no specific sequence-generation detail in a word-limited journal. The supplementary protocol (sh_109cceda14485a1b, page 54, lines 15-19) describes a balanced, center-stratified IWRS randomisation, which differs from the published report; stratification does not by itself change the sequence-generation judgement.

The primary analysis is intention-to-treat. The protocol defines the ITT population as all patients who signed consent and were randomized, regardless of adherence or deviation from the protocol. The report's flow diagram shows 2728 (aspirin) and 2710 (clopidogrel) included in the intention-to-treat analysis. The per-protocol analysis is secondary and is not the basis for this Result.

The report counts 35 patients (0.6%) who used a different antiplatelet regimen from the allocated group: 22 in the aspirin group and 13 in the clopidogrel group. The protocol-specified loading handling for ticagrelor and prasugrel users is described separately. No reason is given for the switches, and the search for the phrase found no stated cause. The guidance allows No information when trialists do not report whether deviations arose from the trial context, so it is not possible to tell whether these switches arose from trial context.

The report states that participants and study investigators were not masked to the assigned group. The protocol describes the study as prospective, randomized, open-labeled. Participants were therefore aware of their assigned antiplatelet monotherapy.

The report states that study investigators were not masked to the assigned group, and the protocol describes an open-label design. Carers and people delivering the interventions were therefore aware of assignment, which is the relevant condition for question 2.3.

Primary endpoint ascertainment was complete in 5338 of 5438 randomised participants (98.2%), and vital status was cross-checked in all randomised patients. Figure 1 shows the per-arm losses: clopidogrel 41 lost to follow-up and 8 withdrew consent; aspirin 50 lost and 1 withdrew, about 1.8% and 1.9% of randomised participants. Patients who changed antiplatelet regimen (13 clopidogrel, 22 aspirin) remained in the intention-to-treat analysis. Outcome data are therefore available for all or nearly all randomised participants.

The protocol states that an independent clinical event adjudication committee, whose members are all masked to the assigned arm, classifies clinical events, and that an external CEC blinded to treatment reviews at least all deaths and safety endpoints. The main article says all endpoints were adjudicated by an independent committee unaware of the treatment group. Participants and investigators were not masked, so the blinded adjudicators are the outcome assessors for the primary events.

Both arms had the same scheduled follow-up at 12 and 24 months (plus or minus 3 months), with active surveillance for events at each visit and extra visits at physician discretion. All endpoints used standardised definitions and were adjudicated by an independent committee. The CEAC was to develop event-classification rules at study onset, so ascertainment methods were the same in both groups.

The primary composite is built from hard clinical events (all-cause death, non-fatal MI, stroke, readmission for ACS, BARC type 3 or greater bleeding) with standardised definitions in the appendix. Nothing in the report suggests these methods could not detect plausible treatment effects.

The intention-to-treat analysis reported here is the prespecified primary analysis in the SAP, with per-protocol analysis also prespecified as supportive; the reported intention-to-treat hazard ratio is the one matching the request, so the choice of analysis was not driven by results.

The reported result is the prespecified primary composite; the report states that the composite was analysed as the primary endpoint and that other composites (a thrombotic composite and any bleeding BARC 2 or greater) are post hoc, so the reported measurement was not chosen from several eligible composites in the outcome domain.

The clinical investigational plan's statistical analysis plan (supplement pp. 61-62) prespecifies the primary composite of all-cause death, non-fatal MI, stroke, major bleeding and readmission due to ACS, analysed by intention-to-treat at 2 years, with per-protocol as supportive. The registry (NCT02044250) records the primary outcome with a 2-year time frame and was first posted 2014-01-23, before the start of enrolment in 2014-02. The plan's date relative to unblinded data is not stated, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.

The authors report that baseline characteristics "were similar, except for a greater incidence of HELLP syndrome ... among mothers in the expectant-management group" (p.5, lines 11-16), with Table 1 giving HELLP syndrome 7 (5.1%) versus 1 (0.7%) (p.6). Other key prognostic factors are closely matched: median gestational age 26.1 versus 26.0 weeks, median birth weight 863 versus 825 g, and group sizes of 136 and 137 match the intended 1:1 ratio. A single nominal difference in a maternal characteristic among roughly 20 compared variables is compatible with chance, and the 7 versus 1 contrast is far from the P<0.001 level the guidance treats as indicating a randomization problem. Baseline data cover all randomized infants (N = 136 and 137), so the comparison is intention-to-treat.

The protocol states: "The randomization is coordinated centrally and web-based. This trial will be protected from selection bias by using concealed, stratified and blocked randomization" (protocol p.24, VII.2). The main report describes a centrally coordinated Web-based randomization system (p.2). Allocation was therefore remote and controlled by a central system independent of the enrolling clinicians, which is the Yes example in the guidance for telephone, web-based or interactive randomization services.

The main report states that after consent infants were "randomly assigned" and that randomization was "coordinated centrally with the use of a Web-based system," stratified by centre and gestational age, with block sizes of 4 to 8 (p.2). The protocol says "Eligible patients are randomly allocated to early pharmacological treatment or expectant management per centre and stratified according to gestational age" with "Block size varies from four to eight" (protocol p.98). A random component is therefore stated, and a central web-based system with a large multicentre trial supports a random sequence. Neither source names the generation method (for example computer-generated numbers), and neither states explicitly that the order within blocks was random, so this is not a firm Yes.

The primary analysis is intention-to-treat over all randomized infants (136 expectant, 137 early ibuprofen), with primary-outcome data for all 273. The per-protocol analysis is reported as secondary and is not used here. The analysis therefore follows the official guidance that ITT analyses are appropriate.

Deviations from assigned intervention were few and appear consistent with routine care outside the trial. One infant in the expectant arm received open-label treatment, which the protocol permits when prespecified criteria are met (protocol: such infants remain in follow-up). Two early-ibuprofen infants did not receive ibuprofen, and second courses were withheld on clinician request (2) or parent request (1). Nothing in the sources links these changes to the trial context, such as awareness of allocation driving a decision to deviate.

The trial was unblinded by design. The protocol states that a blinded study was 'obviously not possible' because the two groups differ in intention (active closure with COXi versus accepting the PDA), and the main report says unblinded echocardiography was allowed. Participants and parents knew the assigned strategy.

Clinical staff delivering the interventions knew the assigned strategy. The protocol states a blinded study was not possible, and the expectant arm is defined by the absence of a treatment intention, which staff would see when managing the infant.

The main report states that at 36 weeks PMA, data for the composite primary outcome were available for all 273 randomized infants (136 expectant, 137 early ibuprofen). The CONSORT diagram shows all randomized infants in the intention-to-treat populations (136 and 137). The composite includes death, and the report gives no missing primary-outcome counts. The protocol SAP expects minimal missing values because the primary outcome is assessed at 36 weeks PMA, generally before discharge, and missing data before discharge are not imputed.

The trial was unblinded by design, and the protocol states that blinding was not possible. The clinicians who classified NEC, managed oxygen therapy and recorded death therefore knew the assigned group. Only the BPD severity classification in six infants without an oxygen reduction test was made by a committee blinded to assignment.

Outcomes were defined and measured at the same time point (36 weeks PMA) with the same definitions in both arms. The protocol schedules extra routine echocardiography after each ibuprofen course, which adds contacts in the ibuprofen arm, but the events are NEC, oxygen-dependent BPD and death, which are unlikely to be detected more often because of echocardiography. The ibuprofen arm's additional contacts are therefore unlikely to have produced differential ascertainment.

Death is an objective outcome, and NEC uses standard staging criteria. The report gives no sign that the treating clinicians held strong expectations about the composite outcome that would have shifted their classification. The protocol's rationale that ibuprofen reduces NEC is a general belief about the intervention, but the report does not show it influencing how outcomes were classified.

NEC staging by Bell criteria and the classification of oxygen dependence and BPD severity both involve clinical judgment, and the assessors knew the assigned group. Such judgment could be influenced by that knowledge, so the composite outcome could have been influenced. Death is an objective event and is unlikely to be influenced.

The primary outcome is a standard clinical composite of NEC (Bell stage IIa or higher), moderate-to-severe BPD defined by supplemental oxygen or ventilatory support at 36 weeks PMA after at least 28 cumulative days, with an oxygen reduction test where indicated, and death at 36 weeks PMA. These are established methods that can detect plausible intervention effects; the report gives no sign that any method was unsuitable.

The reported composite is the prespecified primary ITT analysis, and the per-protocol analysis is reported as a secondary analysis. The SAP and appendix prespecify sensitivity analyses (mild-BPD classification, GEE for multiple births, and adjusted logistic regression), and the main report says these are in the supplement. The primary-analysis result was not selected from these alternatives. Whether the prespecified sensitivity-analysis results were reported in full was not confirmed in the text read.

The registered and protocol primary outcome is a single composite measured at 36 weeks PMA, and the reported result is that composite. The BPD and NEC components are reported separately in Table 2, not as alternative measurements of the primary outcome. No alternative time point or scale for the primary outcome is described in the registry or SAP.

The registry record, first submitted 2016-04-01 and before the trial start on 2016-12-23, registers the primary outcome as a composite of mortality, NEC and BPD at 36 completed weeks PMA. The original protocol (version 1.71, dated 28-08-2016) specifies the same primary outcome and a noninferiority analysis. The SAP states that ITT is primary and per-protocol is secondary, and that analyses start only after database lock and submission of the SAP. The main report's analysis matches these plans. The SAP is not date-stamped against unblinding, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.

Results (p. 5): "No statistically significant differences were found in the characteristics of the patients between the 2 treatment groups" (p. 4 lines 61-63 and p. 5 lines 1-7); mean age 26 years in both groups and weight 75 vs 77 kg (Table 1). Pre-operative pivot shift (P = .761) and pre-operative KT-1000 (P = .364) are not significant (Tables 2 and 3, p. 6). Group sizes were 53 and 50 analysed (56 and 54 allocated), close to the intended 1:1 ratio. No imbalance suggests a problem with the randomization process.

Because group membership was determined by birth date (p. 2, lines 43-47), the assignment of each patient was known or derivable by the enrolling surgeons and clinic staff before enrolment and assignment. Nothing reported (no central, remote or sequentially numbered sealed-envelope allocation) protects the next assignment. Under RoB 2 Box 4 (1.2), reason to suspect that the enrolling staff knew the forthcoming allocation gives No.

Methods (p. 2, lines 43-47): "We randomized the patients into 2 treatment groups based on their birth dates. Group A ... patients who were born on an odd-numbered day, while patients of group B ... were born on an even-numbered day." Allocation by date of birth is a systematic, predictable method that the RoB 2 guidance (Box 4, 1.1; section 4.3.1) lists as a No answer, despite the word 'randomized' in the abstract (p. 1). No random element is reported.

Analysis is by allocated group: 53 in group A and 50 in group B were analysed (p. 2, lines 47-51, Figure 1). Only the Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U tests are described (p. 4, lines 50-59), with no per-protocol or as-treated analysis. The 7 patients who left the country were excluded for missing follow-up, which is a modified ITT analysis and is appropriate for this domain. The report does not explicitly use the term intention-to-treat.

Both groups followed the same postoperative rehabilitation (p. 4, lines 32-49). No crossover, contamination or non-protocol co-interventions are reported. Exclusions were due to patients leaving the country, which is not a deviation from the intended intervention. Any non-adherence that is reported would occur outside a trial context.

Limitations (p. 8, lines 12-14): "we were not able to blind the participants from knowing their treatment group." Group A had an additional ALL reconstruction (p. 4, lines 3-4), so participants knew their assignment. Only the outcome examiner was masked (p. 2, lines 65-68).

One experienced surgeon performed all operations with 2 assisting surgeons or residents (p. 2, lines 62-64). The ALL reconstruction was added only for group A (p. 4, lines 3-4), so the operating team could not have been unaware of assignment. Only the assessors were blinded (p. 2, lines 65-68).

Figure 1 (p. 2, lines 79-95) shows 56 allocated to group A with 3 lost to follow-up and 53 analysed, and 54 allocated to group B with 4 lost and 50 analysed. Overall 103 of 110 (93.6%) had outcome data, with 7 missing (group A 94.6%, group B 92.6%). The outcome is continuous, where about 95% availability is usually needed, so this is just below the threshold and not clearly nearly all. Imputed data are not reported.

The statistical analysis (p. 4, lines 50-59) reports only Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U tests on observed data. No imputation, weighting or sensitivity analysis for the 7 missing participants is reported, and no assumptions about their outcomes are stated.

All 7 non-completions are attributed to leaving the country (p. 2, lines 49-51). Emigration is a documented reason that is plausibly unrelated to knee laxity or the other outcomes. The report gives no reasons that suggest missingness was related to recovery, failure or adverse events.

The operated knees were covered by a white stocking to ensure blinding of the examiner, and this covered the clinical examination and instrumented joint laxity testing with the KT-1000 (p. 2, lines 65-75). The examiner is described as a different surgeon from the one who operated.

Both groups were assessed at the same time points by the same independent examiner using the same KT-1000 protocol (p. 2, lines 65-75). The outcome is a pre-specified instrumented measurement, not passively collected, so there is no opportunity for differential detection.

Instrumented laxity was measured with the KT-1000 arthrometer at 20 lb with standardized limb positioning at 30 degrees of flexion and 15-25 degrees of external rotation (p. 2, lines 71-75). This is a validated, standard method for anterior laxity. The report gives no evidence that the instrument is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity.

For the KT-1000 measurement, the article reports one comparison in full: medians by group with the Mann-Whitney U test (P < .001; Table 3, eh_034e59af6d1bd684). It also reports the categorical result of anterior translation greater than 5 mm (0% vs 6%; eh_3615e10745f6d4fd), alongside the preoperative values in Table 3. Reporting a categorical analysis next to the continuous one is evidence against selection among analyses. The Methods describe only Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U tests (p.4, lines 50-59), with no adjusted or change-score KT-1000 analysis described, so no omitted alternative analysis is shown. This rests on the article alone, because no SAP is captured.

The outcome domain (knee laxity and function) was measured in several eligible ways in this article: KT-1000 at 20 lb, Lachman, anterior drawer, pivot shift, Lysholm, Tegner and IKDC (eh_856650d03e713227, eh_3615e10745f6d4fd). Tables 2-4 report each of these measurements in full, with P values, not only the KT-1000 result (eh_034e59af6d1bd684, eh_8caf62ac8bf55da6). Because the other measurements are reported and none appears omitted, there is no sign that one measurement was chosen from a subset on the basis of its results. This is an inference from comparing the Methods with the Results, since no protocol confirms the intended measurements (guidance 8.3.2). The KT-1000 is the only measure with a significant difference, which is the pattern selection would produce; the complete reporting of the other measures is what limits that concern.

The captured Sources contain only the journal article. No protocol, SAP or registry record dated before unblinded outcome data were available is captured; the registry outcome list and registration dates are empty. Lexical searches for 'analysis plan' and 'registered' returned no hits (sr_f67dc95c3562e4e1, sr_1564586054770fe1); zero hits are not evidence of absence. The Methods describe a Fisher exact and Mann-Whitney U analysis in SPSS 17.0 (p.4, lines 50-59), but no dated plan for it. The Limitations state that no power analysis or sample size calculation was performed (eh_96abe54fd3d677ad), which does not show that an analysis plan was fixed before unblinding.

Table 1 (main report p.7, ITT, n = 49; intervention 25, reference 24) shows similar groups for age (63 vs 60.5 years), male sex (72 % vs 83 %), SAPS II (47 vs 52.5), weight, height, BMI, admission Glasgow coma score and the main reasons for respiratory failure, with no differences large enough to suggest a randomization problem. Table 1 has no p values, so differences are judged descriptively; none is suggestive of failed randomization.

Main report p.3 lines 56-58: "Randomisation was accomplished by using opaque sealed envelopes. The randomisation envelopes contained a card stating the group to which the patient was randomised." The sequence was generated by a statistician not involved in enrolment (p.3 lines 52-55), and no report suggests that enrolling staff knew the next allocation. The report does not state that envelopes were sequentially numbered or opened only after irreversible assignment, so the answer is Probably yes rather than Yes.

Main report p.3 lines 52-53: "A computer-generated 1:1 randomisation was used, generated by a statistician who was not involved in determination of patient eligibility or outcome assessment." A computer-generated random sequence is a random component.

The intention-to-treat analysis includes all randomised patients except those who withdrew consent, did not meet inclusion criteria or improved before intubation (p.5 lines 5-8). One reference patient was excluded because SpO2 could not be recorded (p.5 lines 19-22); that is missing outcome data, assessed in Domain 3. Table 2 reports the day-28 survival denominators as the ITT population (n = 49; 25 and 24), and per-protocol analysis is secondary.

Delivery is described for both arms: HFNC was applied in the intervention group throughout the procedure, and no oxygen flow was given through the cannula in the reference group (p.3; p.9 lines 14-16). The only protocol deviations reported are two per-protocol exclusions for NIV contraindications (p.5 lines 22-28). These are not deviations caused by the trial context, and no crossover or non-protocol co-intervention is reported.

The reference group received a sham: the nasal cannula was positioned on the patient without flow, the tube was hidden under a sheet, and a second cannula at 60 L/min was run into the room to mimic HFNC noise (p.3 'Randomisation and masking'). The design aimed to conceal allocation from the patient, and the blinded observer was independent. Nothing reported suggests participants identified their group.

The operator performing intubation was partly masked by a large sheet over the oxygen flow meter (p.3). The main report nonetheless states the operator 'could not be blinded, given the flow of the HFNC' (p.9 lines 12-14), and the registry records masking as NONE. Only the outcome assessor was independent and blinded (p.9 lines 9-12). Operators could therefore have known the allocation during intubation.

Fifty patients were randomised (25 per arm; p.3 'Randomisation and masking'), and the ITT analysis includes 25 and 24 patients (p.5 lines 15-22). Table 2 gives day-28 survival denominators of 25 and 24 (total 49), so the mortality denominators cover 49 of 50 randomised patients (98%). One reference patient was excluded because SpO2 could not be recorded, not because of death or loss to follow-up. The 17 deaths observed (8 intervention, 9 reference) far outnumber the one missing participant, so that participant could not plausibly change the estimate much.

The main report states 'the assessor was an independent observer who did not know the group of inclusion' and 'One strength of the study was the blinded assessment' (p.9 lines 9-13). Its Methods state 'The study was blinded to the observer collecting the data' and that the blinded observer was 'one of the ICU residents, a nurse or a member of the trained local research team' (p.3). The report also says the intubation operator could not be blinded, but the operator is not the outcome assessor for day-28 vital status. Blinding of the observer is therefore reported, but the report does not state explicitly that the blinded observer also recorded day-28 vital status, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

Day-28 mortality was to be recorded for all randomised participants by the same procedure (registry lines 75-78). The intervention is a single preoxygenation procedure during intubation and does not add routine ICU visits or diagnostic testing that would create more opportunities to detect death in one group. Both arms were managed in the same ICU under the same protocol apart from the sham HFNC during preoxygenation. No difference in ascertainment method between arms is reported.

The requested outcome is all-cause vital status at day 28 after randomisation. The registry states 'Length of mechanical ventilation, length of stay in ICU, mortality at day 28 will be recorded' (NCT02530957, lines 75-78), and Table 2 of the main report reports 'Patient alive at day 28' by arm. Death is an objective outcome with no room for interpretation, so the measurement method is unlikely to be inappropriate. The method of ascertaining vital status is not described in the main report, which is an unresolved detail but not evidence that the method was unsuitable.

The registry's statistical analysis section describes a chi-square or Fisher test for qualitative variables (lines 86-90), and Table 2 reports the day-28 survival counts by arm in the intention-to-treat population (n=49) with a single p value of 0.686. No adjusted mortality model is described, so there is only one obvious analysis. The supplement also contains a per-protocol mortality row, which is a second analysis population; both populations are reported and neither is presented as the favoured one, which is evidence against selection.

Day-28 vital status is one way to measure the outcome domain of all-cause mortality over this window. The registry describes 'mortality at 28 days' as a morbidity-in-ICU secondary outcome (lines 84), and the main report reports 'Patient alive at day 28' by arm (Table 2). No alternative mortality measures or time points are described in the captured Sources, so there is no evident selection among eligible measurements. The registered primary and secondary outcomes concern other domains (oxygen saturation and intubation complications).

The registry record shows the study started on 2015-06-23 (actual) and was first submitted on 2015-08-07, after enrolment had begun. Registered outcomes list 'Lowest oxygen saturation' as primary and 'Number of complications related to intubation' as secondary. Day-28 mortality appears only in the registry description ('mortality at day 28 will be recorded'; 'mortality at 28 days'), not as a registered outcome. The main report cites a protocol (ref 25, BMJ Open 6:e011298) that was not captured as a Source, so its date and content cannot be checked. No source dated before outcome data were available is in the captured Sources, so whether the day-28 mortality analysis was fixed before unblinded data is not established.

Table 2 reports similar baseline characteristics across the three arms of 100 patients: male sex 66/69/70, median age 28.5/27.5/30, baseline ALT 17.1/19.1/17, haemoglobin and creatinine clearance comparable, and similar hepatitis B/C counts. No difference is described as statistically significant, and no imbalance in key prognostic factors is apparent. Daily rifampicin dose differs by design and is not a baseline imbalance.

Participating centres were supplied with sealed, serially numbered, opaque envelopes, and the schedule was made by an independent person (eh_0f6cc095ccf9d55a). This matches the guidance's description of appropriate envelope use. The sentence 'No attempt was made to conceal the treatment regimen after randomisation' refers to blinding after allocation, not to concealment of the sequence before assignment, so it does not change this answer. The report does not say whether envelopes were opened sequentially and only after enrolment was irreversibly recorded, or whether they were tamper-proof, so a judgement is needed; hence probably yes rather than yes.

The report says patients were randomised 1:1:1 in blocks of nine, and that a randomisation schedule was created by an independent person (eh_0f6cc095ccf9d55a). It does not say how the sequence was generated or that the order within blocks was random. The guidance says blocked allocation without an explicit random component should generally be answered No information.

The denominator for each arm is 100, equal to the randomised group size, which suggests the reported safety result includes all randomised participants. However, the text labels the analysis population as patients who received at least one dose, and the number randomised but not dosed is not stated. If no participants were excluded, the analysis is consistent with an intention-to-treat approach for this result.

The report describes differing supervision methods by centre (staff-observed versus DTM after week 8; Santa Cruz 66% staff and 30% DTM) and a single interruption for jaundice and grade 3 ALT. These are either protocol-consistent (DOT/DTM design, toxicity-driven interruption) or routine non-adherence. The report gives no evidence that any deviation was caused by the trial context, and states that the DOT method difference did not change losses or doses taken.
The Methods state that no attempt was made to conceal the treatment regimen after randomisation from patients, so participants were aware of their assigned regimen (open-label, no placebo).

The Methods state that treatment regimen was not concealed after randomisation from researchers or health care staff, so people delivering the interventions were aware of assignment. Only the laboratory staff and the SAE-assessing clinician were blinded.

The report gives the extent of missing ALT data: 81 of 1800 scheduled ALT results (15 R10, 38 R15, 28 R20) were not available. The Result's events are 7 grade 3 ALT increases, so the missing results are not small enough to be ignored in relation to the event count. Participant-level outcome availability is not reported, although the 100-per-arm denominators suggest all randomised participants are in the safety analysis.
No sensitivity analysis, imputation, or weighting for the 81 unavailable ALT results is reported. The analysis is a complete-case count of observed grades.

Reason 1 applies: the unavailable ALT results differ between arms (15 of 600 for R10, 38 of 600 for R15, 28 of 600 for R20; roughly 2.5%, 6.3% and 5%). The difference is in the arm with the most events, which is a pattern consistent with missingness related to the outcome. Reasons for missing results are not reported, so this is not confirmed.

The protocol allowed patients to attend at any time if they had side effects, so attendance for scheduled ALT tests could depend on clinical status, which in turn relates to the hepatic outcome. The reasons for the unavailable ALT results are not reported, so dependence on the true value cannot be excluded.

The laboratory staff who performed the ALT assays were blinded to regimen, and the independent clinician who assessed SAEs was blinded. The assessors of the reported outcome were therefore probably unaware of the intervention received.

ALT was scheduled identically across arms and measured by laboratory staff who were blinded to regimen, so the ALT measurement is unlikely to have differed between groups. Ascertainment of non-hepatic events relies partly on patient-initiated attendance, which could differ by arm, but the reported outcome is the ALT grade.

The reported outcome is a laboratory ALT grade, measured by serial ALT tests at 2, 4, 8, 12 and 16 weeks and graded against ULN multiples. ALT is an objective, appropriate method for detecting the hepatic component of the target. The reported endpoint is labelled only as grade 3 AEs with no definition, and the approved target is broader (hepatic and non-hepatic AEs and SAEs), so that scope gap is assessed in Domain 5, not here.

The reported result is a count per arm with a trend test, but the same ALT data could have been analysed by test or by participant, with different event definitions, as the report itself notes that results were available on 1719 of 1800 scheduled tests. Without analysis intentions, the report does not show whether other analyses were considered. The reported analysis uses the at-least-one-dose population with 100 per arm, which is stated in the report.

The outcome domain of grade 3 or 4 AEs and SAEs could have been measured in several eligible ways: ALT grades recorded at every test (Table 3), non-hepatic AEs (Table 4), and SAEs described in the text. Without analysis intentions, it cannot be established whether the reported grade 3 ALT count was chosen from these measurements on the basis of its results. The text says all non-hepatic AEs were grade 2 or lower and that the only grade 3 ALT increases were the seven reported, so the reported count covers the grade 3 events the report describes, but this does not establish that no other measurement was considered.

The captured sources contain only the main article. No registry record, protocol or statistical analysis plan dated before unblinded outcome data was available is captured, so no dated intention specifies this grade 3 ALT count or its analysis. The report describes the RIFATOX trial design and the 16-week ALT and AE assessments, but no pre-specified analysis of this result is documented.

Table 1 covers all 145 randomized patients (72 conservative care, 73 early surgery) and the authors state there were no significant between-group differences. The article describes the groups as generally well balanced. The one visible difference, coronary artery disease at 1/59 versus 5/72, involves very small counts and is compatible with chance. No substantial imbalance in group sizes or in key prognostic factors is reported.

Assignment was made through a Web-based interactive response system, so allocation was remote and controlled by an external system rather than by enrolling staff. The guidance lists internet-based randomization services as Yes-type examples. The report does not state that the service was independent of enrolling investigators or describe how the sequence was hidden until registration, so Probably yes rather than Yes.

The Methods state that the allocation to each group was computer-generated and stratified by center using a permuted-block sequence with variable block size. A computer-generated permuted-block list has a random component, which meets the Yes criterion in the signalling-question guidance.

The analysis was performed on an intention-to-treat basis, and the primary and secondary end points, including death from any cause, are reported for all randomized patients: 73 early surgery and 72 conservative care, with no patients lost to follow-up. The per-protocol analysis is reported only as a supplementary analysis.

Four early-surgery patients crossed over to conservative care, one of whom did not have surgery, and two conservative-care patients crossed over to early surgery. The article reports the counts and that three of the four early-surgery crossovers later had surgery after symptoms developed. It does not give the reasons for the other crossovers, or whether they arose from knowledge of allocation or from the trial context. The protocol's deviation section (pp. 19 and 40) gives no reasons either. Section 5 guidance notes that No information may be appropriate where trialists do not report whether deviations arose from trial context. The question cannot be answered from the reported information.

The trial is described as an open-label trial, and the authors state that because the trial was not blinded, nonfatal outcomes could have been influenced by the clinician's knowledge of the treatment. Early surgery versus conservative care cannot be hidden from participants.

The same open-label design applies to carers and clinicians. The authors state the trial was not blinded and that clinician knowledge of treatment could have influenced nonfatal outcomes, so the clinicians delivering the interventions knew the assignment.

The article states that no patients were lost to follow-up, and the intention-to-treat analysis includes all 145 randomized patients (73 early surgery, 72 conservative care) with death from any cause as a prespecified secondary end point, during follow-up to April 2019. Outcome data for all randomized participants are therefore reported as available, with no missing participants to account for. Because the outcome is death, ascertainment depends on the reported follow-up completeness. The statement of no loss to follow-up is direct support for the answer, and the protocol was not checked for how vital status was verified.

The trial was open-label, as stated in the article's design and in its limitation that non-blinding could have let clinician knowledge of treatment influence outcomes. The protocol says the Clinical Events Committee is blinded to treatment assignment, but that applies to the adjudication of clinical events and does not establish that the ascertainment of all-cause death was blinded. The answer is therefore yes, with the blinding of death ascertainment left unresolved.

Death from any cause is a pre-specified outcome with no reported difference in ascertainment method between arms. The article reports no extra clinical contacts or differential detection pathway for death in either group. The procedure used to confirm deaths in each arm is not described in the sources read, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

Death from any cause is an observer-reported outcome that involves no judgement. Knowledge of the assigned intervention is unlikely to change whether a death is recorded, so the outcome is not expected to be influenced even though assessors may have been aware of assignment.

Death from any cause is a prespecified secondary end point, and the method is a count of deaths during follow-up. Nothing in the article, appendix or protocol suggests that this method is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity. The question does not assess whether all-cause death is a sensible outcome, which the trial specifies as a secondary end point.

The SAP prespecifies one analysis set for each secondary end point: Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence with log-rank test, and a Cox hazard ratio. The article reports both the Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence and the hazard ratio for death from any cause (Table 2 and p. 6). Subgroup and per-protocol analyses are reported only for the primary end point. No evidence shows that other analyses of death from any cause were run and left unreported.

Death from any cause is one unambiguous outcome, measured only by vital status. The protocol, the article and the registry define a single measure of it, so there is no choice among alternative measurements of death. The registry's differing timeframe concerns the follow-up window, not the measurement.

The only version of the statistical analysis plan (protocol supplement, p. 45-47) prespecifies intention-to-treat analysis of all primary and secondary end points, with Kaplan-Meier cumulative incidence and log-rank tests and hazard ratios from a Cox model. The reported death-from-any-cause result is a hazard ratio from a stratified Cox model with Firth correction, a variant of the prespecified Cox model. The article (p. 3) names death from any cause as a prespecified secondary end point, and the registry (NCT01161732) lists All-cause death as a registered secondary outcome. The protocol's original version is dated February 2010, before enrolment began in July 2010, which supports a plan finalized before unblinded outcome data existed.

The main report states the demographic and clinical characteristics were similar in the two groups (main report p.4, Table S2 referenced), and the baseline subgroup table (p.8) shows group sizes nearly equal (4668 vs 4672) with proportions similar in most categories. Individual differences (for example in the Asian subgroup or the eGFR strata) are the kind expected by chance across many comparisons and are not presented as a key prognostic factor imbalance of a size indicating a randomisation problem.

Allocation was made by a trial-specific interactive voice/web response system (IV/WRS), accessible by internet and telephone, with access restricted to authorised persons (protocol p.170, sections 10.1 and 10.3). This is a remote, centrally administered allocation independent of enrolling site staff. Study drug is visually identical and dispensed by pen-injector (protocol p.57, section 9.1), so the blinded assignment cannot be read from the product.

The main report states patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio, stratified by baseline eGFR (main report p.3). The protocol describes randomisation as a session run by the trial-specific IV/WRS for all subjects, 1:1 (protocol p.170). Neither captured source names the sequence-generation algorithm; searches for 'computer generated' returned no hits. For a large industry-run trial by an experienced unit, with a 1:1 allocation and an interactive randomisation system, a random sequence is a reasonable assumption, so Probably yes rather than No information.

The main report states that all patients who underwent randomization were included in the primary and exploratory analyses (p.3 lines 101-104), and that patients who discontinued the trial without an outcome were censored from the day of their last visit (p.4 lines 4-5). The analysis is a Cox model with treatment as the covariate (p.3 lines 84-85), with 9340 randomized and the reported analysed groups of 4668 and 4672. This matches an intention-to-treat analysis by assignment. The report also says results were similar in a per-protocol sensitivity analysis (p.4 lines 22-27 region, Fig. S3), which is a secondary analysis and does not change the primary-analysis answer. Unknown: the protocol SAP describes censoring at permanent discontinuation plus 30 days in some sensitivity analyses (protocol p.257 lines 15-18), which is not the primary analysis reported here.

The main report describes the trial as double-blind and placebo-controlled (p.2 lines 32-33). The protocol states that the placebo and active drug are visually identical and that the liraglutide/placebo arm is double-blind (p.57 lines 22-23, 28-29). Nothing in the inspected text reports a failure of blinding. Unknown: the protocol and report do not state a blinding-integrity assessment, and the GI side effects that the protocol says were managed by gradual dose titration (p.85 lines 16-20) could in principle hint at allocation, but no unblinding is reported.

The main report describes the trial as double-blind (p.2 lines 32-33). The protocol states that the placebo and active drug are visually identical and that the IV/WRS allocates the trial product dispensing unit number at each dispensing visit, so the dispensing investigator receives a DUN rather than an allocation (p.57 lines 22-23, 41-43). The protocol says randomisation and code access are restricted to authorised persons (protocol p.170 lines 15-45, read in Domain 1). Unknown: the report does not itemise which personnel were masked beyond the general term double-blind.

The main report states that vital status was known for 99.7% of patients and that 96.8% completed a final visit, died, or had the primary outcome (eh_98aeb114f761ed71, NEJM p.4). The registry participant flow for the same trial gives per-arm figures: 4668 and 4672 started, 139 (liraglutide) and 159 (placebo) did not complete, of which 12 and 17 were lost to follow-up or withdrawn without contact, and 127 and 142 were alive (eh_64366374776f3599). Non-completion is therefore about 3.0% in liraglutide and 3.4% in placebo, and the outcome was ascertained for nearly all randomized participants. Under the RoB 2 guidance for this question, data available for nearly all randomized participants supports a probably-yes response.

The trial was double-blind and the primary composite events were adjudicated in a blinded fashion by an external, independent event-adjudication committee (eh_7eb5f7d1e13c4716, NEJM p.3), and the committee is named in the appendix (eh_da9781bc570ca1af, appendix p.4). Blinded adjudication indicates that outcome assessors were unaware of assignment for the events they classified. Earlier clinical records completed by investigators are not explicitly described as blinded, which keeps this at probably no rather than no.

Scheduled follow-up visits were specified as months 1, 3 and 6 and every 6 months thereafter for all randomized patients, and the same adjudication committee reviewed events in both groups (eh_98aeb114f761ed71, NEJM p.4; eh_7eb5f7d1e13c4716, NEJM p.3). The protocol specifies one follow-up schedule for both arms, so the opportunity to detect events was not designed to differ between groups.

The primary composite (first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI including silent, or nonfatal stroke) is prespecified and was adjudicated by an external event-adjudication committee (eh_7eb5f7d1e13c4716, NEJM p.3). The guidance expects a probably-no answer for prespecified adjudicated outcomes. Nothing in the captured text suggests that the method is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity.

The article describes the reported composite analysis as a Cox proportional-hazards model with treatment as covariate, the prespecified primary analysis, and states that prespecified sensitivity analyses were conducted. The article reports sensitivity analyses with alternative censoring, including a per-protocol analysis, and states that the magnitude of the differences was similar, so the reported result is not the only analysis in the sources.

The registry lists the primary composite and the cardiovascular outcomes as registered outcomes, and the registry results report the primary composite, the expanded composite, all-cause death and the individual components. The article reports the primary composite and the cardiovascular outcomes in Table 1 and the supplementary figures. There is no sign that a cardiovascular outcome measurement was measured and then withheld on the basis of results.

The registry record (first submitted 2010-08-06, before the 2010-08-31 start) registers the primary outcome as the same composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI or nonfatal stroke, time from randomisation to first event, that the article reports. The protocol states that the SAP will be finalised before database release and that no unmasked or between-group analyses will be performed before database closure. The SAP (version 3.0, status Final) is dated 04 December 2014, before the planned closeout ended in December 2015.

Table 1 reports baseline characteristics for the 77 placebo and 79 dronabinol participants. The footnote states there were no statistically significant differences between groups except MCQ: Emotion, at P = .05, which is compatible with chance (p.5 lines 3-113). Group sizes match the 1:1 intended allocation (77 vs 79).

Allocation was done by a research pharmacist independent of the research team (p.2 lines 115-117). Study capsules for dronabinol and matching placebo were prepared by the institute pharmacy in identical gelatin capsules with equal riboflavin content and looked identical for both conditions (p.2 lines 94-97). This is an independent pharmacy-based allocation with identical study medication, which supports a probable yes. The report does not describe sequentially numbered containers or envelopes, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.

The main article states only that participants were randomized at the end of the placebo lead-in using a fixed block size of 4, stratified by joints per week and psychotropic medication use (p.2 lines 90-93), and that a research pharmacist independent of the research team conducted the randomization (p.2 lines 115-117). No random generation method (computer-generated numbers, random number table, or random ordering within blocks) is described. Blocked allocation without an explicit statement that the order within blocks was random falls under the guidance for No information. Registry results and descriptions contain no randomization method.

The primary analysis used the intention-to-treat population (p.3 lines 63-143, 'All analyses were conducted on the intent-to-treat population'), and the flow diagram shows all randomized participants analysed in their assigned arms (79 DRO, 77 PBO; p.4 lines 1-59). Missing weeks 7-8 data were scored as use, so no participant was excluded from the analysis.

The reported deviations are consistent with the protocol and would occur outside the trial. Dose reductions were made for side effects under the protocol's flexible dosing (titration to 20 mg bid 'or the maximum dose the participant was able to tolerate', p.2 lines 117-120; 13 reductions, p.6 lines 40-49). Adherence was high (median 92%; riboflavin marker 94% vs 100%, P = .26; p.6 lines 35-40). No contamination or non-protocol co-intervention by trial personnel is reported.

The report describes the trial as double-blind with identical matching capsules (p.2 lines 85-97), so participants were intended to be unaware. However, dronabinol produced reported intoxication more often than placebo (3 DRO vs 1 PBO) and increased blood pressure in 2 DRO participants (p.6 lines 40-47). Under the RoB 2 guidance, side effects participants could recognise as specific to one arm justify a Probably yes answer, so this is answered conservatively and the trial-context question is then assessed.

Study medication was prepared by the hospital pharmacy as identical capsules, and randomization was conducted by a research pharmacist independent of the research team (p.2 lines 94-97 and 115-117). Those arrangements conceal allocation from the staff who dispense and deliver the medication, so carers and deliverers were probably not aware of assignment.
