The trial reports 61 of 79 DRO and 47 of 77 PBO participants retained to week 8 (77% vs 61%; p.4 section 3.3.1, lines 1-92), so about 30 of 156 randomized participants (about 19%, PBO 30 and DRO 18, by inference from those figures) lack the weeks 7-8 data that the primary outcome requires. Scoring missing weeks 7-8 as cannabis use (p.4) means the analysed counts (79 and 77) include participants whose outcome was imputed, not observed. Counts of observed weeks 7-8 outcomes are not reported. Given a low abstinence rate, the missing participants could plausibly change the result, so 'nearly all' is not met.

The authors report a tipping-point sensitivity analysis: the trial would be positive only if, in the DRO group, missing participants were at least 10 times more likely to be abstinent than non-missing participants, and in the PBO group at least 5 times less likely (p.4 section 3.2, lines 1-92). Given observed abstinence of about 23% in DRO and about 25% in PBO, those conditions require implausibly high abstinence among dropouts in DRO, so the null direction is robust under plausible scenarios. The last-two-week analysis (DRO 16/76, PBO 14/72) also shows no difference, which is consistent with this.

The participant is the outcome assessor for TLFB self-report. The article describes the trial as randomized and double-blind, with identical capsules for both conditions. The guidance treats blinded participants in a matching-placebo trial as unaware unless the Sources report that blinding was broken. Searches of the Sources for blinding terms returned only 'double-blind' descriptions and no report of unblinding, so participants were probably unaware of their assignment.

Both arms used the same TLFB self-report method. The registry describes study visits twice each week for the whole study. Missing weeks 7 and 8 were scored as use in both arms, so the outcome definition did not depend on how often each arm was assessed. Retention differed between arms (77% dronabinol vs 61% placebo, P = .02), which could change how many participants were observed. That is an attrition question for Domain 3, not a difference in measurement method, thresholds or detection opportunity.

The approved outcome is self-reported cannabis use by TLFB, with abstinence defined as no marijuana use in weeks 7 and 8. The main article validated TLFB self-report against urine drug screens in the placebo group (log-linear regression, P = .003) and cites prior trials showing self-report corresponds with UDS when elicited non-judgmentally. This supports a method sensitive to the endpoint and not shown to be invalid. UDS could not be used in the DRO group because oral dronabinol produces positive THC screens, so validity was checked only in the placebo arm. That is a limitation of the validation, not evidence the instrument was inappropriate.

No analysis intentions are available for this outcome, and more than one analysis of the TLFB measure was possible: observed proportions, a logistic mixed-effects model adjusted for baseline dollars, and a last-two-weeks variant. Under the guidance, this is No information. The article reports the observed and modeled results together (both P = .69 and counts 14/79 vs 12/77), and the last-two-weeks analysis (16/76 vs 14/72) is also reported with a null result. All the analyses reported are concordant, which argues against selection among analyses, but this is not a substitute for a pre-specified analysis plan.

The requested outcome is two consecutive weeks of abstinence by TLFB self-report in weeks 7 and 8. The registry lists one primary outcome with this measure and time frame, and the registry results report only that outcome measure. The article reports the same measure and window. Urine drug screens were also collected, but the article states they could not serve as the main measure because oral dronabinol produces positive THC screens. Under the eligibility rule, the requested TLFB measure is the only eligible measurement, so there was no choice among measurements.

The only pre-specified source captured is the ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT00217971. Its first submission date (2005-09-16) is after the recorded trial start (2005-03), so the entry was made after enrolment began and cannot show what was fixed before unblinded outcome data existed. The registry lists the same primary outcome as the report (abstinence from marijuana during weeks 7 and 8), but it gives no analysis detail. No protocol or statistical analysis plan is among the captured Sources, and the registry capture lists no linked documents. Under the guidance, this is No information.

Table 1 (N=122; 61 per arm) shows similar age, sex, race and baseline MCQ and withdrawal scores with no imbalance that would suggest a problem with the randomization process; differences such as sex (73.8% vs 63.9%) and MCQ total (40.1 vs 42.4) are compatible with chance.

The sequence was generated and held by a Ph.D. statistician independent of the research team (eh_9588dc874feb0231, eh_d38938aa441c4e2e), and study medication was prepared by a pharmacy in matching capsules (eh_d38938aa441c4e2e). This supports remote, independent allocation, but the report does not state sequential numbering or how assignments were delivered to enrolling staff, so Probably yes rather than Yes.

The Methods state the allocation used "computer generated random blocks of sizes 4, 6, and 8, with a 1:1 allocation ratio" (eh_9588dc874feb0231), a random component under the guidance's definition of Yes.

The primary analysis included all randomized participants, 61 per arm, analysed by intention to treat (eh_56eb479e9681cabb; CONSORT flow on p4 lines 682-714). This is the ITT approach the official guidance regards as appropriate for the effect of assignment.

Reported non-adherence and co-interventions are not described as arising from the trial context. Self-reported adherence was about 95% in both arms and riboflavin use 100% in both (p5 lines 757-832). The placebo lead-in excluded placebo responders before randomization (p2 lines 1041-1167), which is a pre-randomization exclusion rather than a post-randomization deviation. Any deviations that did occur are consistent with those expected outside the trial.

The report describes the trial as double-blind with matched gelatin capsules (equal riboflavin, lactose filler) and participants blinded to allocation (eh_d38938aa441c4e2e). However, the adverse-event table shows marked between-arm differences in dronabinol-typical effects (dry mouth 6 vs 27; intoxication 2 vs 13), which participants could plausibly attribute to their assigned drug. The report does not assess whether participants correctly guessed their allocation, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.

The report states that participants, investigators and study staff were blind to allocation (eh_d38938aa441c4e2e). Medication was prepared by an unblinded pharmacy, but it dispensed packaged, matched capsules, so there is no indication that people delivering the intervention knew the allocation.

The registry flow shows 61 started per arm, with 35 completers in the placebo arm and 32 in the lofexidine-dronabinol arm, so 26 and 29 participants did not complete (registry, sh_14163899f929e7ca p1 lines 1-379). The paper reports about 35% did not complete maintenance and that their abstinence status is not known (eh_076442417fe3b712). Missing participants (26 and 29 per arm) far outnumber the events in each arm (18 and 17), so the outcome is not available for nearly all participants.

The paper does no sensitivity analysis for missing outcomes. The authors state that it 'would seem a reasonable assumption that most dropouts continue to use cannabis' (eh_076442417fe3b712), but this is an untested assumption, not a correction or a sensitivity analysis showing the result is robust.

Reported reasons differ between arms: adverse-event discontinuation was 5 in the lofexidine-dronabinol arm and 1 in the placebo arm (registry flow, sh_14163899f929e7ca p1 lines 1-379). Adverse experiences of one intervention relate to the true value of the outcome under the guidance (section 6.1.4.2). The authors' own statement that dropouts most likely continued to use cannabis, combined with about 45% non-completion and no sensitivity analysis, makes outcome-dependent missingness likely. The overall non-completion counts are similar across arms (26 vs 29), which weighs against it.

Reasons for dropout include loss to follow-up (21 placebo, 18 lofexidine-dronabinol), adverse events (1 vs 5) and not interested (4 vs 4) (registry flow, sh_14163899f929e7ca p1 lines 1-379). Dropout from a cannabis treatment trial could plausibly relate to continued use or withdrawal, which relates to the abstinence outcome.

The paper reports that participants, investigators and study staff were blind to allocation. The primary outcome is participant-reported, so the participant is the outcome assessor. Blinding was reported as successful, but dronabinol produced markedly more intoxication and dry mouth than placebo (for example intoxication 2 vs 13 and dry mouth 6 vs 27 in Table 3). Participants could therefore plausibly infer their assignment, and the report does not test whether they did. I judge awareness probably yes, consistent with the Domain 2 answer on participant awareness.

Both arms used the same TLFB self-report at the same visit schedule (twice-weekly clinic visits, with use between visits measured), and the same weekly self-report instruments. The dronabinol-specific urine problem applies to measuring the outcome by urine, which was not used in either arm for the primary result, so it does not create differential ascertainment between arms.

The outcome is a behavioural event (whether cannabis was used on each day), recalled with TLFB anchoring and a surrogate for quantity, and it has relatively little room for judgement. Belief in a benefit from dronabinol could bias some reporting, but the guidance treats this as likely only when expectations are strong and the outcome involves judgement. The main article reports no difference between arms and does not report a large differential in self-reported use. I judge that influence was probably not likely. This is a material judgement that falls within the 'Some concerns' range.

The outcome is participant self-report of cannabis use, the category the guidance identifies as capable of being influenced by knowledge of intervention. The participant is the assessor, and the participant could have had knowledge of the assigned intervention given the differential side effects (Table 3), so the assessment could have been influenced.

The outcome is self-reported cannabis use by timeline follow-back (TLFB), the standard instrument for this outcome. The main article describes the TLFB as the method used at each visit and reports that self-report was validated against urine in prior work. The paper also acknowledges that urine toxicology could not be used for this trial because dronabinol produces positive THC urines, but that limits the choice of a second method rather than making the TLFB unsuitable. The measurement is therefore not inappropriate for the approved Result.

For the primary outcome, the Methods specify one analysis (logistic regression adjusted for baseline amount of use) and the Results report one test with crude proportions (p3 lines 703-727; p5 lines 405-460). No sensitivity analysis or alternative adjusted model for the primary outcome is reported in the passages read, and none is shown to have been run and selectively omitted. The alternative analyses that are reported (longitudinal outcomes and secondary dichotomous outcomes) are analysed as their own outcomes, not as alternatives for the primary result.

The registry lists one registered primary outcome, the 21-day TLFB abstinence measure, which matches the reported primary result (registry p1 lines 114-124 and 252-267). The main article also reports a secondary dichotomous abstinence in the last two weeks of maintenance, which was 12/61 in each arm (p5 lines 503-606). That secondary measure is reported with its own null result, so the reported primary is not the only result for the outcome domain. The Methods define the primary aim as the 21-day measure before the data were analysed, and no passage suggests the 21-day measure was chosen for its results.

The registry entry (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01020019) was first submitted 2009-11-24 and the trial started 2010-01, so the entry predates enrolment. It names the primary outcome '21 Days of Consecutive Abstinence as Measured by the Time-line Followback' with a daily time frame (registry p1 lines 22-33 and 114-124). The Methods state the same primary aim and specify a logistic regression of consecutive abstinence on treatment and baseline amount of use (main article p3 lines 591-727). The Results report the primary outcome as 17/61 vs 18/61 with a single test (X2(1) = .17, p = .68; p5 lines 405-460), consistent with the registered outcome and time frame. The Methods-to-Results match is not perfect because the Results report only the single test and not the adjusted model, so I answer probably yes rather than yes.

Table 1 (main article p. 4) shows baseline characteristics that are broadly similar across arms, with no formal baseline tests reported. Group sizes (14/16/14) are close to the intended 1:1:1 ratio. The authors note imbalances in weight/BMI and sex, and median urine protein and eGFR differ between arms (for example eGFR median 91.2 in placebo vs 70.2 in 240 mg). With 14 per group these are compatible with chance. None is shown to be large and very unlikely to be due to chance, so Probably no.

Main article p. 2: "Eligible patients were centrally randomized 1:1:1 ... stratified by proteinuria." The sequence was centrally generated and used by all 21 centres, so allocation was controlled by a central process rather than by site staff. The report does not describe how assignments were delivered to sites (for example IWRS or telephone) or whether the central unit was independent of enrolling staff, so Probably yes rather than Yes. Placebo and active drug were identical injections, which supports concealment of the next assignment.

Main article p. 2: "Randomization was performed using a minimization algorithm, which was centrally generated and used by all centers." Official guidance (Box 4, 1.1) states minimization generally includes a random element and should generally be considered random. The report does not state that a random element was used in this trial, and the registry search (sr_9a4a3c1bd312e2b4) for "random" returned no allocation-method text. Hence Probably yes rather than Yes.

The full analysis set analysed all randomized participants by randomized group regardless of adherence or protocol violations, which follows intention-to-treat principles. Missing outcome data were imputed using last observation carried forward. Imputation is a missing-data matter addressed in the missing outcome data domain, not a deviation from intention-to-treat analysis.

The main article reports only that two placebo-group participants discontinued treatment prematurely because of local COVID-19 outbreaks. This is a deviation inconsistent with the protocol, but it is not described as arising from the trial context such as recruitment or engagement activities or personnel undermining protocol delivery. No non-protocol co-interventions attributable to the trial context are reported.

The trial was described as double-blind with placebo, so participants were intended to be unaware of assignment. However, telitacicept produced injection-site reactions in 19/30 (63.3%) of 240 mg/160 mg recipients versus 0/16 placebo, which participants could plausibly attribute to their assigned intervention. This makes awareness of assignment probable, consistent with the guidance that participants aware of intervention-specific side effects should be answered Probably yes.

The main article reports that all study personnel and participants were blinded during the trial, and that randomization used a centrally generated minimization algorithm with central allocation, which is consistent with allocation concealment. Injection-site reactions could in principle signal assignment to personnel, but no report links these to non-protocol care decisions by personnel.

The main article reports 42 of 44 randomized participants completed treatment, and the full analysis set imputed missing outcome data by LOCF. Imputed values count as missing, and both non-completers were in the placebo group (placebo n=14; telitacicept 240 mg n=14). Outcome data were therefore available for 12/14 (86%) of the placebo comparison arm, which is not nearly all of that arm, and the comparison of interest depends on that arm.

The only missing-data method reported in the read main article is last observation carried forward. The guidance states that LOCF should not be assumed to correct for bias from missing outcome data, and no sensitivity analysis exploring plausible outcomes for the two missing placebo participants was found in the pages read.

The main article attributes the two premature treatment discontinuations in the placebo group to local outbreaks of COVID-19. That is a documented reason unrelated to proteinuria, so missingness is unlikely to depend on the true value of the outcome. Because the reason is external, it does not by itself indicate that the outcome was affected by the participants' proteinuria.
The article states that all study personnel and participants were blinded during the trial, which indicates outcome assessors were not aware of assignment.
The same 24-hour urine protein measurement was applied to all randomized groups under the same protocol. Nothing in the passages read suggests the method differed between arms.

The outcome is 24-hour urinary protein, a quantitative laboratory measurement that is reported as an LS means difference with a 95% CI. The passages read do not describe a judgement-based measurement method.

The analysis intentions are not available in sufficient detail to show whether the reported analysis (change from baseline, LS means, full analysis set, LOCF) was one of several eligible analyses that was selected. Several analyses of the same measurement were plausible (for example, adjusted or final-value models, or other missing-data strategies), so no information is the appropriate answer.

The registered primary outcome (24-hour urine protein at week 24) is the outcome measurement fully reported as the primary result, with the same time point. The report describes it as the primary endpoint, which is consistent with the pre-specified measurement rather than a choice made on the results.

The registry entry (first submitted 2020-02-27, first posted 2020-03-02, start 2020-04-13) pre-dates enrolment and registers the primary outcome as change from baseline in 24-hour urine protein at week 24. The report uses the same outcome, time point and change-from-baseline analysis (LS means difference, full analysis set, LOCF), as the methods describe. Per the guidance, a pre-enrolment registry entry naming this measurement and time point supports Probably yes even though it gives no analysis detail.

Table 1 (main report p. 5) shows the groups well balanced at baseline (for example age 62 vs 63, ECOG 0 61.4% vs 60.5%, newly diagnosed 34.1% vs 33.8%, visceral disease 59.0% vs 58.7%), and the report states baseline characteristics were well balanced (p. 4). Group sizes are 334 per arm, matching the 1:1 ratio. No imbalance suggests a randomization problem.

The same protocol passage (p. 46) states the allocation is concealed from patients and investigator staff and is delivered by an external IRT provider. Remote, centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment staff meets the minimal criterion for Yes in Box 4 and Table 2. Protocol section 6.5.3 (p. 207) adds that randomization data are kept strictly confidential until unblinding.

Protocol section 6.5.2 (p. 46) states the randomization list is produced by an Interactive Response Technology provider using a validated system that automates the random assignment of patient numbers to treatment, with a 1:1 ratio stratified by liver/lung metastases. This is a computer-generated random component, which is the criterion for Yes. Main report Methods (p. 2) confirms random assignment of patients.

The reported Result is the intention-to-treat analysis of all randomized participants: the Figure 1 numbers at risk start at 334 per arm (668 in total), and the Figure 1 and Results text refer to the intention-to-treat population. The safety population (334 vs 330) is a separate summary, not the analysis for this Result. The Result is therefore analysed by assignment, not by treatment received, and no naive per-protocol or as-treated analysis is used.

Question 2.3 is active because 2.1 is Probably yes. The protocol (section 4.1.2, sections 6.5.2 and 6.5.3) describes central IRT randomization and a fully blinded, placebo-controlled design with dosing specified by protocol. The sources reviewed do not describe crossover, contamination or non-protocol co-interventions arising from trial recruitment, engagement or personnel beliefs. Any deviations that might exist in the reviewed text are of the kind that could occur outside a trial, so the answer is Probably no. The main report's adherence and dose-intensity data were not located and inspected for this question.

The protocol (section 6.5.3, p.68) states the trial is double blind: patients are blinded to treatment identity until database lock, and investigational drug is identical in packaging, labelling and appearance to matching placebo. The main report states ribociclib caused a markedly different adverse-event profile: neutropenia of any grade 74.3% vs 5.2%, nausea 51.5% vs 28.5%, diarrhoea 35.0% vs 22.1%. Guidance for 2.1 says side effects known to be specific to one intervention support Yes or Probably yes. The sources do not state whether participants recognised these effects as drug-specific, so the answer is Probably yes rather than Yes.

The protocol (section 6.5.3) states that investigators, study team and anyone involved in study conduct remain blinded to treatment identity, and that randomization data are kept strictly confidential. Section 6.5.2 states randomization numbers are concealed from patients and investigator staff, and the IRT assigns them centrally. The main report describes a placebo-controlled double-blind design (Methods, p.2). Nothing in the sources reports a personnel unblinding.

The main report analyses all randomized participants by intention to treat: 'All randomized participants analysed by intention to treat (668 randomized; 334 per arm)', and the Figure 1 numbers at risk start at 334 in each arm. PFS is a time-to-event outcome, so 'missing' means censored before progression or death for reasons related to loss of follow-up. The protocol and main report state that tumour assessments continue until progression 'including in patients who discontinued treatment for reasons other than progressive disease', and PFS is censored only at the last adequate tumour assessment (protocol p.128 and p.58). This design makes loss of PFS ascertainment unlikely to be large, so outcome data are probably available for nearly all participants. The main report and protocol passages read do not report the number of censored participants per arm, so the answer is Probably yes rather than Yes.

The protocol section 6.5.3 (p.68) states that 'The local (or Novartis-designated) radiologists will remain blinded to the identity of the treatment from the time of randomization until final database lock', and 'patients, investigators, study team, or anyone involved in the study conduct will remain blinded'. Section 7.2.1.1 (p.58) states the central review 'will be carried out in a blinded fashion'. The main report states the independent review committee 'whose members were unaware of treatment assignments prospectively reviewed all imaging data'. The primary endpoint is local investigator/radiologist assessment, so the local radiologist blinding is the relevant element. Blinding is a planned design feature in the protocol and is not confirmed as executed in the main report, so the answer is Probably no rather than No.

Tumour imaging is the same method, using the same RECIST 1.1 criteria and the same schedule for both groups: 'every 8 weeks during the first 18 months, every 12 weeks thereafter until disease progression' (main report p.3), with the protocol defining the same imaging assessment (p.58). Imaging of progression is not triggered by arm-specific toxicity in the reported schedule. The ribociclib arm had additional ECG and laboratory monitoring (main report p.3, safety monitoring), but these are not tumour assessments and do not add opportunities to detect progression. No source reports extra imaging in one arm.

The approved Result is investigator-assessed PFS by RECIST 1.1, the pre-specified primary endpoint. The main report states 'Tumor assessments (computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging) were performed at screening, every 8 weeks during the first 18 months, every 12 weeks thereafter until disease progression'. Protocol section 7.2.1.1 (p.58) states 'Tumor response will be assessed locally and centrally according to ... RECIST Version 1.1'. RECIST 1.1 is the standard imaging method for progression in advanced breast cancer and is capable of detecting progression of the kind that PFS measures. Nothing in the sources suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity.

The protocol and main report both specify the stratified log-rank test and stratified Cox model as the primary efficacy analysis, and the reported hazard ratio is that prespecified analysis. The protocol also prespecifies a sensitivity analysis of PFS based on recalculated lesion responses, which is not reported in the main article. Its absence from the report does not by itself show selection on the results.

The protocol prespecifies investigator-assessed PFS as the primary endpoint and BIRC-assessed PFS as a supportive analysis, and the registry lists one primary PFS outcome. The reported result is the prespecified primary measurement, and no source indicates that a different eligible PFS measurement was omitted because of its results.

The registry record (NCT01958021) was first submitted on 2013-10-04, before the 2013-12-17 start, and registers investigator-assessed PFS by RECIST 1.1 as the single primary outcome with a stratified Cox hazard ratio, matching the reported Result. The protocol primary endpoint (local investigator PFS by RECIST 1.1, stratified by liver/lung metastases) and the main-report stratified log-rank and Cox methods are consistent with the registered plan. The statistical analysis plan module (RAP Module 3) carries a date stamp of 11-Feb-2016, which postdates the interim data cutoff of the reported analysis. This means the RAP date does not establish that the analysis plan was finalised before unblinded outcome data existed, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.

Table 1 (main article p.3) shows closely matched groups: median age 63.0 in both arms; ECOG 0 at 64.0% vs 65.3%; lung or liver metastases 50.0% in both arms; prior endocrine therapy treatment-naive 49.2% vs 53.3%; visceral sites 60.5% vs 60.3%. The only notable difference is metastatic sites of 4 (7.9% vs 14.0%), which is not one of the stratification factors and is not a key prognostic imbalance of the kind that indicates a randomization problem. Differences are compatible with chance.

Protocol p.64 states allocation is made remotely through the IRT after the investigator confirms eligibility, and that the randomization numbers are concealed from patients and investigator staff; the randomization number is not communicated to the caller. Protocol p.65 adds that randomization data are kept strictly confidential until unblinding and that identical packaging and labelling conceal treatment identity. This matches the central/remote allocation criterion for Yes.

Protocol p.64 (Prot_002.pdf, section 6.3.2) states the patient randomization list is produced by a validated Interactive Response Technology system that automates random assignment of patient numbers to randomization numbers. The main article (p.2, Study Design) reports random assignment at a two-to-one ratio, stratified by lung or liver metastases and prior endocrine therapy. A computer-generated random component is therefore described.

The primary PFS analysis used all randomly assigned patients (full analysis set: 484 ribociclib plus fulvestrant, 242 placebo plus fulvestrant), analysed by randomized group. The SAP (p.66) specifies a stratified log-rank test and a stratified Cox hazard ratio, consistent with the protocol's FAS analysis by randomized group and IRT strata (protocol section 10.4, p.125). No post-randomization exclusions from the primary analysis are reported, so the analysis is intention-to-treat as required.

The protocol (section 6.3.3, p.65) states the trial was double-blind: patients were blinded until database lock, with identical packaging, labelling, schedule and appearance of ribociclib and matching placebo. The main article (p.2) describes the study as double-blind and placebo-controlled. Section 4.1 (p.53) states there was no crossover to the experimental arm after a positive PFS result, and patients remained blinded. No source reports participants learning their assigned intervention.

The protocol (p.65) blinds investigators, study team and radiologists to treatment assignment, with matching placebo, and the main article describes a double-blind design. No source reports that personnel learned assignment. However, the ribociclib adverse-event profile (neutropenia, QTc prolongation; main article p.4) is specific to one arm, and the sources do not report whether personnel could infer assignment from it, so the answer is not 'no'.

The primary PFS analysis includes all randomized patients in the full analysis set (484 ribociclib plus fulvestrant, 242 placebo plus fulvestrant), so no randomized participant is excluded from the analysis (main article p.2 CONSORT; p.4 Results). PFS is a time-to-event outcome, so a participant without progression or death is censored, not missing, unless censoring is due to loss to follow-up or withdrawal. The protocol (p.95, section 7.1.7) requires survival follow-up every 12 weeks regardless of treatment discontinuation until death, loss to follow-up, or withdrawal, and the SAP (p.65, Table 3-3) censors at last adequate assessment only for non-progression reasons. Of 726 randomized, 361 had a PFS event (210 ribociclib, 151 placebo). The publication does not report the per-arm number censored for loss to follow-up or withdrawal, so the extent of censoring for non-event reasons cannot be confirmed; the answer is probably yes rather than yes because the design and follow-up rules point to near-complete outcome ascertainment.

The protocol states that the local (or Novartis-designated) radiologists remain blinded to treatment identity from randomization until final database lock (protocol 6.3.3, p.65), and the main article describes the study as double-blind. Blinding of the assessors of the local investigator-assessed PFS is therefore the design, though the sources do not report confirmation that it was implemented for every local assessment.

The protocol specifies one local RECIST 1.1 assessment process applied to all randomized patients, with no arm-specific imaging rule in the inspected passages. The main article reports no arm-specific imaging frequency or differential detection pathway, so there is no positive evidence of systematically different ascertainment of progression between arms.

The approved Result is locally assessed PFS per RECIST 1.1 (protocol p.96 and p.125; registry PFS definition). RECIST 1.1 imaging-based progression is a standard, sensitive method for detecting progression, and nothing in the inspected sources suggests the method cannot detect plausible intervention effects or has poor validity. The question does not assess whether PFS itself is a sensible endpoint.

The SAP pre-specifies one primary analysis (stratified log-rank test and stratified Cox HR on the FAS; SAP p.66) and sensitivity and supportive analyses (SAP p.66-68), including BIRC-based PFS and an audit-based approach. The reported result is the pre-specified primary analysis. The main article does not report the alternative PFS censoring derivation or the sensitivity analyses, so there is no direct evidence that a favourable analysis was chosen from among several.

PFS is the only outcome measurement for the domain that the protocol and SAP specify as primary: locally assessed PFS per RECIST 1.1 (protocol p.33). BIRC-assessed PFS is a pre-specified supportive measurement; it is registered as a secondary outcome and its result is reported in the registry results (outcome measure 3) and the main article (HR 0.492 in the 40% audit sample, p.4). The reported local-PFS result therefore corresponds to the intended measurement and no alternative eligible PFS measurement was left unreported in the captured sources.

The registry record (first submitted 2015-04-01, before start 2015-06-09) names the same primary outcome, PFS per investigator assessment, censored at last adequate assessment, and the FAS of all randomized participants. The SAP version history shows version 1.0 is dated 2015-08-27, before this trial's primary PFS analysis, and specifies a stratified log-rank test with a stratified Cox hazard ratio on the FAS using local RECIST 1.1 PFS (SAP p.66). The protocol (p.33) names the same local PFS primary analysis. The reported primary analysis (HR 0.593, FAS of 484 vs 242) follows that plan. Later SAP amendment 1 (dated 2017 in the history table, 24-Jul-2018 on the cover) changed censoring options and the supportive BIRC audit, not the primary local PFS analysis.

Table 1 shows closely matched arms (ribociclib n=335, placebo n=337): age 43 vs 45 years (median), ECOG 0 in 73% vs 76%, bone metastases 75% vs 73%, visceral 58% vs 56%, previous endocrine therapy 38% vs 42% (eh_aa460064002091a3). No baseline difference is described as an imbalance that would suggest a randomisation failure.

Allocation was made remotely through IRT. The protocol states that the randomisation number 'will not be communicated to the caller' and that the list is 'concealed from patients and investigator staff' (eh_8bc58611d0914a12; supplement copy eh_49dd2d27bc10571e). Investigators register patients into IRT with identifying information before assignment (eh_565143e46d03c263). Study drug packs are identical in packaging and appearance, so the next allocation cannot be read off the dispensed product before assignment.

The main report states patients were randomised 1:1 by permuted block randomisation through interactive response technology (eh_565143e46d03c263). The protocol describes the randomisation list as produced by a validated IRT system that automates the random assignment of patient numbers to randomisation numbers (eh_8bc58611d0914a12). A random element is therefore documented, and the block scheme is random-permuted.

The primary PFS analysis used the full analysis set of all randomised patients, per the intention-to-treat principle, with a stratified log-rank test and stratified Cox model (eh_ce8e555ae4f92682). The cited passage states no exclusions after randomisation.

The main report describes the trial as 'randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled' (eh_ea502717b1a442c7). Protocol section 6.5.3 states patients remain blinded to treatment identity from randomisation until database lock (eh_9bf59088797db85d). Participants were therefore not aware of their assigned intervention.

Protocol section 6.5.3 states that investigators, the study team and anyone involved in conduct remain blinded to treatment identity from randomisation until database lock (eh_9bf59088797db85d). The main report describes the trial as double-blind (eh_ea502717b1a442c7). Personnel were therefore not aware of the assigned intervention.

The primary PFS analysis covers all randomised patients (full analysis set, ITT; eh_ce8e555ae4f92682), and the trial profile accounts for the randomised groups (335 assigned to ribociclib; eh_e14d6575086568c8). PFS is a time-to-event outcome with a sponsor-specified data cutoff set before unmasking, so participants without an event by the cutoff are censored rather than missing. The Kaplan-Meier at-risk tables show censoring counts per arm (eh_34af0af8bb648c7f) that are small relative to the 318 events analysed. They do not separate administrative censoring from loss to follow-up before progression, so probably yes rather than yes.

Protocol section 6.5.3 states that investigators, the study team and anyone involved in conduct, and the local or designated radiologists, remain blinded to treatment identity from randomisation until database lock (eh_9bf59088797db85d). The main report describes the trial as double-blind (eh_ea502717b1a442c7). The investigator-assessed PFS was therefore recorded by assessors unaware of the intervention received.

One pre-specified endpoint definition (RECIST 1.1 progression or death) applies to both arms (eh_4d91257ff1637803), with the same tumour assessment method in both groups (eh_ada2dfb7b5586a46). No group-specific assessment schedule or extra imaging is reported in the cited passages, so the measurement method is probably not different between groups.

The primary endpoint is investigator-assessed PFS, defined by RECIST version 1.1 progression or death from any cause (eh_4d91257ff1637803). Protocol section 9 describes tumour response assessed locally and centrally by RECIST 1.1 (eh_ada2dfb7b5586a46). This is the standard, pre-specified imaging-based measurement for PFS, so the method is not inappropriate.

The primary PFS analysis is a stratified unadjusted Cox model with the stratified log-rank test, as specified in the SAP (eh_72e80a7bdac88ca5) and reported in the article (eh_ce8e555ae4f92682). The reported HR therefore corresponds to the pre-specified primary analysis, and no alternative primary model is shown to have been available for selection. Probably no rather than no because the supportive analyses were not confirmed as fully reported.

The sole registered primary outcome is PFS by investigator assessment, using RECIST 1.1 (eh_4d91257ff1637803). The SAP lists masked BIRC PFS as a supportive analysis (eh_b87ab59d8414c680), and the article reports investigator PFS as the primary endpoint with central review as supportive. Both measurements were reported, so the reported investigator-assessed result was not selected from several eligible measurements.

The article states the primary PFS analysis (stratified Cox, log-rank, 329 events) and that the 20-Aug-2017 data cutoff was set before unmasking (eh_ce8e555ae4f92682). The SAP document history records a first approved SAP on 18-Feb-2015 and Amendment 1 on 5-Jun-2017 (eh_2b5045bb729ace6d), both before the cutoff. The SAP's primary analysis is a stratified unadjusted Cox model (eh_72e80a7bdac88ca5), matching the report. The registry describes the same PFS outcome and stratified Cox analysis, was first submitted 22-Oct-2014, and enrolment began 20-Nov-2014. Protocol Amendment 4 (24-Feb-2017) set the 329-event final analysis before unblinding. Amendment 2 (27-Sep-2017) lists clarifications, not changes to the primary PFS analysis (eh_47d8e7a7b9909045). Probably yes rather than yes because unblinding dates and the earlier SAP text are not confirmed.

The main report states 'Patients had well-balanced baseline characteristics (Table 1)'. Table 1 shows 446 vs 223 patients, matching the intended 2:1 ratio, and similar distributions of ET resistance (primary 24.9% vs 26.0%), metastatic site (visceral 54.9% vs 57.4%) and other key prognostic factors. No imbalance suggests a problem with randomization.

Protocol section 9.3 says that after informed consent site personnel access the IWRS to assign a patient number, and that patients meeting enrolment criteria are then randomly assigned through the IWRS. The sequence is therefore held by a remote, centrally administered system independent of enrolment staff, and is revealed only after enrolment and assignment. The main report describes the same interactive web-based scheme. Identical appearance of study drug containers is not explicitly quoted in the passages read, but the remote assignment mechanism alone meets the Yes criterion for remote or central allocation.

Protocol section 9.3 states that assignment 'will be determined by a computer-generated random sequence using the IWRS'. The main report (p3) states 'Using an interactive, web-based randomization scheme, patients were assigned ... in a 2:1 ratio.' Both describe a random component for the allocation sequence.

The main report states that 669 patients were randomly assigned and that the PFS Kaplan-Meier analysis (Fig 2A) is of the 'intent-to-treat population', with all 669 randomized patients analysed. The protocol (section 12.2.7) specifies that the primary test of PFS compares the two treatment groups using a log-rank test stratified by the randomization factors, in the ITT population. This is an analysis by assignment with all randomized participants included, which is appropriate for the effect of assignment.

The protocol describes the study as 'randomized, double-blind' with 'Blinded study drug' (abemaciclib or placebo, supplied as identical-form capsules dosed Q12H). Section 8.2 states that 'patients, investigational sites, and the sponsor study team do not have immediate access to treatment assignments'. Placebo control supports blinding of participants. Probably no rather than No because the main report's adverse-event table (Table 3, abemaciclib diarrhoea 86.4% vs placebo 24.7%) shows large between-arm differences in side effects, which participants could use to infer their allocation. No report says participants were unblinded.

Protocol section 8.2 states that investigational sites and the sponsor study team 'do not have immediate access to treatment assignments for any patients', and section 9.3 says site personnel use the IWRS to assign the blinded study drug and fulvestrant, so assignment is not visible to them. The Result's comparison uses identical blinded drug. Probably no rather than No because the adverse-event profile differs between arms, which could let investigators infer allocation.

The main report's CONSORT-style flow (p2, lines 47-61) shows an intent-to-treat population of 669 with 'Lost to follow-up (n = 6)' in one arm and '(n = 4)' in the other, so 10 of 669 randomized participants (1.5%) were lost to follow-up. The results text (p4, lines 42-50) confirms 669 randomized (446 and 223) and a data cut-off of February 14, 2017. For this time-to-event outcome, the outcome is observed or censored for all but about 1.5% of randomized participants, and the lost participants are few enough that their outcomes could make no important difference to the hazard ratio. Yes, rather than probably yes, because the counts are explicitly reported.

The protocol (section 8.2) states that 'patients, investigational sites, and the sponsor study team do not have immediate access to treatment assignments for any patients', and section 9.3 says assignment is made through the IWRS. Investigational sites are the assessors of the investigator-assessed PFS, so they were masked to treatment assignment. The main report adds a blinded central analysis, which 'demonstrated consistent PFS results' (p5). Probably no rather than No because the report does not state explicitly that the investigators assessing progression were blinded, and the protocol refers to access to assignments rather than to blinding of each assessment.

The same imaging schedule (every 8 weeks in year 1, every 12 weeks thereafter, and within 2 weeks of clinical progression) applied to both arms (p3). Progression is therefore detected on a common schedule rather than through passive collection. The abemaciclib arm had more dose reductions and interruptions for adverse events (p4: 189 patients, 42.9%, versus 3, 1.3%), which could add clinic contacts, but the report does not indicate that this led to additional scans. Probably no rather than No because the extra clinic contacts in the abemaciclib arm are not quantified.

The main report (p3, lines 1-165) states that tumours were measured by CT or MRI 'according to RECIST version 1.1' at baseline, 'every 8 weeks the first year, every 12 weeks thereafter, and within 2 weeks of clinical progression', and p1 names investigator-assessed PFS as the primary end point. RECIST 1.1 is a standard, validated imaging-based progression criterion that is sensitive to the plausible effects of a CDK4/6 inhibitor on tumour progression. Probably no rather than No because the report does not give the measurement details beyond the RECIST reference.

The reported HR (0.553) is the registered and delivered-protocol primary PFS analysis, a stratified log-rank comparison in the ITT population (section 12.2.7, eh_7d28a22c7952d76b). The main article reports this analysis together with its median PFS values and a Kaplan-Meier figure, without alternative PFS analyses being reported for selection. No evidence was found that an alternative analysis was run and omitted.

The registered primary outcome and the reported result are both PFS. Investigator-assessed PFS is the reported primary result, and a blinded independent central review of PFS is also reported (Fig 2B; text states consistent PFS results, eh_b95b85f08c13a3fa; eh_764d476b7edca898). Both measurements of the outcome are reported, so there is no evident selection among measurements of PFS based on results.

The statistical analysis plan (SAP_005, I3Y-MC-JPBL v4) carries an approval date of 08-Jul-2016, which precedes the data cut-off of February 14, 2017 reported in the main article (eh_fb1928fdfde8f4a5). The delivered protocol specifies the PFS primary test as a stratified log-rank test in the ITT population (section 12.2.7), matching the reported HR 0.553 (95% CI 0.449 to 0.681; log-rank P < .001; eh_19f40ceb4f6db8c5). The registry record lists PFS as the registered primary outcome with the same time frame (sh_c6f3bfda13490426). No amendment or unblinded interim use is documented in the sources read.

The Table 1 baseline characteristics are similar between arms (median age 63 in both; visceral metastases 52.4% vs 53.9%; ECOG 0 58.5% vs 63.0%; PgR positive 77.7% vs 77.0%). The 328:165 group sizes approximate the intended 2:1 ratio, and no baseline difference is reported as suggesting a randomization problem.

Section 9.3 of the protocol states that sites access the IWRS upon obtaining informed consent to receive a patient number and that assignment is made by the IWRS, so allocation was remote and administered by an external system independent of enrolment staff. This matches the guidance example of an interactive web response randomization service for Yes.

The registry-linked protocol (Prot_004 p.36 and Prot_000 p.36, section 9.3) states that assignment to treatment groups 'will be determined by a computer-generated random sequence using the IWRS', which is a random component of the kind the guidance lists as Yes.

The primary analysis included all patients in the intent-to-treat population, with log-rank testing stratified by metastatic site and prior endocrine therapy. The reported analysis covers all 493 randomized patients (328 abemaciclib and 165 placebo) analysed by allocated arm. The CONSORT diagram shows 2 abemaciclib and 3 placebo patients did not receive allocated intervention, and one placebo patient received abemaciclib in cycle 1, but all were kept in their randomized arm for efficacy.

The main article describes a double-blind, randomized trial of abemaciclib or matching placebo plus an NSAI. Participants were not told their arm in the reported design, and no unblinding or guessing analysis is reported. Diarrhoea was the most common adverse event in the abemaciclib arm, so participants could partly infer their arm from side effects, but the article reports no such unblinding.

The main article describes a double-blind design with matching placebo, and allocation was made centrally through an interactive web response system. Investigators and trial personnel were therefore not reported as aware of assignment.

The JCO main article reports the efficacy population as all 493 randomized patients (328 abemaciclib plus NSAI, 165 placebo plus NSAI), and the supplement CONSORT diagram likewise shows all 493 analysed for efficacy with still-on-treatment and discontinued-intervention counts. PFS is defined from randomization to progression or death, and the SAP censoring rules censor participants without events at their last adequate assessment rather than excluding them, so PFS data are available for essentially all randomized participants. The registry outcome record reports censored counts (190 abemaciclib, 57 placebo) among evaluable participants, which indicates follow-up data exist for the remainder.

The outcome is investigator-determined, so the assessors are the treating investigators. The trial is described as double-blind, but the captured passages do not state whether investigators assessing tumour progression were masked to arm. A bounded search for blinding and tumour-assessment terms returned dosing and unblinding-plan passages, not an assessor-masking statement. Under the guidance, absence of a statement means no information, so awareness cannot be excluded.

The protocol applies the same investigator-determined RECIST v1.1 PFS definition to both arms, with the same tumour-assessment framework, so measurement method and thresholds are the same across groups. The trial is described as double-blind with matching placebo, which makes differential scheduling or detection less likely. The per-arm assessment schedule was not directly inspected.

Influence is likely only with strong beliefs about the treatment effect. The independent blinded central review of the same PFS endpoint gave a hazard ratio of 0.51 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.72), closely matching the investigator-assessed hazard ratio of 0.54 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.72). Concordance between an independent review and investigator assessment argues against meaningful influence of investigator awareness on progression assessments.

Investigator-determined RECIST progression involves judgement from imaging, and the assessor is the treating investigator. Under the guidance, observer-reported outcomes that involve judgement can be influenced by knowledge of the intervention received, so influence is possible if the assessors were aware.

The approved outcome is investigator-assessed PFS, defined in the protocol as investigator-determined objective progression per RECIST v1.1 or death from any cause. RECIST imaging-based progression is a standard, sensitive method for PFS in metastatic breast cancer, and the question concerns method validity rather than whether PFS is a sensible endpoint. Nothing in the captured sources indicates an inappropriate measurement method.

The reported hazard ratio (0.54) comes from the stratified Cox model that the SAP pre-specifies as the primary PFS analysis (SAP_002 p.19, eh_978e65e42584930f). The same passage lists a restricted mean difference in PFS as a further planned analysis, which the report does not present. The investigator-assessed and BICR hazard ratios agree (0.54 and 0.51), so the reported analysis is not a clear outlier among the captured analyses. The absence of the restricted mean difference is an unresolved question rather than evidence that it was dropped for results.

The registry and protocol specify one primary outcome, investigator-assessed PFS (Prot_003 p.64, eh_037869041e9359c3; registry eh_daa1d78f6e564a1d). The BICR-assessed PFS is a second reading of the same outcome that the report presents alongside the investigator-assessed result (eh_9d17fbf52ff5ef2f). The reported hazard ratio uses the investigator-assessed measure, which is the registered primary, and the BICR hazard ratio (0.51) is close to it. No evidence in the captured passages shows that eligible measurements were dropped in favour of the reported one.

The registry entry was first submitted 2014-09-18, before the 2014-11-06 start date, and its primary outcome is PFS from randomization to progression or death under RECIST v1.1 (registry lines 31-43 and 125-129). The SAP (SAP_002 p.19) pre-specifies the PFS Kaplan-Meier curves, medians and a Cox model stratified by nature of disease and prior endocrine therapy, which matches the reported hazard ratio method. The report states that the analysis is intent-to-treat and that the interim analysis was run by the DMC. The SAP's version date and finalization relative to unblinded outcome data were not established in the captured passages.
The main report states that baseline characteristics were well balanced between treatment arms in cohort A and cohort B. No reported imbalance suggests a problem with the randomization process.

Assignment was made through an interactive web response system, with site personnel entering patient details and receiving the assignment only after enrolment. This is a remote, independently controlled allocation method, matching the Box 4 example of an internet-based randomization service. The protocol confirms IWRS-based assignment and blinded study drug.

The main report states that treatment was determined by a computer-generated random sequence (2:1, block size 6, stratified). The protocol Section 9.3 confirms assignment by a computer-generated random sequence using the IWRS.

The report analyses efficacy in the intent-to-treat population, which includes all randomly assigned patients. The SAP defines the ITT population as all randomized patients, grouped by randomized treatment.

The report states that patients, physicians and investigators were masked to treatment allocation, and the protocol describes matching placebo capsules and a double-blind design. No source reports that participants were unblinded during the trial. Toxicity profiles could in principle reveal allocation, but no unblinding is reported.

The protocol states that the investigational treatment is double-blind, with patients, investigational sites and the sponsor study team lacking immediate access to treatment assignments. Blinded study drug was supplied as capsules, and the report describes no unblinding of personnel.

Cohort A randomized 207 patients to abemaciclib plus NSAI and 99 to placebo plus NSAI, and the ITT analysis includes all of them (main report p.5; supplement trial profile). The registry participant-flow table reports study-level non-completion by reason: lost to follow-up 1 and withdrawal by subject 3 in the abemaciclib arm, and lost to follow-up 4 and withdrawal by subject 1 in the placebo arm. Those are the participants whose PFS status is most likely missing, about 1.9% (4/207) and 5.1% (5/99). Observed PFS events were 66 of 207 and 53 of 99 (main report p.5), so the number of participants with possibly missing outcomes (9) is far smaller than the observed events (119). Under RoB 2 Box 8, that makes the bias necessarily small, so the outcome is probably available for nearly all randomized participants. The SAP censoring rules (Table JPBQ.6.1) also treat progression-free status as known for participants censored administratively at the last adequate assessment, which is not missing outcome data.

The main report states that patients, physicians, and investigators were masked to treatment allocation, and that matching placebo was used (main report p.4). The protocol describes the study as double-blind, with investigational sites and the sponsor study team without access to assignments (protocol sections 8.2 and 9.5). The investigator-assessed PFS outcome was therefore assessed by blinded investigators.

The imaging schedule and RECIST criteria are the same for both arms, and both arms received matching placebo or active drug with the same NSAI and imaging schedule (main report p.4; protocol section 10.1.1). No arm received extra scans or visits that the other did not, so ascertainment of progression was not expected to differ between arms.

PFS was assessed by CT or MRI according to RECIST version 1.1 at baseline and at scheduled intervals, with bone scintigraphy at baseline and every sixth cycle from cycle 6 (main report p.4; protocol section 10.1.1). RECIST-based imaging is a standard method for progression in this setting, and the endpoint was prespecified. Nothing in the sources suggests the method was insensitive to plausible effects.

The reported result is the prespecified primary analysis: a stratified Cox hazard ratio with a stratified log-rank test in the ITT population (SAP section 6.7.1; main report p.5). The SAP also prespecifies a restricted mean difference in PFS as an additional analysis (SAP section 6.7.1.3.2), but the main report does not report it. Reporting the primary analysis rather than alternatives is not evidence of selection on the results.

PFS in cohort A is measured in a single way: investigator-assessed progression by RECIST v1.1 on CT or MRI, or death from any cause (registered primary outcome 1; main report p.4). The registry lists PFS in cohort B as a separate secondary outcome in a different comparison, so it is not an alternative measurement of the same result. The other registered outcomes (overall survival, response rate, and so on) are different outcome domains. No other eligible PFS measurement, such as a different definition or time point, appears in the Sources.

The registry record, first submitted 2016-05-04 before enrolment started on 2016-12-05, lists the registered primary outcome as PFS from randomization to RECIST v1.1 progression or death from any cause (registered primary outcome 1). The main report analyses PFS on that definition, and its statistical methods (stratified Cox model, Kaplan-Meier, ITT population) match the SAP's primary PFS analysis (SAP section 6.7.1). The SAP (version 2, approved 25 April 2019) and protocol (approved 14 May 2019) both post-date the interim data cutoff of 29 March 2019, so they cannot show that the analysis was fixed before unblinded interim data existed. An earlier SAP version is not among the Sources. The answer rests on the dated registry entry and on the report following the documented plan.

The report states that 'Patient demographics and baseline characteristics were balanced across the treatment groups' (eh_a4c4e80491e611c1). It notes more diabetes (16 vs 8) and pre-diabetes (71 vs 50) in the Nefecon group but gives no test for these and does not treat them as a problem with randomization. These differences are compatible with chance and are not key prognostic imbalances in the sense of Box 4.

Allocation was made through an interactive response technology system run by a separate CRO team (eh_ab220bdb098eee00). The protocol (eh_206dabd1708fd91c) states that the IRT randomization triggers the first shipment of study drug and that the investigator dispenses the assigned drug after randomisation. Remote, centrally administered allocation independent of enrolment staff meets the criteria for Yes in Box 4.

Main report p3 (eh_ab220bdb098eee00): 'Patients were randomly assigned (1:1)... The randomisation list was generated by a separate unmasked contract research organisation team using an interactive response technology system... stratified... in permuted blocks of four.' The list was generated by an IRT system and described as permuted blocks, which implies a random ordering within blocks. The report does not explicitly say the within-block order was random, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.

The requested estimate (2·95, 95% CI 1·67–4·58) is from robust regression of multiply imputed values in the full analysis set of 364 patients (182 per arm). The Table S3 footnote states that it excludes data observed after rescue medication. This censors post-randomisation data from patients who received rescue medication (20 Nefecon, 27 placebo), so it is not a strict ITT analysis. However, all randomised patients in the FAS remain in their randomised group, and the all-data sensitivity analyses were consistent with the primary analysis (p 7).

The main report states that patients, investigators and site staff were masked to treatment assignment throughout the 2-year trial, and that Nefecon and placebo capsules were matched in taste, smell and appearance (p 3). Protocol section 5.3 (p 35) describes the same blinding. Three patients were unmasked in an emergency, which does not indicate a general loss of participant blinding.

The same masking statement covers investigators and site staff (p 3). Randomisation was by an interactive response system run by an unmasked contract research organisation team, so allocation was concealed from site staff at the point of enrolment (p 3).

Only 2 randomised patients were excluded from the FAS, for pre-specified randomisation errors. Post-rescue data were excluded for 47 patients (20 Nefecon, 27 placebo) out of 364. The main report states that all-data supplementary analyses were consistent with the primary analysis (p 7), so the exclusions are unlikely to change the conclusion materially.

Of 364 randomised patients (182 per arm), 161 (Nefecon) and 165 (placebo) had at least one valid eGFR at 24 months, so 21 and 17 patients respectively (38 total, about 10%) lacked the 24-month outcome (p 7). Ten percent missing is not 'nearly all' for a continuous outcome, where about 95% availability is usually needed. The 2-year slope does use earlier eGFR values, so the effective missingness is smaller than 10%, but it is not negligible.

The 2·95 estimate uses robust regression of multiply imputed 2-year eGFR values (supplement p 5). Multiple imputation reduces bias only when missingness depends on measured variables included in the imputation model, and the trialists give no MNAR sensitivity analysis showing that plausible values of the missing outcomes would not change the estimate. The supplementary analyses (random coefficients 1·82, linear spline 2·78) are all based on the same observed-data assumption, and the random-coefficients estimate is about 40% smaller, so the result is sensitive to the analysis model.

The completion counts are similar in both arms (21 vs 17 patients without 24-month data, a difference of four), and no reasons for missingness that differ between arms are reported in the passages read. The analysis uses multiple imputation from the observed longitudinal eGFR trajectory, which is the measured variable most likely to explain missingness related to progression. This suggests that missingness was probably not strongly dependent on the outcome. The reasons-for-missingness data needed to confirm this were not located.

The main report states that patients who discontinued study treatment were followed up 'unless they withdrew their consent' (p 3). Withdrawal and loss of 24-month eGFR could be related to health status or to the progression of IgA nephropathy, so missingness could depend on the true value of the outcome.

The main report states that patients, investigators and site staff were masked to treatment assignment throughout. The central laboratory is not named as masked, so its awareness of assignment is not confirmed.
eGFR was calculated by a central laboratory at each timepoint for all participants, so the measurement method is the same in both arms at comparable time points.
eGFR is a creatinine-based calculated value with no judgement involved in its assessment, so knowledge of assignment is unlikely to influence it.

eGFR (CKD-EPI, central laboratory) is the standard kidney-function measure for IgA nephropathy trials and is sensitive to the 2-year slope difference estimated here (2·95 mL/min per 1·73 m² per year). Nothing in the cited passages suggests the method is inappropriate for the outcome.

Table S3 (appendix p10) reports three 2-year slope analyses of the same eGFR data: the pre-specified random coefficients model (1·82, 95% CI 0·50–3·13), robust regression (2·95, 1·67–4·58), and the pre-specified linear spline (2·78, 1·39–4·17). All three are reported with CIs, all favour Nefecon, and the reported method is justified in the text (§1.4.3). The spline, which was pre-specified before unblinding the full study, gives an estimate close to the reported one. This makes it unlikely that the reported estimate was selected from the alternatives on the basis of its results.

The requested outcome is the 2-year eGFR slope, measured by central-laboratory eGFR at each timepoint. The registry's primary outcome is the time-weighted average of eGFR (Part B), and the 2-year slope is registered neither as primary nor secondary. The alternative eGFR summaries are different analyses of the same measurement and are assessed under 5.3, so they do not add a separate measurement choice here.

The protocol (§9.2.1.2, p61) pre-specifies the 2-year eGFR slope analysis as a random coefficients model. The reported 2·95 estimate uses a different method, half the between-arm difference in mean change from robust regression on multiply imputed log-eGFR, which the supplement (§1.4.3, p5) introduces after saying the random coefficients method 'underestimates' the effect. The supplement says the random coefficients analysis was planned before Part A unblinding, but does not date the robust-regression method. The linear spline was pre-specified before unblinding the full study, but the reported slope does not use it.

Table 1 shows baseline characteristics well balanced across the 2:1 groups (444 vs 222). The authors report no significant differences except ECOG performance status (P=0.004), a single difference that is compatible with chance among the many comparisons shown. Visceral disease (48.2% vs 49.5%), prior hormonal therapy (56.1% vs 56.8%) and DFI (40.1% vs 41.9% for >12 months) are closely matched. The group-size ratio matches the intended 2:1 allocation.

Protocol Section 5.1 requires the site to submit a pre-randomization form for sponsor approval and then enroll via a centralized internet/telephone registration system (IRT), which assigns the patient number and study medication. Allocation was therefore administered remotely by a unit independent of enrolment staff, and assignment was irreversible at the point of registration. Placebo is matching and identical in appearance (p.59), so the blinded assignment was not visible to recruiters.

The article (p.2) and the protocol (p.42 of Final Protocol; Prot_000 p.57) state that eligible patients were 'randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio' to palbociclib-letrozole or placebo-letrozole, stratified by site of disease, DFI and prior hormonal therapy, via a centralized internet/telephone registration (IRT) system. No passage read names the random-number method itself, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes: a random component is stated and the sponsor-run central IRT trial makes a random sequence reasonable to assume.

Figure S1 (appendix p.12) lists 666 randomized patients in the Full Analysis (Intention-to-Treat) population, with 444 analyzed in the palbociclib-letrozole group and 222 in the placebo-letrozole group, and zero patients receiving a different treatment from the one allocated. The SAP specifies the primary PFS analysis as a stratified log-rank test in the ITT population (protocol SAP p.37, section on the primary analysis). The analysis is by assigned group, with no naive per-protocol or as-treated primary analysis and no post-randomization exclusion.

The protocol specifies dose interruption, delay, and reduction for treatment-related toxicity (Prot_000 p.61, section 5.3.4; protocol p.47, section 5.3.4.2.3). The large dose-reduction difference (36.0% vs 1.4%) therefore reflects protocol-consistent toxicity management, which the guidance says is not a deviation from intended intervention. The report does not describe non-protocol co-interventions or contamination arising from the trial context. Discontinuation for progression is also protocol-consistent. The few protocol-violation discontinuations are small in number and not described as arising from trial context.

The design is described as double-blind with matched placebo (main article p.2). However, palbociclib produced toxicities that were markedly more frequent than with placebo, including grade 3-4 neutropenia (66.4% vs 1.4%), alopecia (grade 1 30.2% vs 14.9%), and stomatitis (15.3% vs 5.9%) (p.8). Participants can therefore plausibly infer their arm from their own side effects, so blinding of participants is probably incomplete. The report does not state whether participants guessed their allocation, so this answer is an inference from the toxicity profile, not a documented unblinding.

The treating investigators made palbociclib dose reductions in 160/444 (36.0%) of palbociclib-letrozole patients versus 3/222 (1.4%) of placebo-letrozole patients (main article p.7). These reductions were driven by toxicities that are specific to palbociclib, mainly neutropenia (grade 3-4 66.4% vs 1.4%, p.8). Investigators who manage those toxicities can infer the arm, so carers and people delivering the intervention probably knew the assigned intervention. The report does not state how personnel were masked to hematologic results.

The main article reports PFS for all 666 randomized patients (444 vs 222) in an ITT analysis, with numbers at risk shown at each time point for both arms (Figure 1, p.9). The protocol (section 7.3, p.482) says no values are imputed for PFS and non-event observations are censored, so every participant has a PFS observation as event or censored time. The relevant question for missing data is therefore whether censoring is balanced across arms, which is addressed in 3.2 and 3.3 rather than here. The only outcome-availability gap identified is that the number censored for reasons other than progression or death is not reported by arm.

The registry record for NCT01740427 lists masking as QUADRUPLE, with participant, care provider, investigator and outcomes assessor all masked (registry page 1, lines 73-75). The main article describes a double-blind study (p.2). Guidance asks whether outcome assessors were blinded, and this record says they were. The answer is probably no rather than no because the registry is a sponsor record and does not describe how investigator-assessed progression dates were blinded in practice.

Both arms followed the same protocol with matched placebo, and progression was defined by the same radiologic RECIST 1.1 criterion in both arms (main article p.3). The guidance identifies extra healthcare contacts as a route to differential detection, but for a radiologically defined end point the detection route is the imaging schedule, which is protocol-driven.

The prespecified primary end point is investigator-assessed PFS by RECIST 1.1, defined as time from randomization to radiologically confirmed progression or death (main article p.3). Radiologic progression is a standard, sensitive measure for a PFS end point, and the blinded central review in Figure 1B (HR 0.65) reproduces the direction and size of the investigator-assessed effect.

The reported hazard ratio of 0.58 comes from the investigator-assessed PFS analysis in the intention-to-treat population, which the report and the SAP identify as primary. Other analyses (central review, subgroups and sensitivity analyses) are reported alongside it, and the central review HR of 0.65 agrees in direction. The reported primary analysis therefore does not appear to have been chosen from several eligible analyses on the basis of results.

Investigator-assessed PFS by RECIST v1.1 is the single prespecified primary end point. The SAP describes the investigator radiologic assessment as the primary basis, with blinded central review as a supporting assessment. The report presents both (Figure 1A and 1B), with the investigator result as primary. The reported measurement therefore does not appear to have been selected from several eligible measurements on the basis of results.

The registry record was first submitted on 26 November 2012, before enrolment began on 22 February 2013 (registry lines 30-41). It names progression-free survival as assessed by the investigator, defined by RECIST v1.1 as time to first documented progression or death, as the primary outcome (registry lines 121-124). The protocol header reads 'Final Protocol, 30 October 2012' (protocol p.69). The report presents this prespecified primary outcome, so the measurement and its definition appear to have been fixed in advance. The later SAP describes the same end point and does not show a change.

Table 1 (main report p4) reports baseline characteristics that are similar between the oral semaglutide and placebo arms, with no imbalance evident in the characteristics shown. Stratification by cardiovascular risk status was pre-specified and applied at randomisation.

Allocation is made only after eligibility is confirmed, through a trial-specific IV/WRS that is accessed centrally by the investigator by internet or telephone, with access restricted to authorised persons (protocol p43-44, Section 11 and the IV/WRS description). Site staff therefore cannot foresee the next assignment from a list held locally, which is consistent with allocation concealment.

The main report states that patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio and stratified by cardiovascular disease, CKD, or risk factors only (p2 lines 90-98). Protocol v3.0 Section 11 (p43 of 79) states that the investigator must use IV/WRS, which ensures random assignment 1:1 and even distribution within the strata. The sequence-generation algorithm is not named, but allocation by a trial-specific central interactive system is a probable computer-generated random sequence.

The statistical analysis section states that 'all analyses involved the full analysis set, which included all randomly assigned patients' (main report p3 lines 58-59). The primary outcome analysis is a stratified Cox model with trial group as a fixed factor, which analyses participants in their randomized groups, regardless of treatment received. This is an intention-to-treat analysis, and the report does not describe a per-protocol or as-treated primary analysis.

The main report states that patients were randomly assigned to oral semaglutide or placebo 'in a double-blind fashion' (p2 lines 90-94). The protocol describes identical tablets for the two arms, so participants could not distinguish the assigned treatment by appearance, and no report describes unblinding or intervention-specific side effects that would reveal assignment.

The same double-blind statement applies to carers and people delivering the interventions, and the allocation was made centrally by IV/WRS with restricted access, so site personnel had no routine knowledge of assignment (protocol Section 11, p43 of 79). The source does not separately name each class of personnel as masked.

The main report states that 3172 of 3183 randomized patients (99.7%) completed the trial and that vital-status information was collected for the 11 patients who did not complete it, accounting for all patients who took part. Outcome data are therefore available for all or nearly all of the 3183 randomized patients (1591 oral semaglutide, 1592 placebo). At most 11 participants (about 0.7% of the full analysis set) lack trial-completion data, and vital status was collected for all of them, so the number with missing primary-outcome data is small enough that it could make no important difference to the hazard ratio of 0.79 (95% CI 0.57 to 1.11) for this Result. The per-arm split of the 11 non-completers is not reported in the main article, but the total is too small to alter the conclusion.

The main report states that cardiovascular events were adjudicated by an independent external event-adjudication committee whose members were unaware of the trial-group assignments (eh_f4dfdfe3e8bb765e). The protocol describes the committee as performing adjudication in an independent and blinded manner (eh_286a9a9992925f2d). The outcome assessor for the composite is therefore blinded to intervention received.

Both arms were followed with the same visit schedule (every 6 to 7 weeks in person or by telephone, eh_010a870297e0bb3c) and the same central adjudication process for the same prespecified events (eh_f4dfdfe3e8bb765e; eh_286a9a9992925f2d). Because the composite events are confirmed centrally rather than detected passively through differing care contacts, there is no obvious mechanism by which the oral semaglutide arm had more opportunity to have events identified than the placebo arm.

The outcome is a prespecified composite of cardiovascular death (including undetermined causes), nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke. The main report states that cardiovascular events were adjudicated by an independent external event-adjudication committee (eh_f4dfdfe3e8bb765e), and the protocol specifies ongoing adjudication of predefined cardiovascular events by an external event adjudication committee (eh_286a9a9992925f2d). Adjudicated, prespecified clinical events of this kind are usually sensitive to plausible effects, and the sources raise no concern about instrument validity. The question concerns method rather than whether the composite is a sensible choice, and no source describes a method that could fail to detect these events.

The protocol and SAP prespecify one primary analysis for this endpoint, a stratified Cox model on the full analysis set over the in-trial period (protocol p.63; SAP p.11), and the report presents that analysis. Prespecified sensitivity analyses (protocol p.64; SAP p.12) are described in the main article as exploring robustness, and the reported result is the prespecified primary analysis rather than a sensitivity analysis chosen on the basis of results.

The protocol prespecifies the primary MACE composite, a confirmatory secondary expanded composite (adding unstable angina and heart failure hospitalisation), an all-cause-death composite, and each individual component (protocol pp.10, 20, 65). The main report's Table 2 reports every one of these cardiovascular measures with its hazard ratio and CI, so no eligible intended measurement was left out of the report, and the primary composite is not selected from among unreported alternatives.

Protocol v3.0, dated 12 February 2016 and so before enrolment began on 17 January 2017 (registry start date), states the primary estimand as time from randomisation to first MACE and analyses it by a stratified Cox model on the full analysis set over the in-trial observation period (protocol p.61; primary endpoint text at p.63). The registry record was first submitted 23 February 2016 with the same MACE composite outcome, and the main report's methods and Table 2 (HR 0.79, 61/1591 vs 76/1592) follow this plan. The SAP v2.0 (1 November 2018, Final) also specifies the same primary analysis but is dated after the trial's primary completion (25 September 2018), so it does not by itself establish finalisation before unblinding; the probable answer rests on the pre-enrolment protocol.

Table 3 shows the groups similar at baseline: gestational age (p=0.76), birth weight (p=0.94), antenatal steroids (p=0.29) and other characteristics mostly non-significant.
