The one nominal difference, male sex (50% vs 62.5%, p=0.07), is compatible with chance and not a key prognostic factor with a very small p-value.

The paper describes a computer-generated random sequence but gives no account of how assignments were delivered to enrolling staff or protected until assignment (no central or remote allocation, sealed envelopes or matched drug containers are described). The trial was open-label, so the circumstances do not support a probable answer either way. The registry record carries no allocation-concealment description.

The main report states that randomization was performed using a computer-generated random sequence of numbers, and that the particular pharmacological agent was selected randomly using the same method (p.732).

The primary analysis is intention-to-treat, with all 104 randomized infants per arm (p.733, eh_45c78ce52e2fc8a3; Table 1, eh_904c6661ef641353). Per-protocol results are reported as a secondary analysis, and the primary conclusion rests on the ITT result (p=0.39).

Rescue treatment in the expectant arm followed protocol-specified rescue criteria. Eight of 104 expectant infants received rescue treatment at a median age of 7 days (p.733, eh_45c78ce52e2fc8a3). The paper reports no non-protocol co-interventions and no crossover, and nothing indicates that the trial context itself caused protocol departures.
The main report states the trial's limitations include the lack of blinding (p.737, eh_4cfc7f221ae0440e). The registry masking field is NONE, so participants knew their assigned strategy.

The expectant arm was managed with the intention not to treat the PDA, and the paper describes open-label treatment criteria (p.732, eh_161b55260b8270c6). The paper also names the lack of blinding as a limitation (eh_4cfc7f221ae0440e). Carers and treating staff therefore knew the assigned strategy.

The ITT analysis includes all 104 randomized infants per arm, and the BPD/death counts are reported on those denominators: 47 (45) of 104 in the early treatment arm and 41 (39) of 104 in the expectant arm (p.733 and Table 1, eh_45c78ce52e2fc8a3 and eh_904c6661ef641353). The denominators equal the randomized counts, so outcome data appear to be available for essentially all randomized infants. The paper does not state explicitly that no infants were lost to follow-up.

The trial was open-label. Registry masking is NONE (eh_974b1d8de69e9327), and the main report names the lack of blinding as a limitation (eh_4cfc7f221ae0440e). No blinded outcome assessor is described, so the people recording BPD and death were presumably aware of the assigned strategy.

The same BPD definition and the same routine monitoring standards applied to all infants in both arms (p.733, eh_45c78ce52e2fc8a3). The paper does not describe different measurement methods, thresholds or timing by arm for the composite.

Influence is more likely when the comparator is no treatment (the expectant arm was managed with the intention not to treat the PDA, eh_161b55260b8270c6) and when the people assessing the outcome also delivered the care (eh_4cfc7f221ae0440e; open-label). Both conditions apply to the BPD component. Outcome timing at 36 weeks PMA is long after the 72-hour intervention, which lowers the likelihood, but does not remove it for a judgement-based respiratory-support criterion.

BPD is defined partly by a treatment decision, the need for oxygen or respiratory support at 36 weeks PMA or discharge (eh_45c78ce52e2fc8a3). Such decisions are made by the treating team, who knew the assigned strategy. Death is an objective outcome, so the influence applies to the BPD component of the composite.

BPD was defined by the NICHD consensus (need for oxygen or respiratory support at 36 weeks PMA and/or discharge), and death is an objective outcome. Standard protocols were applied to all infants (p.733, eh_45c78ce52e2fc8a3). Nothing suggests the measurement method is insensitive or invalid for this composite.

The paper reports both the intention-to-treat analysis (primary, all randomized, 47 (45) vs 41 (39), p=0.39) and the per-protocol analysis (35 (36) vs 19 (...), p=0.21) in Table 1, and the methods state both were performed (eh_45c78ce52e2fc8a3). Reporting both analyses is evidence against selection among analyses. The reported Result uses the intention-to-treat population, which matches the registered and intended population. No alternative analysis of the composite is reported, and none is shown to be omitted.

The outcome domain is BPD or death. The registry registers one primary measure of it (BPD or mortality at 36 weeks PMA, lines 115-120). The registered secondary measures of its components, BPD and mortality at 36 weeks PMA (lines 156-163), are both reported in Table 1 (eh_904c6661ef641353), so no eligible registered measurement is withheld. The components are not alternative measures of the composite outcome requested here. No evidence in the Sources shows a second eligible measurement of the composite that was dropped.

The registry record was first submitted on 2019-02-16 (start 2019-02-15), before recruitment began in March 2019 as the paper states (eh_45c78ce52e2fc8a3). That dated entry registers the primary measure as incidence of BPD or mortality at 36 weeks PMA (registry lines 115-120), which matches the reported composite and time window. The paper analyses the outcome with the chi-square tests its methods describe, and reports the intention-to-treat and per-protocol analyses it says it performed (eh_904c6661ef641353). Under the guidance, a pre-enrolment registry entry naming this measurement and time point supports Probably yes even without analysis detail. The registry record is the current version (last update 2022-04-13), so the earlier registered wording is not directly verifiable.

Table 1 reports baseline characteristics for all randomised participants (4949 dulaglutide, 4952 placebo), with near-identical group sizes and characteristics (for example age 66.2 (6.5) in both groups; female 46.6% vs 46.1%; cardiovascular disease 31.5% vs 31.4%; HbA1c 7.3% vs 7.4%). The few differences in medication use (for example DPP-4 inhibitor 5.4% vs 6.0%) are small and compatible with chance. No imbalance suggests a problem with the randomisation process.

Allocation was made through an interactive web response system with stratification by site, and the study drug and placebo were identical in appearance preloaded syringes. Remote, centrally administered allocation by a web system that is independent of enrolling investigators meets the RoB 2 criteria for Yes (section 4.3.2, Table 2 minimal criteria). The report says that investigators and participants were masked to allocation.

The main report states that randomisation was done by a computer-generated random code (Summary and Methods, Randomisation and masking). A computer-generated random code is a random component under RoB 2 section 4.3.1.

The primary outcome is reported as a comparison of all randomly assigned participants analysed by intention-to-treat irrespective of adherence (4949 dulaglutide, 4952 placebo) (eh_af1af7f4fec6c3d4), with the trial sponsor's analysis using the randomised groups as assigned. This matches the ITT principle required by signalling question 2.6, so the analysis is appropriate for the effect of assignment.

The main report states that all investigators and participants were masked to treatment allocation and that the study drug and placebo were identical in appearance (eh_e69e8ab0a2909647), so participants were blinded to assignment. The trial is placebo-controlled and the Methods/abstract describe a double-blind design (eh_14dab36c8bf73af5). However, the trial reports a substantially higher rate of gastrointestinal adverse events on dulaglutide (47.4% vs 34.1%; eh_46862ecc8890c440), which could allow some participants to infer their allocation. No report states that participants actually recognised their allocation, so the answer is probably no rather than yes.

The main report states that investigators and participants were masked to treatment allocation and that the study drugs were identical in appearance, and randomisation used a computer-generated code within an interactive web response system (eh_e69e8ab0a2909647). Trial personnel were therefore not aware of assigned intervention during follow-up.

The main article reports that the primary composite outcome status was known in 9610 (97.1%) participants during a median follow-up of 5.4 years (eh_990dad4a5b11d84d). Of 9901 randomly assigned participants, this leaves about 291 (2.9%) with unknown status across both arms. Those unknown participants are small relative to the 1257 primary composite events (594 dulaglutide plus 663 placebo; eh_46862ecc8890c440). Following the guidance that when observed events greatly outnumber participants with missing outcome data the bias is necessarily small, outcome data are available for nearly all randomised participants.

The main article states that all investigators and participants were masked to allocation, so outcome assessors in the trial were not reported as aware of treatment group. The residual uncertainty is that GI adverse event differences could have partly revealed allocation to participants, and that adjudicator blinding is not confirmed in the inspected text.

The article reports that investigators and participants were masked, with identical-appearing weekly injections, and that the same primary outcome was ascertained across both arms over the same follow-up. No differential ascertainment method or threshold is reported between arms.

The approved Result is a pre-specified composite of non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke, and CV or unknown death, analysed as time to first event. The main article reports the composite as the primary outcome with a stated ITT analysis of all randomised participants (4949 vs 4952), and the component event definitions are standard CV endpoints. Nothing in the inspected text suggests the measurement method was inappropriate for the outcome.

The protocol and registry specify one primary intention-to-treat Cox analysis with hazard ratio and 95% CI, adjusted for the interim look. The reported HR, CI and p-value match that analysis, and the report discloses that its CV death category includes unknown-cause deaths. The inspected sources show no alternative composite or adjusted analysis that was run and left unreported.

The registry lists one registered primary outcome, the composite, and the protocol names the same composite as the primary efficacy measure. The individual components (cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke) and the microvascular composite are registered as secondary outcomes and are reported in Table 2. No eligible alternative primary outcome measurement was found that went unreported.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record was first submitted on 2011-07-13 and started on 2011-07-22, before randomisation began (screening from 2011-08-18). Its registered primary outcome is the time to first occurrence of cardiovascular death, non-fatal MI or non-fatal stroke from randomisation, with the median follow-up of 5.4 years. The protocol's statistical methods (pp. 6 and 90) specify the same primary intention-to-treat Cox hazard-ratio analysis. The report analyses the composite this way. Its Table 2 footnote counts deaths of unknown cause within cardiovascular death, a classification choice disclosed in the report and not a change to the outcome. No SAP date-stamp was found, so the answer is Probably yes rather than Yes.

The Results text (p. 4) states: "Subjects in the HF group were a mean of 5.7 years older. More patients were ongoing or previous smokers in the HF group. Baseline characteristics (Table 1) and baseline measurements (Table 2) were otherwise similar between groups." Table 1 gives age 38.7 ± 10.0 (PEEP, n = 18) versus 44.0 ± 8.8 (HF, n = 20), ASA 1/2 at 6/12 versus 3/17, and previous smokers 2 (11) versus 4 (20). Group sizes are 18 and 20, close to the intended 1:1 ratio, so the Box 4 size criterion is not met. No p-values are reported for the Table 1 baseline comparisons. The age difference is about 0.6 pooled SD, compatible with chance in groups this size, and the smoking and ASA differences are small in count. No key prognostic factor is shown to be imbalanced at p < 0.001, so the imbalance does not on its own indicate a randomization problem; Probably no reflects that the reported imbalances are compatible with chance but not entirely absent.

Section 2.3 (p. 2) reports allocation by "sealed opaque sequentially numbered envelopes". Opaque, sequentially numbered, sealed envelopes are the safeguards Box 4 lists for Yes, and the report describes allocation in advance of enrolment with no reported suspicion of foreknowledge. Full detail is absent: the report does not say the envelopes were opened only after irreversible assignment, or who prepared and held them. Section 4.3.2 warns that a fixed block size of two is a predictability problem when recruiters know the block boundaries and allocations are revealed after assignment; the report says nothing on either point, so the warning is not shown to apply. The trial was unmasked ("There was no masking"), which bears on blinding, not on concealment.

Section 2.3 (Randomisation and masking, p. 2) states: "Randomisation was performed with an allocation ratio of 1:1 and a block size of two using sealed opaque sequentially numbered envelopes." The report names a blocked design but does not say that the order of allocations within each block was random, and does not name a generation method (computer, random-number table or similar). Official guidance section 4.3.1.1 and Box 4 state that blocked allocation without an explicit statement that the within-block order was random should generally be answered No information. The supplement (subgroup tables only) contains no methods.

The CONSORT flow (Figure 1, p. 6) shows 40 randomised, 20 per arm. The analysed population is 18 in the PEEP group, with 2 PEEP participants who withdrew consent before analysis, and 20 in the HF group (Results, p. 4). The 2 failed arterial cannulations affect only the blood gas analysis, not the Table 1 counts. Excluding participants who withdrew or had missing data is a modified intention-to-treat analysis, which Box 6 and Section 5.3.1 treat as appropriate for this domain; the missing-data consequences belong in Domain 3. The report gives no per-protocol or as-treated grouping for this Result. The laryngoscopy-attempt counts are reported descriptively in Table 1 and no analysis of them is reported, so the answer is Probably yes rather than Yes.

Section 2.4-2.5 (p. 2) describe delivery in detail: the PEEP group had a sealed mask with a good seal checked by capnography, and the HF group was instructed to breathe with the mouth closed, with a jaw thrust applied after loss of consciousness. The Discussion (p. 6) suggests that inspiratory flows in the HF group "could have exceeded the flow of HFNC due to deep-breathing leading to entrainment of room air". That is a possible adherence or delivery issue, but the report does not tie it to the trial context (recruitment, consent or personnel undermining the protocol), so it is consistent with ordinary non-adherence. Section 3.4 reports that none of the interventions were aborted. No context-driven non-protocol intervention is described.

The design is described as "single-centre, open-labelled, randomised, controlled trial" (Section 2.1, p. 2) and "There was no masking" (Section 2.3, p. 2). The Limitations (p. 7) state that "subjects and anaesthetists were not blinded to the allocated intervention". The two interventions are physically different (a face mask with PEEP versus a high-flow nasal cannula), so participants could tell which they received.

Section 2.1 and 2.3 describe an open-labelled trial with no masking, and the Limitations (p. 7) state that anaesthetists were not blinded to the allocated intervention. The anaesthetists delivered and managed the interventions (Section 2.5: bag-mask ventilation "performed manually by the attending physician and was not protocolised"), so carers and people delivering the interventions knew the allocation.

Forty subjects were randomised, 20 per arm (CONSORT, eh_6e607b58dc7f11ea). Results (eh_15af7d94235f54d1) state that two PEEP subjects withdrew consent and arterial access failed in two others; 18 PEEP and 20 HF subjects were analysed. The Table 1 laryngoscopy counts sum to 18 (PEEP, 16/1/1) and 20 (HF, 17/1/2), so outcome data are present for 38 of 40 randomised participants (95%). Missingness is limited to two participants with documented consent withdrawal, and the 2 failed arterial cannulations affect only blood gas data. Laryngoscopy attempts are a count with a small number of missing participants, so their outcomes are unlikely to change the result materially.

The trial was open-label. The Limitations state that subjects and anaesthetists were not blinded to the allocated intervention (eh_e6a41ba6badafa98), and Methods report no masking (eh_4071c613f84ec1be). The attempts were made by anaesthetists (Table 1 lists the laryngoscopist's experience; eh_15af7d94235f54d1), so the assessor responsible for recording the count was aware of the group allocation.

Both groups were intubated under the same general anaesthesia process and the same laryngoscopy-attempt framework, and the Results report attempt counts for both groups in the same format (eh_15af7d94235f54d1). No passage describes extra clinical contacts or passive ascertainment that would give one group more opportunity to record a difficult intubation. The intra-induction procedures differed (HF group jaw thrust and mouth-closed breathing; PEEP group manual bag-mask ventilation until laryngoscopy, eh_4071c613f84ec1be), which may change the clinical difficulty of intubation but not how attempts were counted.

The passages report no strong beliefs or expectations among anaesthetists about the benefit or harm of either preoxygenation method, and the comparator is an active standard (face mask with PEEP), not no treatment (eh_4071c613f84ec1be). The difficult intubations occurred in both groups (one in PEEP, two in HF; eh_15af7d94235f54d1), which does not suggest a directional influence. The judgement is that influence was possible but not likely.

The count of attempts depends partly on provider decisions made during intubation, such as whether to repeat laryngoscopy, to switch to a video laryngoscope, or to bag-mask ventilate between attempts (eh_15af7d94235f54d1, PEEP participant with three attempts; eh_4071c613f84ec1be). Such decisions are of the intervention-provider-decision type, which Box 10 notes can be influenced by awareness of the intervention.

The Result is a per-participant count of laryngoscopy attempts (1, 2 or 3) recorded at intubation (Table 1 and Results, eh_15af7d94235f54d1). A count of attempts is a direct observation that is unlikely to be insensitive to plausible effects, and the passages do not report any instrument validity problem. The outcome was not a prespecified primary or secondary outcome, so the method was not designed for this question.

The attempt counts are reported as a descriptive frequency distribution in Table 1 with no test or adjusted analysis (eh_15af7d94235f54d1). Several analyses of this count are possible in principle (e.g. proportion with more than one attempt, adjusted models), but the captured text does not show whether any analysis was planned or run beyond the reported table, so selection among analyses cannot be assessed.

Intubation difficulty could be measured in more than one way (attempt count, time to intubation, glottic view grade, or success at first attempt). Only the attempt count is reported, and the methods do not describe how attempts were counted (eh_15af7d94235f54d1, eh_4071c613f84ec1be). Without analysis intentions, it cannot be determined whether other eligible measures were collected and not reported.

The Result (laryngoscopy attempts 1/2/3, Table 1) is a descriptive count. Section 2.7 and Section 3 list EtO2 at 2.5 and 5.0 min as primary outcomes, with secondary outcomes that do not include laryngoscopy attempts (eh_f1609df2cf8033f8, eh_15af7d94235f54d1). The article says the protocol was registered at ISRCTN (#ISRCTN37375068) (eh_4071c613f84ec1be), but the registry record and any protocol or SAP are not among the captured Sources. Whether the attempt count was a prespecified analysis cannot be determined from the captured text.

Baseline characteristics are reported for all 66 randomized participants (43 ravulizumab, 23 placebo), not only analysed participants (eh_98680d2f58172169; eh_e65410ca3b96e1c4). Differences exist: 24-hour urine protein 2.6 (1.3) vs 3.0 (1.8) g/d, baseline eGFR 76 (30) vs 70 (30), male sex 49% vs 65%, Asia Pacific 12% vs 26%. With 23 placebo participants and the SDs shown, these are compatible with chance, and no source reports a non-chance pattern. The primary analysis also adjusts for baseline log proteinuria and the stratification factor. Answer No.

Allocation was made centrally through an interactive response technology system, with the randomization code maintained by the IRT provider (eh_2f19532ab38a8968; eh_5a8be2a4668e2404). Remote central allocation independent of enrolment personnel is the desirable method under the official guidance (Box 4, signalling question 1.2).

The main report states the trial randomized participants 2:1 to ravulizumab or placebo using interactive response technology, stratified by mean proteinuria (eh_5a8be2a4668e2404). The protocol confirms 2:1 IRT randomization stratified by proteinuria (eh_2f19532ab38a8968). An electronic 2:1 stratified allocation implies a computer-generated random component, but no source states the generation method explicitly, so the answer is probably yes.

The primary analysis uses the full analysis set, defined as randomized participants who received at least 1 dose of study drug (protocol p.89; SAP v3.0 p.15; SAP v4.0 p.16). Official guidance (Box 6, 2.6; section 5.3.1) treats analyses that exclude eligible randomized participants after randomization as inappropriate, and says the dose-received meaning of modified ITT is not the missing-data mITT it accepts. The main report (p.7, Figure 2) analyses 41 ravulizumab and 22 placebo participants against 43 and 23 randomized, and no source states why three randomized participants were excluded. The analysis is therefore not clearly appropriate. Mitigating: the primary analysis imputes post-discontinuation data by multiple imputation, and the treatment-policy supplementary analysis uses the FAS with all observed data (supplement p.56).

"Participants, investigative site personnel, and employees or designees from the study sponsor ... were blinded to treatment assignments. Placebo had identical appearance to ravulizumab" (main report p.3). Protocol p.63 states participants are blinded during the Initial Evaluation Period, with a blinded ravulizumab dose at Week 26 in both arms to maintain the blind. Participants were therefore unaware of their assignment during the effect window to week 26.

Investigative site personnel were blinded, with identical kits and labels and a randomization code held by the IRT provider; the sponsor was unblinded only at week 26 to run the primary analysis (main report p.3; protocol p.63). Individual emergency unblinding is recorded and reported to the sponsor (protocol p.63), which does not indicate routine awareness.

Three of 66 randomized participants (4.5%) were not analysed in the primary FAS: two ravulizumab and one placebo (main report p.4 and Figure 1, p.5; Figure 2, p.7). The supplement's supplementary-analysis rule runs a randomized-set analysis only if the FAS excludes more than 10% (supplement p.56). The primary effect's 90% CI runs from -43.5% to -13.7%, and the placebo arm loses only one of 23 randomized participants. The report describes one ravulizumab participant who withdrew consent and one who was lost to follow-up in the extension period, but does not explain the analysed-count difference. The answer is probably no rather than no because the exclusion reasons are unreported.

Of 66 randomized participants (43 ravulizumab, 23 placebo), 65 completed the Initial Evaluation Period; one ravulizumab participant withdrew consent before completing it (main report p.4, eh_e65410ca3b96e1c4; Figure 1, p.5, eh_d69c4d74e15c75f2). The SAP (v4.0 p.23) states the primary analysis runs after all participants have completed the protocol-required Initial Evaluation Period assessments, so week-26 outcome data should exist for 65 of 66. The primary Figure 2 analysis set has 41 ravulizumab and 22 placebo participants (eh_68b04bb64d59ad84), 63 of 66 (95.5%), above the 95% benchmark for continuous outcomes. Post-discontinuation data are multiply imputed (eh_decaa380ccf00c61) and imputed values count as missing; the number of imputed week-26 values is not reported. The answer is probably yes rather than yes because the reason for three randomized participants being outside the analysis set is unexplained (see Domain 2) and the imputed count is unknown.

Participants, all investigative site personnel and sponsor staff directly involved in the study were blinded to assignment during the Initial Evaluation Period, with identical kits and labels (protocol p.63, eh_2f19532ab38a8968; main report p.3, eh_e667a3194ffb055b). The sources do not say who at the central laboratory analysed the samples, or whether that staff were told which arm each sample came from. The participant contributes the collection diary, and participants were blinded, so the participant route is covered. The central-laboratory assay itself is not described as blinded, so this answer is no information rather than no.

Both arms are assessed with the same 24-hour urine collections at Screening, Week 26 and Week 50 using the same central laboratory and validity criteria (protocol p.75, eh_8aa035f381e5d3c0). Ravulizumab and placebo arms both attend a Week 26 visit with a blinded dose (900 mg ravulizumab or a blinded loading dose of ravulizumab in the placebo arm), so the number of visits and opportunities for measurement does not differ between arms (protocol p.63, eh_2f19532ab38a8968). The outcome is a quantitative lab value, not an event that more visits could detect.

The outcome is a laboratory measurement of urine protein and creatinine, with completeness checked by a rule (creatinine excretion and collection duration, protocol p.75). The central laboratory's analysis involves no clinical judgement, so knowledge of assignment is unlikely to influence the measured value (official guidance p.54, Box 10, 4.4: observer-reported outcomes without judgement are usually not influenced). The participant's role in the collection is recorded as a diary of voids, which is a completeness record, not an assessment of the outcome value, and participants were blinded during the Initial Evaluation Period (protocol p.63).

The primary outcome is 24-hour urine protein from a central laboratory, derived from the mean of two 24-hour collections within 2 weeks of the Week 26 visit (protocol p.75, eh_8aa035f381e5d3c0; main report p.3, eh_a2d1f67fcc031dcb). Collections are checked for completeness by duration (22–26 h), missed voids and creatinine excretion, which makes the measurement sensitive to the proteinuria range in this population (proteinuria 1–3 g/d at baseline, Table 1). Nothing in the sources suggests the method has poor validity or detection limits that would matter for the expected effect.

The pre-specified primary analysis (SAP, eh_75b0dc37a0d34ba0) is the ANCOVA on log proteinuria with baseline and stratum adjustment and MI for post-discontinuation data, and the main report reports exactly that analysis (eh_decaa380ccf00c61). The reported result is therefore the pre-specified primary analysis, not one selected from alternatives. The SAP also pre-specifies sensitivity analyses (placebo-based MI, tipping-point, per-randomized-stratification; eh_6a6178e03cb49cdc), and the supplement describes a randomized-set analysis used only if the FAS excludes more than 10% (eh_2ade4610a064afeb). The FAS here excludes 3 of 66 randomized participants (4.5%), so the fallback analysis was not triggered. Planned sensitivity analyses that the main report does not show are a reporting gap, not evidence that the reported primary was chosen on its results.

For IgAN proteinuria the protocol specifies 24-hour urine protein from central-lab collections as the primary measure (protocol p.49, eh_de163458c35955e2: 'The gold standard for measuring proteinuria is a complete 24-hr urine collection'). The registry lists UPCR only under the LN cohort primary outcome (registry p.1 lines 129-131, eh_e5815a87bc3880c7), so UPCR is not an eligible IgAN primary measurement. The main report does report UPCR for the IgAN cohort (eh_e65410ca3b96e1c4: 240.4% vs 210.9%, treatment effect 233.2%, P 5 0.001) with the same time point. Because the IgAN primary measurement and its alternative are both reported, selection among measurements of this domain is not evident, and the reported primary measure is the pre-specified one.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record for NCT04564339 (first submitted 2020-09-21; study start 2021-01-19 ACTUAL, registry p.1 lines 21-32, eh_64ad32f954649c2a) lists the IgAN primary outcome as percentage change from baseline in proteinuria at week 26, measured by absolute protein from 24-hour urine collections, time frame Baseline and Week 26 (registry p.1 lines 124-126, eh_eedbf448c46c2e61). That entry predates enrolment, so it is a dated plan for this measurement and time point, which matches the reported primary endpoint. The protocol (amendment 4.0, eh_de163458c35955e2) and main report (eh_decaa380ccf00c61) both specify the same ANCOVA on log proteinuria adjusted for baseline and stratum, with MI for post-discontinuation data; the SAP (eh_75b0dc37a0d34ba0) pre-specifies the same primary analysis. The report follows the plan as its methods describe. Dates of the protocol amendment (26 Mar 2024) and SAP v4.0 (21 Apr 2025) come after enrolment and possibly after unblinded data, so they are not used as proof of prior finalization; the registry entry carries the date-stamp.

Table 1 shows closely matched baseline characteristics (for example age 66.0 vs 65.0 years, complex PCI 76.8% vs 75.2%, prior stroke 2.8% vs 2.4%, LDL 1.55 vs 1.56 mmol/L), and the authors describe the groups as well balanced. Differences in this range are compatible with chance and do not indicate a problem with the randomisation process.

Allocation was made by a web-based randomisation service that is external to enrolling staff, which meets the official 'Yes' description of a remote or centrally administered method. The report does not state that the enrolling site saw each assignment only after irreversible registration, and the blocks are small (four) and fixed, so the last assignment in a block could be predicted by someone who tracked earlier assignments. Because the report does not describe how this was handled, the answer is Probably yes rather than Yes.

The main report (p.3, Randomisation and masking) states that allocation used a web-based procedure with computer-generated block randomisation (block size four) in a 1:1 ratio. Computer-generated random allocation is a random component under the official guidance for question 1.1.

The protocol (supplement p.66, section 14.1) specifies intention-to-treat analysis of all randomised participants, regardless of whether the correct treatment was administered or crossover occurred. The Result is reported in the intention-to-treat population of 5506 randomised patients (main report Table 2 note), so the analysis groups participants by assignment and includes all randomised participants.

Supplement Table S1 reports protocol deviations by category: clinician-judged deviations occurred in 32 clopidogrel patients and 64 aspirin patients, and other devices in 87 and 85 patients, with patient-wanted switches (7 in each arm). The table gives counts only. It does not say why clinicians deviated, so it cannot be established whether the deviations arose from the trial context (the official guidance's question) rather than ordinary clinical judgement. The protocol's deviation and monitoring text (supplement p.72-78) does not describe the reasons for these switches either.

The main report (p.3, Randomisation and masking) states that participants and study investigators were not masked to group allocation (open-label design). Participants therefore knew their assigned intervention.

The same passage states that study investigators (the people delivering the interventions and managing patients) were not masked to allocation, and the limitations section (p.10) says the groups were not masked by the physician. Carers and treating physicians therefore knew the assigned intervention.

Trial profile (main p.4): 2752 randomised to clopidogrel, 30 did not complete 1 year (18 withdrew consent, 12 lost to follow-up), so 2722 (98.9%) completed at least 1 year. 2754 randomised to aspirin, 32 did not complete 1 year (11 withdrew, 21 lost), so 2722 (98.8%) completed. Missing outcome data in the 1-year window are about 1% per arm, which is nearly all randomised participants. Protocol 9.4 (eh_8e80aa1d4e6a3072) defines lost to follow-up as participants who do not complete scheduled follow-up and have not withdrawn. Withdrawals and losses are treated as missing outcome data for the time-to-event endpoint, consistent with guidance section 6.1.5.

The trial was open-label: participants and study investigators were not masked to allocation (main p.3, eh_35a1d468f41004e2). For the endpoint events, however, the assessor is an independent clinical event adjudication committee of interventional cardiologists who did not participate in the study; each case was reviewed independently by three members, and all reported events were reviewed in a blinded manner, with discrepancies resolved by majority vote (main p.3). The guidance treats a blinded adjudication committee as unaware of allocation for the events it classifies. The report says 'blinded manner' without specifying the masking, so this is probably_no rather than no.

Both arms received the same follow-up schedule (6 months, 12 months, then annually, with telephone interviews when in-person visits were unavailable) and the same active surveillance for ischaemic and bleeding events at each visit (main p.3). Ascertainment therefore used comparable methods and time points in both groups, and the events were adjudicated by one committee with the same process for both arms.

Main p.3 defines the composite endpoint from standard definitions: MI by the Fourth Universal Definition, stroke as sudden focal neurological signs, and death by cause, with stent thrombosis by Academic Research Consortium criteria. Vital status was cross-checked against the Korean National Health Insurance Service system. These are established, pre-specified measurement methods, and the question does not judge whether the composite is a sensible choice of outcome. Nothing in the pack suggests the method would be insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity.

For an assignment effect, the eligible analyses are the ITT analyses. The SAP plans ITT and per-protocol analyses for secondaries (eh_6168b2b5147a0a56), but per-protocol analysis is not an eligible analysis for the effect of assignment. The report presents an ITT Kaplan-Meier HR for this composite (eh_fe4b47b358f7169e); it reports a per-protocol HR only for MACCE and major bleeding, not for this composite. The SAP also refers to a Cox model adjusted for stratification factors (eh_aa7acbf64a163d81, eh_6a2f55e56cf360d5), but the captured report does not show an adjusted estimate for this composite and does not show that an unadjusted estimate was preferred over an adjusted one. The captured sources therefore show no clear evidence that several eligible ITT analyses were run and only one was reported on the basis of its results.

The registry lists the composite of cardiovascular death, MI or stroke (Secondary outcome 8, lines 152–156) as a registered measurement, and Table 2 of the report (eh_fe4b47b358f7169e) reports this composite with the same definition, along with the other registered secondary measures apart from medical cost. No eligible measurement of this composite appears to have been omitted, so the reported Result does not look like one chosen from several reported measures. The one departure is the time point: the registry and SAP specify 1 year, and the report presents only the 3-year estimate. The captured sources do not show that a 1-year estimate was analysed and then withheld, so there is no evidence that the time point was chosen on the basis of the results.

The approved Result is the 3-year Kaplan-Meier HR (0·73, 0·54–0·98) for the composite of cardiovascular death, MI or stroke, ITT. The ClinicalTrials.gov record (first submitted 2020-06-01, before the 2020-08-10 start) registers this composite as Secondary outcome 8 with a time frame of '1-year after last patient enrollment' (registry lines 152–156). The SAP (eh_6168b2b5147a0a56) also specifies secondary ITT and per-protocol analyses at 1 year after last enrolment, and states that P-values are not presented for secondaries. The report instead presents 3-year Kaplan-Meier estimates for this endpoint (eh_fe4b47b358f7169e) and does not say why the window differs from the plan. The ITT population (all 5506 randomised) does match the SAP (eh_3030b2158e2542f1). Because the analysed window departs from the pre-specified plan without a stated, result-independent reason, the answer is probably no rather than probably yes.

Table 1 shows 80 and 82 participants at the start of the trial phase, close to the 1:1 intended ratio (eh_681847ec0d5383f7). The only significant differences were ARB without ACE inhibitor (30% vs 15%, P=0.034) and maximum daily ARB dose (33% vs 17%, P=0.025). Official guidance treats a small number of P<0.05 differences as compatible with chance, so they do not indicate a randomization problem.

The protocol describes central allocation: the centre faxes eligibility data to the Trial Office randomisation service, which assigns treatment after eligibility is confirmed, using a telephone-based adaptive procedure that the protocol says minimizes concealment bias (eh_76dc52b2e6ce06a3, eh_d8a42980e5233d19). Official guidance gives Yes for remote, centrally administered allocation controlled by a unit independent of enrolment staff.

The 1:1 randomization codes were generated by covariate-adaptive randomization on eGFR and proteinuria (eh_5233a982d46ef47b, eh_2a7025038eaae2a8). Official guidance says minimization generally includes a random element and should generally be considered random, so the sequence is treated as random. The report does not explicitly describe the random element, so the answer is Probably yes rather than Yes.

The full-analysis set (ITT) was the primary analysis (eh_acd6ccb5bc52d5f1), and the requested Result comes from the available-case analysis of secondary endpoints (eh_b8db22ced9738a8c, eh_ca45f5ae2c9b3304). That analysis excludes only randomized participants with missing end-of-trial data (71 of 80 and 72 of 82) and keeps their assigned group. Official guidance treats a modified ITT that excludes participants with missing outcome data as appropriate for this question; the impact of that missingness is assessed in Domain 3, not here. The protocol's full-analysis-set definition (eh_9593d638a6767c72) also excludes only ineligible participants and those without post-randomization data.

The main report does not describe crossover, co-interventions or non-protocol treatment in either arm, and it does not report adherence data. The protocol says compliance could only be monitored indirectly ("compliance can not be monitored by ... monitoring drug levels in serum"; eh_f0dbe37b42c25fcb), and lists non-compliance and non-protocol concomitant therapy as reasons to discontinue (eh_eb939875b9bf3ab0). Whether any deviation arose from the trial context, rather than from ordinary non-adherence or protocol-consistent changes, cannot be determined from the reports read.

The report states: "One limitation of our trial is its open-label nature. Given the complex immunosuppressive treatment regimens, a blinded study did not seem possible" (eh_4793884e3621edac). Participants therefore knew their assigned regimen. Immunosuppression side effects were substantial (infections, weight gain, impaired glucose tolerance), which would also reveal the assignment.

The same open-label design (eh_4793884e3621edac) means carers and people delivering the regimens knew the assigned group. The protocol's concomitant-medication and immunosuppression sections describe group-specific treatment, consistent with the unblinded delivery (eh_c12b718b0a3599e8).

Table 2 analyses the 36-month eGFR change on available cases: 71 of 80 randomized in supportive care (88.8%) and 72 of 82 in supportive care plus immunosuppression (87.8%) had data, so about 11-12% of each arm is missing. The guidance treats about 95% availability as the threshold for a continuous outcome, so 'nearly all' is not met. Figure 1 accounts for 4 post-randomization losses per arm (death, withdrawal of consent, loss to follow-up), but 76 and 78 completed the study, leaving 5 and 6 completers without the endpoint unexplained.

The authors report sensitivity analyses using an available-case set, multiple imputation and a permutation test (p4). The only imputation results shown are for the primary remission end point, and the report says imputation confirmed differences in remission. No imputation or sensitivity result is shown for the 36-month eGFR change, so no analysis is reported that tests robustness to plausible values of the missing eGFR data for this result.

Reasons for post-randomization loss are identical in both arms (1 death, 1 consent withdrawal, 2 lost to follow-up each) and the proportions missing are similar (9 of 80 vs 10 of 82). Nothing in the report indicates that intervention-specific reasons, such as adverse effects, drove differential missingness. The analysis is available-case and does not account for the baseline characteristics that could explain the missingness.

Missingness could depend on the true eGFR value: 2 patients died (1 per arm), and the remaining missing eGFR values in the completers are unexplained. Progressive IgA nephropathy with eGFR decline makes death and loss to follow-up plausibly related to kidney function, so the chance that eGFR is missing may depend on its true value.

The trial was open-label, and the protocol states that unblinding is unnecessary because of the open-label design (protocol p44). The main article acknowledges its open-label nature (p11). No blinding of outcome assessors or laboratory staff is reported, so the guidance says to assume awareness when the sources say nothing to the contrary.

Creatinine and proteinuria were measured by routine clinical laboratories using the same method for both arms (protocol p40, p106). The primary and secondary end points are pre-specified, and both arms followed the same visit schedule. The immunosuppression arm had additional safety laboratory monitoring (protocol p40), but the end point is a scheduled 36-month value, so extra testing is unlikely to have changed its ascertainment.

The outcome is an automated creatinine-based calculation with no clinical judgement involved (protocol p40), so awareness of assignment would not realistically influence the recorded value. Per the guidance, observer-reported outcomes that do not involve judgement, such as automated tests, are usually not influenced by knowledge of the intervention.

The 36-month eGFR change is derived from creatinine measured by the enzymatic method in clinical routine laboratories under quality control (protocol p40), which is a standard, objective, laboratory-based method. The main article describes all end points as objectively measured laboratory values (p11). Nothing indicates the method is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity.

The protocol plans one analysis of this measurement: a repeated-measures model over time with treatment and the two stratification factors, allowing for single missing observations (protocol p115; TSAP p174). The paper reports one analysis for this result, the available-case 36-month values with a P value, and states that secondary endpoints were analysed on available cases with multivariate models (main p4). The sensitivity analyses named in the paper (multiple imputation, permutation test) are described for the primary endpoints, and no evidence shows secondary-endpoint versions were run and withheld. The reported available-case analysis is a stated analysis, not an evidently selected one.

The protocol designates the endpoint measure as CKD-EPI eGFR (protocol v4.1 summary of changes, item 5, which replaced creatinine clearance from 24-hour urine), and the reported absolute eGFR change at 36 months uses that measure. Creatinine clearance is reported only as a sensitivity analysis for the primary eGFR-decrease endpoint (main p6), not as a withheld version of this result. The protocol defines the endpoint at one time point (end of study), so no other intended time point of the same measure exists. Nothing shows the creatinine-clearance version of this endpoint was dropped because of its results.

The protocol v1.0 (dated 12.11.2007, before enrolment) and the registry record (first posted 2007-11-07, start 2008-02) prespecify absolute GFR change at the end of the 3-year period as a secondary endpoint, with a repeated-measures covariance model including the two stratification factors and allowing for single missing observations. The reported Table 2 result (available cases at 36 months, stratified multivariate analysis as stated in main text p4) matches that plan class. Later plan documents (TSAP dated 2012-07-11; protocol v4.1 dated 2012-04-13) changed the model wording from covariance to ANOVA and the GFR measure from creatinine clearance to CKD-EPI eGFR, but the endpoint definition is unchanged. No date-stamp shows the plan was finalised before unblinded outcome data existed, and the trial ran interim analyses, so the answer is probably yes rather than yes.

Table 1 shows group sizes near 1:1 (1500 vs 1509) and baseline characteristics that differ only trivially, and the authors state that they were well balanced. No baseline difference suggests a problem with the randomization process.

Allocation was assigned centrally through the electronic data capture system before hospital discharge, after consent, by a remote system that enrolling investigators did not control. This matches the guidance example of a central or web-based randomization service. The protocol's concealment statement concerns the statistician and analysts, not enrolling staff, so it does not change the answer but also does not establish the enrolment-side safeguard.

The main article and protocol both state that randomization was performed centrally through the electronic data capture system with a stochastic minimization algorithm to balance assignment within centers. Guidance treats minimization as usually including a random element, and the word 'stochastic' indicates one here.

The protocol states that ITT is the main analysis and the full analysis set is randomized participants with assessable data. The reported main analysis, however, excludes 36 participants who withdrew consent after randomization (23 in the 1-month group and 13 in the 12-month group). Guidance treats post-randomization exclusions of eligible participants as inappropriate, so the main analysis is not a clean ITT analysis. Per-protocol and as-treated analyses are secondary and do not serve as the assignment estimate.

The article reports that most patients followed the assigned regimen appropriately, which implies some non-adherence. Nothing in the read passages attributes non-adherence or regimen switching to the trial context (consent process or staff undermining protocol delivery). The protocol instead records adherence and discontinuation through routine web-database entry, which points to ordinary post-randomization non-adherence.

The main article states the STOPDAPT-2 trial was an open-label randomized trial comparing 1 month of DAPT followed by clopidogrel monotherapy with 12 months of DAPT. Participants knew their assigned regimen, so participants were not blinded.

The same open-label design means carers and people delivering the regimens knew the assigned antiplatelet strategy. Only the statistician, the independent clinical event committee, the steering committee and the sponsor were blinded to group assignment, so trial personnel were not blinded.

The 36 post-randomization exclusions are about 1.2% of 3045 randomized participants, and the protocol excludes withdrawn-consent data totally rather than censoring it on outcome. Primary events are 35 vs 55, and it is not established that the excluded participants were prognostic or had outcome events. The effect is nonetheless fairly close to the boundary (CI upper limit 0.98), so impact cannot be fully excluded.

The flow passage reports 1523 and 1522 randomized, with 23 and 13 withdrawing consent and excluded from the analysis (1500 and 1509 analysed). Loss to follow-up was 22 in the 1-month group and 13 in the 12-month group, so 35 of 3045 randomized participants (about 1.1%; 1.4% and 0.9% by arm) lacked outcome data. For this time-to-event outcome, participants censored at loss to follow-up count as missing. At the observed event rates (about 2.4% and 3.7%), the 35 missing participants could contribute only about one additional primary event at most under typical rates, so their outcomes could not plausibly change the estimate materially. Consent withdrawals are a Domain 2 exclusion and are not counted here.

The main article states the trial was adjudicator-blinded, with the independent clinical event committee blinded to group assignment. The protocol states the trial was open-label but blind for the event assessor. Events were therefore classified by assessors who did not know the assigned group.

The composite was pre-specified, the same definitions applied to both arms, and events were adjudicated centrally by a single committee. The protocol describes the trial as open-label, so visit intensity or testing could in principle differ by arm, but no passage reports a difference in ascertainment between groups.

The primary composite (CV death, MI, definite stent thrombosis, ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke, TIMI major or minor bleeding) is pre-specified in the protocol with TIMI bleeding criteria, and the Result reports it directly as a 12-month event count. The passages do not describe a validity or sensitivity problem with the measurement method, so the answer is probably no.

The protocol names the ITT full analysis set as the main analysis and plans per-protocol and as-treated analyses as secondary checks. The report presents the ITT hazard ratio as the primary result and reports the per-protocol and as-treated analyses as secondary. The site random-effects model is labelled post hoc and is not the reported primary result. No unreported adjusted or alternative primary analysis appears in the passages read.

The registered 12-month primary composite is the measurement reported as the primary result in Table 2, and the 12-month CV composite and bleeding outcomes that the registry also lists are reported with the same time window. The primary outcome was not switched to another 12-month measurement in the passages read.

The registry record was first submitted on 2015-11-29 with a registered start of 2015-12, before enrolment, and its primary outcome (12-month composite of CV death, MI, definite stent thrombosis, stroke and bleeding) matches the reported primary outcome. The protocol specifies the ITT full analysis set as the main analysis, the 12-month primary endpoint with a 50% non-inferiority margin, and no hazard-ratio adjustment. The report follows that plan.

Table 1 of the 30-day landmark ITT population (2920 aspirin, 2913 clopidogrel) shows near-equal group sizes and closely matched age, sex, clinical presentation, comorbidities, procedural characteristics and medications. The main article states that the baseline characteristics were well balanced except for PPI prescription at discharge (92.5% vs 83.1%). Discharge PPI use follows randomization and is not a baseline prognostic factor, so it does not indicate a randomization problem.

Allocation was administered centrally by the EDC system (protocol p. 11), which is a remote central method controlled by a unit independent of enrolment staff. Assignment is issued only after the enrolling clinician registers the patient, which matches the minimal criteria for central randomization in Table 2 of the guidance.

The protocol (p. 11, section 4) states that randomization was performed centrally through the EDC system with a stochastic minimization algorithm to balance treatment within institutions and presence of ACS. Minimization generally includes a random element, so the sequence counts as random. The main article (p. 3) states that patients were randomly assigned 1:1.

The reported co-primary result is a 30-day landmark analysis. It excludes 129 randomized patients who died by 30 days or were lost to follow-up, and it counts only events after 30 days. Excluding participants on the basis of post-randomization outcomes and loss is a post-randomization exclusion of eligible participants, which the RoB 2 rules treat as inappropriate. The authors acknowledge immortal-time bias from the landmark design. The trial-wide 1-year analysis reported in the main article (overall composite HR .95, 95% CI .79-1.14) is a broader population, but it is not the requested result.

The 30-to-59-day antiplatelet transition was protocol-mandated, so it is not a deviation. Non-adherence was 11-13% at 60 days in both arms (88.6% vs 87.8% continued assigned monotherapy). The report does not say whether these changes arose from trial context (recruitment or engagement effects, or clinician behaviour driven by knowledge of assignment), so this cannot be determined.
The trial was open-label: group assignments were open to the patients and the attending physicians. Participants were therefore aware of their assigned antiplatelet regimen.
Attending physicians, who delivered the antiplatelet care, were aware of assignment. Only event adjudicators, statisticians, the steering committee and the sponsor were blinded.

The exclusions total about 169 patients (129 dead or lost by 30 days, plus 40 before analysis), about 2.8% of randomized patients. Early deaths are strongly related to prognosis and are themselves cardiovascular composite events, so the exclusions could substantially change the estimate even at this small proportion.

The main article reports that follow-up was completed in 99.3% of participants in both arms of the 30-day landmark analysis. The 129 participants who died by 30 days or were lost at 30 days are excluded from the landmark population (about 2.2% of randomized patients). Their exclusion is addressed under Domain 2, not here. Because the composite outcome is recorded for nearly all participants, the 129 excluded participants are unlikely to change the estimate, but 'yes' is not fully supported because the report does not separate deaths from losses to follow-up within this excluded group.

The main article states that the clinical events related to the co-primary endpoints were centrally adjudicated by three or more event adjudicators blinded to the assigned group. The same passage records that group assignments were blinded to event adjudicators, statisticians and the steering committee, while patients and attending physicians were not blinded. For the composite components, the adjudicators are the outcome assessors and they were blinded, so Question 4.3 is answered No. Clinical decisions made by unblinded attending physicians before adjudication are a separate concern, which Domain 2 addresses.

Events were identified from site reports in the electronic data capturing system and then adjudicated by the same central process for both arms, and the protocol applies the same central monitoring to all patients. No passage describes arm-specific additional visits, imaging or testing that would create extra opportunities to detect the composite events. Because the trial is open label, site reports were not blinded, so differential identification remains a theoretical concern that the Sources do not address directly.

The cardiovascular composite (cardiovascular death, MI, definite stent thrombosis, ischaemic stroke) is a pre-specified co-primary endpoint. The main article states that events were centrally adjudicated by three or more blinded event adjudicators using Academic Research Consortium criteria for MI and stent thrombosis, and that stroke required persistent symptoms over 24 h. The protocol (p. 35, section 10.8.1) assigns definitive rating of all clinical endpoints to a Clinical Events Committee. Nothing reported suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity.

The main article designates the 30-day landmark ITT analysis as the main analysis for 1-year outcomes (p.3 lines 75-123), and the protocol plans the 1-year analysis as exploratory. The supplement also reports 30-day landmark per-protocol, 60-day ITT and per-protocol, and no-staged-PCI analyses (Supplemental Figures 2-5, Table 2). Several analyses were reported, but the reported one is the designated main ITT analysis. Nothing shows that it was chosen on the basis of its result. The paper's discussion notes immortal-time bias from the landmark design, which concerns validity rather than selection.

The reported composite is the co-primary cardiovascular endpoint defined at 1 year in the supplement (Appendix C, p.6), and the main article describes the 30-day landmark as the main analysis for 1-year outcomes (p.3 lines 75-123). The registry's 12-month components (death, cardiovascular death, MI, stroke, stent thrombosis) are separate outcomes, and no 12-month composite appears among them. These records show no sign that the reported composite was chosen from several 1-year cardiovascular measurements based on its results. The registry's 1-month primary composite is a different time frame, not an alternative measurement chosen after results.

The protocol (p.24 lines 24-34) states that exploratory analysis of primary and secondary endpoints at 1 year (365 days) after stenting was planned, with details to be defined in an SAP. The protocol (p.3 lines 20-26) also names a landmark analysis between 1 and 12 months as exploratory. The supplement (Appendix C, p.6) defines the co-primary cardiovascular composite assessed at 1 year from randomisation, which matches the reported endpoint. The reported analysis is therefore described in the protocol before results. Against that, the registry (first submitted 2020-10-23, before enrolment began 2021-01-29) lists both co-primary outcomes with a 1-month time frame, and the main article calls this a secondary analysis with no prespecified power calculation. The protocol does not show that the 30-day landmark population rule (exclusion of 129 patients who died or were lost by 30 days) was prespecified; that rule is only described in the SAP, which is not among the Sources.

Table 1 shows that male sex differed between groups (57% nonintervention vs 40% ibuprofen, P=.04; eh_5be48df20e1f214a). This single nominal difference is compatible with chance among many compared characteristics, and gestational age strata and other characteristics are balanced. The adjusted analysis in Table 3 gives an estimate similar to the unadjusted one (eh_873d429c3a3c120d), so the imbalance does not suggest a problem with the randomization process.

The unblinded part of the trial holds the randomization table and delivers it to the statistics team (protocol p13, eh_769fc8dd20fcb5dc). Study drug or placebo was prepared and administered by an unblinded medical professional not involved in patient treatment (main p3, eh_6be2871ed7206e88). Recruiters and treating clinicians therefore did not have access to upcoming allocations. Explicit statements on sequential numbering and sealed containers are absent, so this is a judgement.

The protocol describes stratified (GA <27 and >=27 weeks) 1:1 block randomization with the allocation table generated in SAS (protocol p9, eh_8e60d8e740a21fcc). The main report describes blocked randomization stratified by gestational age with a SAS-generated code table (p2, eh_0c27de2c41177605). The sequence was computer-generated and blocked; the report does not explicitly state that block sizes or order within blocks were random, so this is a judgement that the sequence was random.

The analysis was per-protocol: the report states that the authors performed a per-protocol analysis instead of an intention-to-treat analysis, and the Results use 142 of 146 randomized infants (72 nonintervention, 70 ibuprofen) after excluding 4 ibuprofen infants for incomplete ibuprofen courses (main p2, eh_0c27de2c41177605; main p4, eh_374c7c9bc3a9a4be). A per-protocol analysis that excludes participants who did not complete their assigned intervention is inappropriate for the effect of assignment. No intention-to-treat estimate was found in the main article or supplements read.

The trial is described as double-blind and placebo-controlled, with blinding of parents, staff and personnel (main p2, eh_0c27de2c41177605; main p3, eh_6be2871ed7206e88). The placebo was saline at equal volume and schedule (registry and protocol, eh_458a319a50e9ade8). Nothing in the report says participants recognised their group, and no intervention-specific side effects are reported as unblinding participants.

Study drug and placebo were prepared and administered by an unblinded medical professional who was not involved in patient treatment (main p3, eh_6be2871ed7206e88). Carers and clinicians were otherwise blinded, and the unblinded staff were excluded from endpoint reporting (protocol p9, eh_8e60d8e740a21fcc). Because the unblinded person did not deliver care, carers were probably not aware of the allocation.

Four of 74 randomized ibuprofen infants (about 5%) were excluded (CONSORT, main p4, eh_374c7c9bc3a9a4be). Even if all four had the outcome, the ibuprofen proportion would rise from 35/70 to 39/74 (about 53%), giving a risk difference near 8 percentage points, which remains well above the -0.2 noninferiority margin. The excluded infants therefore could not reverse the noninferiority conclusion, although the per-protocol analysis is not the intended analysis of assignment. Table 2 shows the reported group values (eh_eba0bb33546716d1).

Of 146 randomized infants, 142 (72 nonintervention, 70 ibuprofen) are reported in the analysis; the only exclusions are 4 ibuprofen infants for an incomplete ibuprofen course (CONSORT, main p4, eh_374c7c9bc3a9a4be). Those 4 are about 2.7% of randomized participants, and the outcome had 67 events (32 and 35, Table 2, eh_eba0bb33546716d1). Events greatly outnumber the possibly missing participants, so their outcomes could make no important difference to the estimate.

The main article states that parents, hospital and research staff, and medical personnel directly involved in patient care were all blinded to group allocation throughout the study (eh_6be2871ed7206e88, lines 2-4). The protocol says blinding is maintained until the end of the trial, that unblinded personnel are excluded from reporting endpoints and analysis, and that unblinding is limited to medical emergencies (eh_8e60d8e740a21fcc, protocol p9 lines 24-36). The ClinicalTrials.gov record lists outcomes assessor among the masked roles (NCT02128191). The main article does not name the outcome assessor separately, and the protocol's delegation log was not read, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

Both groups received the same follow-up schedule, with serial echocardiography at 1, 2 and 4 weeks, at 36 weeks GA and at discharge (eh_6be2871ed7206e88, lines 38-42). The placebo was given at the same volume and schedule as ibuprofen (lines 1-3). The main article does not report extra visits or tests in the ibuprofen arm, and the outcome is a pre-specified composite, so measurement is likely comparable.

The outcome is BPD at 36 weeks PMA, defined as need for supplemental oxygen and/or positive pressure to keep SpO2 above 90%, or death before discharge (main p3, eh_6be2871ed7206e88, lines 43-46). These are standard, objective clinical measures for this population, and the method is not shown to be insensitive or invalid. The question does not judge whether BPD is a sensible choice of outcome.

The protocol pre-specifies both a FAS and a per-protocol analysis set (protocol p12, eh_28a02351bc95f79b). The report analyses only the per-protocol set for the primary result, stating 'instead of intention-to-treat analysis' (eh_6be2871ed7206e88), and gives an adjusted OR for BPD or death (aOR 1.61, 95% CI 0.72 to 3.63; Table 3, eh_873d429c3a3c120d). The planned FAS result is not reported in any Source read. Whether the reported per-protocol estimate was chosen on the basis of its results cannot be determined from the Sources read.

The registered and protocol BPD measures both concern BPD at 36 weeks PMA, and the reported result is the registered composite primary outcome (eh_8c7b1fa93d4e4681, eh_28a02351bc95f79b). The report's separate BPD incidence (Table 3, eh_873d429c3a3c120d) corresponds to the registry's secondary BPD outcome at 36 weeks, so the reported BPD results are not selected from alternative measures. The protocol lists oxygen or ventilator dependency at 40 weeks as a secondary endpoint (protocol p12, eh_28a02351bc95f79b), and the main text does not show its result. That gap does not by itself show selection on the basis of results.

The ClinicalTrials.gov record, first submitted 23 April 2014 before enrolment began in July 2014, registers the primary outcome as 'Incidence of moderate to severe BPD or mortality at 36 weeks PMA' (eh_8c7b1fa93d4e4681). The report instead analyses 'BPD (O2 or positive pressure at 36 weeks PMA) or death' (main p3, eh_6be2871ed7206e88), so the measured outcome differs from the registered one. The protocol (ver 7.0, undated) defines both a FAS and a per-protocol population (protocol p12, eh_28a02351bc95f79b). The report's primary analysis is per-protocol, adopted 'instead of intention-to-treat' (eh_6be2871ed7206e88), with a CONSORT-based reason. No source dated before unblinded data shows per-protocol as the planned primary population, and the registry's 'moderate to severe' wording was not carried into the report, so the report departs from the registered plan.

Table 1 and the text report baseline characteristics as similar across the four groups, and the table footnote states that there were no significant differences between groups except for duration of type 2 diabetes (P=0.048). One nominal difference among many baseline comparisons is consistent with chance and does not by itself indicate a problem with the randomisation process.

Allocation was performed centrally by the IV/WRS after the participant was registered as screened at Visit 1 and at the Visit 2 randomisation step, and the IV/WRS assigned the dispensing unit number; code breaks are controlled through the IV/WRS and Novo Nordisk, with notification rules. A central, third-party allocation system after enrolment is the kind of concealment that prevents foreseeing assignment.

The protocol states that a randomisation session is carried out by the interactive voice/web response system (IV/WRS), that eligible subjects are randomised 1:1:1:1, and that randomisation is stratified within 12 strata; the main report states randomisation was stratified by CVD status, insulin treatment and eGFR. Random allocation by a central system is described, but the sequence-generation algorithm (for example, computer-generated random numbers and block size) is not stated in the inspected passages, so 'yes' is not supported.

The main report states that all results were analysed on an intention-to-treat basis including the full analysis set of all patients randomized according to the planned treatment. The appendix defines the full analysis set as all randomised patients, evaluated intention-to-treat as randomized. The primary Cox model analysed randomized groups. The as-treated analysis is limited to the safety set and not the primary outcome.

The main report states the trial was randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled, with volume-matched placebo that maintained blinding within dose. The matched placebo design makes it unlikely that participants knew their assigned intervention. The report does not describe any unblinding of participants during follow-up.

The protocol describes a double-blind, once-weekly dose of semaglutide or equivalent placebo, randomized by IV/WRS. Code-breaking is restricted to a defined procedure in which the site contacts Novo Nordisk before breaking the code, which indicates that carers and staff were not routinely aware of assignment.

The main article reports that of 3297 randomized patients, 3232 (98.0%) attended the last follow-up visit, were contacted by telephone, or died during the trial, and that vital status was known for 99.6% by the end of the trial (main article p4 lines 4-11). The primary composite outcome counts (108 of 1648 semaglutide; 146 of 1649 placebo) are reported against the full randomized denominators, consistent with outcome ascertainment for nearly all randomized participants. The SAP defines lost to follow-up for vital status as participants whose vital status is not obtained (protocol p271 lines 15-17), so the unknown-vital-status group is the relevant missing set. Missing outcome data are therefore about 2% overall, and with 254 primary events in total the number missing is small relative to observed events. Probably yes rather than yes because the inspected passages give no arm-specific count of participants with unavailable composite outcome data, and the 98.0% figure is not split by arm.

The primary composite events were adjudicated in a blinded fashion by an external, independent event-adjudication committee (main article p3 lines 30-33, eh_6a89f0b087734a01). The trial was described as double-blind with volume-matched placebo (main article p2, not re-inspected here). Blinded independent adjudication indicates that the assessors who classified the primary events were unaware of assignment. Probably no rather than no because the inspected passage does not explicitly state that the adjudicators were blinded to treatment assignment, as opposed to blinded in general.

Patients in both arms were scheduled for quarterly site visits and were encouraged to receive the same glycaemic management, with additional non-investigational antihyperglycaemic therapy permitted in both arms (main article p3 lines 4-14, eh_6a89f0b087734a01). The same adjudication process applied to events in both groups (p3 lines 30-33). No arm-specific difference in event detection or visit frequency is reported, so the measurement method appears comparable between groups.

The primary composite is a prespecified outcome defined as the first occurrence of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction (including silent) or nonfatal stroke (main article p3 lines 15-19, eh_6a89f0b087734a01). Its components are standard clinical events, and each outcome except peripheral revascularization was adjudicated by an external, independent committee (p3 lines 30-33). Nothing in the inspected text suggests the method is insensitive to plausible effects or has poor validity.

The reported Result is the pre-specified primary analysis: a stratified Cox model over the full analysis set on the in-trial observation period (SAP, sensitivity analysis 9 describes the same model per dose level). The SAP also specifies an on-treatment sensitivity analysis of the primary endpoint and the appendix specifies per-protocol analyses 10 and 11. Choosing the pre-specified primary FAS analysis, rather than a post hoc alternative, is not evidence of selection on the results, and the main article reports the primary and the protocol-listed secondary analyses.

The protocol defines the primary endpoint as the MACE composite and lists the eligible secondary measurements of cardiovascular events (expanded composite, its components, and all-cause death/MI/stroke). Table 2 reports the primary composite together with the expanded composite, all-cause death/MI/stroke, each component and the other listed events, so the eligible cardiovascular-event measurements are all reported and the Result is not selected from among them.

Protocol v5.0 (dated 19 May 2014, before the trial's 16 March 2016 primary completion and before unblinded outcome data were available to investigators) specifies the primary endpoint as time to first MACE (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) with the same definition and a noninferiority objective, and the report follows it. The SAP (dated 16 March 2016) specifies the primary analysis as a stratified Cox model in the FAS over the in-trial observation period, and its listed changes from the protocol are clarifications of endpoint selection and censoring rather than changes to this measurement or analysis. Per-protocol sensitivity analyses 10 and 11 were specified post hoc (appendix p33), but they are not the reported Result.
Table 1 of the main report shows baseline characteristics similar across the methylprednisolone and placebo groups, with no imbalance reported as important.

Allocation was generated and held centrally: the randomisation schedule was produced by the code administrator, the Master Randomisation List was kept in a password-protected, encrypted system, and access was restricted to authorised senior staff. Participants were randomised centrally, so enrolling staff could not see the next assignment.

The protocol (supplement, p218 lines 16-25) states that participants were randomised 1:1 using a minimisation algorithm run by a central web-based system. The main report (p3 lines 5-10) says the minimisation algorithm was centrally generated and used by all centres. Neither passage states a random element within the minimisation, so the sequence is probably but not certainly unpredictable.

The main report states that all analyses were conducted by analysing all patients according to the group to which they were randomised, regardless of adherence or protocol violations (p3 lines 76-78). The SAP v1.0 specifies the same ITT principle (supplement 1 p274 lines 13-17).

The report describes discontinuations for IDMC decisions, serious adverse events, participant choice and one investigator decision (p4 lines 73-81), and the halt for futility and safety (p2 lines 47-54). These changes are inconsistent with the protocol or are consistent with protocol-driven withdrawal, and nothing in the report indicates deviations arising from trial context (recruitment or engagement) that the protocol did not allow.

The main report states that participants recruited up to the 13 Nov 2015 halt were unblinded (p9 lines 43-47), and that all participants and investigators were informed of the halt (p2 lines 47-54). Participants recruited after that point were presumably aware of their arm. The protocol v1.0 design was open PROBE, with both patient and staff aware of assignment, which supports awareness at least in part of the trial. The report's general statement of masking and double-blind design weighs against awareness, but the 2015 unblinding is the specific, later-stage information.

The report states that investigators and site staff were masked to treatment assignment (p3 lines 5-10), and that the trial was double-blind placebo-controlled (p2 lines 37-38). Allocation was centrally generated and concealed through a web-based system accessible only to senior staff (protocol). The 2015 unblinding is described for participants (p9 lines 43-47) and does not state that personnel learned allocations.

The main report states that 503 participants were randomised (257 methylprednisolone, 246 placebo) and that the primary analysis included 257 and 246 (p4 lines 25-31 and Figure 1). It states that almost all participants were followed up to the end of the trial, with negligible missing data, and that all available data points were analysed (p4 lines 3-7). The flow chart records 20 participants lost (about 14 of 257 methylprednisolone, 5.4%; 6 of 246 placebo, 2.4%), which is a small proportion for a continuous eGFR-slope outcome. The slope uses all available eGFR values, so participants lost after some measurements still contribute. Footnote d notes that lost participants may have received, completed or discontinued the intervention. Reading the flow-chart line order, the 7/5/2 and 3/2/1 breakdowns appear to belong to the methylprednisolone and placebo arms respectively, but this is a layout inference.

The protocol (version 5, 13 May 2015) states that both the patient and study personnel at each site are blinded to treatment assignment, as are members of the Endpoint Adjudication Committee (protocol v5 p130 lines 33-36). The published report states that patients, investigators, site staff and sponsors were masked to treatment assignment (main p3 lines 5-10). eGFR is a laboratory-derived value from serum creatinine rather than a judgement-based clinical assessment, so awareness of assignment is unlikely to matter. Blinding of the laboratory staff who measured creatinine is not stated explicitly, which is why this is probably no rather than no.

The protocol states that the follow-up schedule of data collection should be maintained after any unblinding, so that all patient data are analysed (protocol v5 p130 lines 21-22). The analysis population is all randomised participants by group, and the eGFR slope is calculated from the same scheduled measurements in both arms, so measurement method, thresholds and timing are presented as comparable. A remaining possibility is that more creatinine measurements were taken in the methylprednisolone arm because of excess hospitalisations (serious adverse events 28 vs 7, main p8 lines 1-9); the sources do not say whether this happened, so the answer is probably no rather than no.

The outcome is the annual eGFR slope from all eGFR values during follow-up. eGFR is calculated from measured serum creatinine (CKD-EPI, main report p2 lines 69-72), a standard laboratory method. The method can detect the effect size reported (2.46 mL/min/1.73 m2 per year, main p7 lines 29-33), so it is not an insensitive instrument. The question does not judge whether an eGFR slope is an appropriate outcome; that is outside this domain.

The reported estimate (2.46; group means -2.50 and -4.97) matches the unadjusted difference in mean slopes that the SAP and main text specify (t-test on the mean rate of decline, SAP p277 and main p3 lines 95-97). The pre-specified sensitivity excluding high-dose months (2.65, main p8 lines 1-9) is also reported, which goes against selection. Footnote g describes a linear model adjusted for stratification factors with a random site effect.
